skills.name: connectors
skills.desc: Walks a developer through connectors end to end - the terms, turning them on in the router, connecting an account, giving an agent a connector's tools (one app account or each user's own), a channel such as the Slack bot, and what to check when something stays silent. Read before you connect a connector to an agent, set one up locally or on staging, or debug one.
skills.body:
---
name: connectors
description: Walks a developer through connectors end to end - the terms, turning them on in the router, connecting an account, giving an agent a connector's tools (one app account or each user's own), a channel such as the Slack bot, and what to check when something stays silent. Read before you connect a connector to an agent, set one up locally or on staging, or debug one.
---

# Connectors

A connector lets an agent call tools at a provider (GitHub, Linear, Slack) with an account
that someone connected. The router keeps the credential sealed and adds it to each call.
The agent's own code never sees a token.

Connectors replaced plugins. The router refuses a config naming `plugins`, `plugin_events` or
`mcp_servers` and opens none a stored config still names.

To add a new connector to the catalog, read the `add-connector` skill.

## Terms

One word, one meaning. The full table is in `acceleration/internal/connectors/core/AGENTS.md`.

| Term | What it is | Example |
|---|---|---|
| connector | One provider the router can reach. Built-in, or the app's own (`custom_…`) | `linear`, `slack_bot`, `custom_demo_deepwiki` |
| connection | One account at one connector, owned by the app or by one end user | the app's GitHub token; Ann's Linear login |
| binding | What one agent config may use from one connector: which connection and which tools | `connectors[]` on the agent config |
| `fixed` | The binding always uses one app connection | the support bot reads one GitHub org |
| `session` | The binding uses the connection of the session's verified end user | each user files Linear issues as themselves |
| provider app | The app the customer has at the provider, for a connector that receives messages | a Slack app with its signing secret |

```
connector (linear)
  └── connection (Ann's Linear login, owner: user ann)
        ▲
binding on agent config "support": name linear, connection.type session, tools [list_issues]
```

## 1. Turn connectors on in the router

| Setting | Why |
|---|---|
| `ROUTER_CONNECTORS_ENABLED=true` | Off by default |
| `ROUTER_DEV_KEK` on a laptop or in CI; `ROUTER_AUTH_KMS_KEY` + `ROUTER_AUTH_KEK_V<n>_WRAPPED` (+ `ROUTER_AUTH_KEK_VERSION`) on a hosted router | Seals the credentials. The router refuses to start without it when connectors are on, and refuses `ROUTER_DEV_KEK` beside a KMS setting. Changing it makes stored credentials unreadable. README, «The key encryption key in Cloud KMS» |
| `ROUTER_PUBLIC_URL` | The provider sends the browser back to `<ROUTER_PUBLIC_URL>/v1/agents/connectors/oauth/callback`. The dashboard shows this redirect URI on each OAuth connector |
| `DASHBOARD_BASE_URL` | The consent popup reports back only to this origin, unless the consent was started with a `return_url` (`createAuthorization`'s, or for a login or step-up the chat asks for, the session's own from `createSession`), which then replaces it. Unset, a consent without one reports to the wrong place and the dashboard waits forever |
| `ROUTER_CORS_ORIGINS` | The dashboard origin, when the browser calls the router directly |
| `<ENV>_MCP_CLIENT_ID`, `<ENV>_MCP_CLIENT_SECRET` | Stream's own OAuth client for a connector whose manifest lists `operator` (for example `SLACK_MCP_CLIENT_ID` for `slack`, `SLACK_BOT_MCP_CLIENT_ID` for `slack_bot`). Without it, the app must set its own client |

Full list: `acceleration/README.md`, «Configuration». Local setup: the `dashboard` skill.
Restart the router after a change.

## 2. Connect an account

In the Volt dashboard: **Library › Connectors**. It has two tabs.

1. **Connectors**: the catalog. Open a connector to see its auth, scopes and redirect URI.
   For an OAuth connector that needs the app's own client, set **OAuth client** (client id
   and secret, write-only). **New connector** adds a custom MCP server.
2. **Connections**: **New connection**. Pick the connector, the owner (the app, or an end
   user id) and the auth: OAuth opens a consent popup; a bearer token or API key is typed
   in. **Validate** checks the credential at the provider.

The same with the API (operations in `acceleration/api/openapi.yaml`):

| Step | Operation |
|---|---|
| The catalog | `GET /v1/agents/connectors` |
| The app's own OAuth client | `PUT /v1/agents/connectors/{id}/oauth-client` |
| A custom MCP or HTTP API connector | `POST /v1/agents/connectors` (`id` starts with `custom_`; `endpoint` or `http`) |
| A connection | `POST /v1/agents/connections` (`connector_id`, `owner`, `auth_scheme`) |
| OAuth consent | `POST /v1/agents/connections/{id}/authorizations` → open `launch_url` in a popup |
| A token or key | `PUT /v1/agents/connections/{id}/credentials` |
| Check it | `POST /v1/agents/connections/{id}/validate`, then `GET /v1/agents/connections/{id}/tools` |

### Direct calls from your backend

Your backend can call the provider's own API with a connection's credential:
`/v1/agents/connections/{id}/proxy/<path>` sends `<path>` under the connector's `api_base`.
Only a connector whose manifest has an `api_base` takes direct calls.

| Built-in | `api_base` | Example path |
|---|---|---|
| `github` (revision 4) | `https://api.github.com` | `repos/octo/hello/issues` |
| `slack_bot` (revision 5) | `https://slack.com/api` | `chat.postMessage` |
| `linear_app` (revision 1) | `https://api.linear.app` | `graphql` (POST a GraphQL body) |

A provider's `Link` header (RFC 8288) that names a URL under `api_base`, such as GitHub's
`rel="next"` page, comes back naming the same path and query under this connection's proxy
URL (`ROUTER_PUBLIC_URL` + `/v1/agents/connections/{id}/proxy`), so a client that follows it,
Octokit's paginate included, stays on the proxy. URLs in a body (`url`, `comments_url`) still
name `https://api.github.com`: never send the router's credential there; call their path
through the proxy. With `ROUTER_PUBLIC_URL` unset the router has no proxy URL to name, so it drops every
`Link` (fail closed): a connection then loses GitHub's pagination until the URL is set.

Every other built-in, `linear` included, is MCP-only: a direct call answers 400 «connector
"linear" has no api_base endpoint». Why Linear has none is in `linear.yaml`.

For Linear's GraphQL API, connect `linear_app` («Linear (own OAuth app)») instead. It signs in
with your own Linear OAuth app, and its token serves both the GraphQL API and Linear's MCP
tools:

1. Read the callback URL: `GET /v1/agents/connectors/linear_app`, field `redirect_uri`.
2. In Linear, create an OAuth app at https://linear.app/settings/api/applications/new with
   that callback URL.
3. Give the router its client id and secret: `PUT /v1/agents/connectors/linear_app/oauth-client`.
4. Create a `linear_app` connection and run its OAuth consent as for any connector.

Gong needs its tech admin first. In Gong: **Admin center › Settings › MCP** (under Ecosystem) **› MCP
servers › New MCP server integration**
([Gong's guide](https://help.gong.io/docs/create-an-integration-to-connect-to-the-mcp-server)).
Set the redirect URI to the connector's `redirect_uri`, and the registration type to
**Automatic** for `dcr` (Manual issues your own client id and secret; the type cannot be changed later). Until then Gong refuses every consent with
`unauthorized_client`, «This MCP client is not authorized for your company». The connection
stays pending, and its last validation says why.

A `linear` connection stays as it is; it does not move to `linear_app`. A connection keeps
the revision it was made on, so a `github` connection made before revision 4 takes direct calls
only after its next consent or token save.

## 3. Give an agent the tools

Dashboard: open the agent › **Tools** › **Connectors** › **Add connector**.

1. Pick the connector.
2. Under **Whose account**, choose **One app connection** (`fixed`) or **Each user’s own** (`session`). The list then shows «App connection <name>» or «Each user’s own account».
3. **Connect** lists the connection's tools. Tick the ones the agent may call. There is no
   wildcard: a tool that is not ticked is never offered.
4. Save.

The agent sees each tool as `<binding name>__<tool>`, for example `github__get_me`.

`github` (revision 5) offers GitHub's Actions tools beside its default ones: `actions_list`,
`actions_get`, `actions_run_trigger` and `get_job_logs`. The manifest asks for them with the
`X-MCP-Toolsets: default,actions` header. A binding's `tools` still narrows them: a tool that is
not granted is never offered. A connection made before revision 5 lists them after its next
consent or token save.

With the API, the binding goes in `connectors[]` of the agent config
(`AgentConnectorBinding`):

```json
{
  "name": "linear",
  "connector_id": "linear",
  "connection": {"type": "session"},
  "tools": [{"name": "list_issues"}]
}
```

A `fixed` binding names `connection.connection_id` and pins each tool's `schema_digest`.
A `session` binding may grant a tool by name alone.

Test it in **Playground**. For a `session` binding the end user may have no connection yet.
The call then waits for them to sign in on its own `ai_tool_call` step, which is
`awaiting_authorization` and carries an `authorization` with the `provider`, `title`, `url`,
`handoff_token` and `expires_at`. The reply also carries a `connector_authorization` card, which
the dashboard renders. **Connect** opens the consent popup, and once they consent the same call
runs in the same reply. A `tool_approval` with only the `tool_call_id` and `allowed: false`
declines it, and a consent that is refused, fails or is not finished in ten minutes ends it.
Either way the model is told, and nothing runs. A native app opens
`url#handoff_token=<handoff_token>` in its web authentication sheet, with its own scheme as the
session's `return_url`. On iOS that is StreamChatAI's `AIToolAuthorizationView`, which
`examples/voice_agents/swift_assistant` uses for Gmail and Linear. A spoken turn on a call has
no reply to show it on, so by voice the binding answers that it is not available.

`require_approval: ["create_issue", "delete_*"]` on a binding holds each call of a tool it names
until the session's user allows it. The call's step is `awaiting_approval`, addressed to them, and
nothing reaches the provider before they answer with `tool_approval` (`tool_call_id`, the reply's
`request_id`, `allowed`), on their socket or their backend's. They answer as the kind of caller
that opened the session, as they reach it (`session.Owner.Reaches`): a guest token with a signed-in
user's id is not them. Declined, or not answered in ten
minutes, the call is not sent and the model is told. A session with nobody to ask (incognito, a
run, a shared chat, an MCP event's) refuses the call at once. In a channel of a type
`chat_channels` names, the call asks the writer of the message the reply answers, who answers
with their own user token through `POST /v1/agents/conversations/{cid}/tool_approvals` while a
member of the channel. The hook names the writer by id alone, so any verified token of that id
answers for them, unless they are the session's own user (a session opened through the API
answering in the channel), who is asked as the kind of caller that opened it; the backend may
answer any (`api/conversations.go`, AI-3154). There the
writer has two minutes, not ten, when the Router opened the session for the message, as it does
unless a session opened through the API answers in the channel: it answers one message for at
most two minutes (`askTimeout`, `api/messagehooks.go`) and then closes that session, which stops
the call, and an answer after that is a 404 (`answerHosted`, `api/threadhooks.go`). The model gets
no round to say why, so the reply ends with a line that the approval expired, that the step
waiting did not run (an earlier call of the reply may have), and that the person can ask again, and the step says "Not allowed in time" (`ExpireApprovals`, `conversation/parts.go`, AI-3302). An entry must match a tool the
binding grants, and `sandbox: true` is refused beside it (`session/connector_approval.go`).
Beside a sensitive connector (Nessy), a binding's write tool needs `require_approval`: the
config is refused unless each tool it grants only reads (`read_only_tools`, or an http tool's
`read_only` at the digest the grant pins: one granted by name or at another revision's digest
does not) or is held, and a `tool_patterns` binding needs an entry such as `*` that matches each pattern as written
(`connectors/sensitive`, `ConfigComplaint`; across a parent and its child agents, `GraphComplaint`). In agent.yaml it is `require_approval:` on
the connector entry. Tools a caller declares at createSession are not checked. The caller runs
them, or a person's device does (`executor: client`). The router sends a client tool's
arguments to the caller on the events socket (`api/sessionws.go`). Every channel member can
also read them in the conversation's tool part, but only when they are 512 bytes or fewer
(`conversation/parts.go`, `maxClientArguments`) (AI-1642). If one of them
sends data on to anyone else, declare it with `approval`. On a voice call the router then asks
the user and sends the call only on yes. In text the router does not ask: the caller's client
must wait for `tool_approval` before it runs the tool.

For a session your backend creates, pass the end user's connection in
`connector_bindings: [{"name": "linear", "connection_id": "…"}]`. Leave it out and the
router uses the user's only connected connection to that connector, if there is exactly one.

`agent.yaml`: the sync API accepts `connectors`, and the Go SDK folder reader reads the block
(`sdks/go/agents/config.go`, `connectorBindings`). An entry whose `connection:` the app does not have
is left out with a warning, and the rest of the agent syncs; `required: true` makes it an error. `sandbox: true` lets code in the session's sandbox call the connector's API with the binding's connection.
The left-out entries go to the router as `left_out_connectors` and are served on the agent config.
Other SDKs: unverified, check `git grep connectors sdks/js/src plugins/stream` before relying on it.

### Sandbox access

A binding with `sandbox: true`, on a config with `sandbox: daytona`, lets `run_code` call the
connector's API. Code reads a placeholder (`dtn_secret_…`) from the env var the manifest's
`sandbox.env` names, such as `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and sends it as `Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN`
over HTTPS to a host in `sandbox.hosts`. Daytona's egress swaps it for the token there
(https://www.daytona.io/docs/en/secrets.md); code never reads the token.

  with such a binding is refused. Each session's secret is `va_<prefix>_<session>_<binding>_<8 hex>`.

  share a prefix delete each other's secrets.
- With the Daytona broker, the grant's hosts join the sandbox's domain allow list; a config with
  `network: true` or a `network_allow_list` keeps its own.
- A connection saved before its connector had a `sandbox` block (GitHub revision 5) gives the
  sandbox nothing, with a WARN «reconnect to use sandbox access»; a `required` binding refuses
  the session. Where a later revision has the block, every `run_code` result says to ask the
  user to reconnect, which takes effect from the next session (`Result.Reconnect`).
- Google Drive has a block from revision 5 (`GOOGLE_DRIVE_TOKEN`, host `www.googleapis.com`; AI-1958),
  so its connections of revisions 2-4 give the sandbox nothing until reconnected. Its token
  carries `drive.file`, so code can also create files and change files the app opened. A
  `session` Drive binding of a user with no connection gets a late grant (below).
- Linear has a block on `linear_app` from revision 2 (`LINEAR_ACCESS_TOKEN`, hosts `api.linear.app`
  and `uploads.linear.app`; AI-2082): code sends `Authorization: Bearer $LINEAR_ACCESS_TOKEN`,
  and under the proxy broker a POST to `/graphql` passes only with queries; a mutation gets 403.
  Its connections of revision 1 give the sandbox nothing until reconnected. `linear` (DCR) has
  no block: its token, issued for `mcp.linear.app`, gets 401 from `api.linear.app/graphql`
  (probe 2026-10-27).

  code reads with GETs and with jobs.query (`client.query_and_wait`), and under the proxy broker a

  whatever the code did: if the code needed the binding (a 401 from the grant's hosts), call

  binds the grant: at once behind the proxy, within 18 to 24 s as a Daytona secret, whose run that
  binds it says to wait 20 s on a 401 (`Result.Connected`; a run the login finished during says it
  too). A login on a connection whose revision has no `sandbox` block, or another env var or
  hosts, binds nothing: every run after it says to ask the user to reconnect, which takes effect from the next session (`Result.Reconnect`).

  session gets no grant.

  reconnect, or was deleted, withdraws it, and so does a binding the agent config dropped, no
  longer marks `sandbox`, or binds to another connector or connection (AI-1686, as the tool

  the placeholder stops at once; it costs one agent config read per request. The Daytona broker
  withdraws a grant by putting `va_withdrawn` in its secret, which it deletes at Close: deleted,
  the placeholder left in the env var got 502 «could not reach upstream host», which code cannot
  tell from the host failing; now the request reaches the host without a token, and GitHub
  answers 401 (live probe, 2026-10-29, AI-1876). Daytona refuses a request that carries a placeholder it
  does not substitute (another host, the query, another session's): 502 «could not reach upstream
  host».

  granted host when the value is not Base64-encoded (live Basic-auth check, staging 2026-10-21).
  It also substitutes inside a Base64-encoded Basic header, which is how git sends it (live
  staging E2E, 2026-10-22, session `01a16514-923c-7843-9214-40a94453f194`: `git ls-remote` of a public repo with

  only reads (above).

  host that echoes the token escaped or encoded would hand it to the sandbox. Wave 14's proxy
  broker closes it.
- Known limit (any header, AI-1976, accepted): Daytona substitutes the placeholder in any request
  header to a granted host, not only `Authorization` (https://www.daytona.io/docs/en/secrets.md,

  reconnect), Daytona keeps substituting it for a while. The withdrawal is an update, which takes

skills.bodyMd:
# Connectors

A connector lets an agent call tools at a provider (GitHub, Linear, Slack) with an account
that someone connected. The router keeps the credential sealed and adds it to each call.
The agent's own code never sees a token.

Connectors replaced plugins. The router refuses a config naming `plugins`, `plugin_events` or
`mcp_servers` and opens none a stored config still names.

To add a new connector to the catalog, read the `add-connector` skill.

## Terms

One word, one meaning. The full table is in `acceleration/internal/connectors/core/AGENTS.md`.

| Term | What it is | Example |
|---|---|---|
| connector | One provider the router can reach. Built-in, or the app's own (`custom_…`) | `linear`, `slack_bot`, `custom_demo_deepwiki` |
| connection | One account at one connector, owned by the app or by one end user | the app's GitHub token; Ann's Linear login |
| binding | What one agent config may use from one connector: which connection and which tools | `connectors[]` on the agent config |
| `fixed` | The binding always uses one app connection | the support bot reads one GitHub org |
| `session` | The binding uses the connection of the session's verified end user | each user files Linear issues as themselves |
| provider app | The app the customer has at the provider, for a connector that receives messages | a Slack app with its signing secret |

```
connector (linear)
  └── connection (Ann's Linear login, owner: user ann)
        ▲
binding on agent config "support": name linear, connection.type session, tools [list_issues]
```

## 1. Turn connectors on in the router

| Setting | Why |
|---|---|
| `ROUTER_CONNECTORS_ENABLED=true` | Off by default |
| `ROUTER_DEV_KEK` on a laptop or in CI; `ROUTER_AUTH_KMS_KEY` + `ROUTER_AUTH_KEK_V<n>_WRAPPED` (+ `ROUTER_AUTH_KEK_VERSION`) on a hosted router | Seals the credentials. The router refuses to start without it when connectors are on, and refuses `ROUTER_DEV_KEK` beside a KMS setting. Changing it makes stored credentials unreadable. README, «The key encryption key in Cloud KMS» |
| `ROUTER_PUBLIC_URL` | The provider sends the browser back to `<ROUTER_PUBLIC_URL>/v1/agents/connectors/oauth/callback`. The dashboard shows this redirect URI on each OAuth connector |
| `DASHBOARD_BASE_URL` | The consent popup reports back only to this origin, unless the consent was started with a `return_url` (`createAuthorization`'s, or for a login or step-up the chat asks for, the session's own from `createSession`), which then replaces it. Unset, a consent without one reports to the wrong place and the dashboard waits forever |
| `ROUTER_CORS_ORIGINS` | The dashboard origin, when the browser calls the router directly |
| `<ENV>_MCP_CLIENT_ID`, `<ENV>_MCP_CLIENT_SECRET` | Stream's own OAuth client for a connector whose manifest lists `operator` (for example `SLACK_MCP_CLIENT_ID` for `slack`, `SLACK_BOT_MCP_CLIENT_ID` for `slack_bot`). Without it, the app must set its own client |

Full list: `acceleration/README.md`, «Configuration». Local setup: the `dashboard` skill.
Restart the router after a change.

## 2. Connect an account

In the Volt dashboard: **Library › Connectors**. It has two tabs.

1. **Connectors**: the catalog. Open a connector to see its auth, scopes and redirect URI.
   For an OAuth connector that needs the app's own client, set **OAuth client** (client id
   and secret, write-only). **New connector** adds a custom MCP server.
2. **Connections**: **New connection**. Pick the connector, the owner (the app, or an end
   user id) and the auth: OAuth opens a consent popup; a bearer token or API key is typed
   in. **Validate** checks the credential at the provider.

The same with the API (operations in `acceleration/api/openapi.yaml`):

| Step | Operation |
|---|---|
| The catalog | `GET /v1/agents/connectors` |
| The app's own OAuth client | `PUT /v1/agents/connectors/{id}/oauth-client` |
| A custom MCP or HTTP API connector | `POST /v1/agents/connectors` (`id` starts with `custom_`; `endpoint` or `http`) |
| A connection | `POST /v1/agents/connections` (`connector_id`, `owner`, `auth_scheme`) |
| OAuth consent | `POST /v1/agents/connections/{id}/authorizations` → open `launch_url` in a popup |
| A token or key | `PUT /v1/agents/connections/{id}/credentials` |
| Check it | `POST /v1/agents/connections/{id}/validate`, then `GET /v1/agents/connections/{id}/tools` |

### Direct calls from your backend

Your backend can call the provider's own API with a connection's credential:
`/v1/agents/connections/{id}/proxy/<path>` sends `<path>` under the connector's `api_base`.
Only a connector whose manifest has an `api_base` takes direct calls.

| Built-in | `api_base` | Example path |
|---|---|---|
| `github` (revision 4) | `https://api.github.com` | `repos/octo/hello/issues` |
| `slack_bot` (revision 5) | `https://slack.com/api` | `chat.postMessage` |
| `linear_app` (revision 1) | `https://api.linear.app` | `graphql` (POST a GraphQL body) |

A provider's `Link` header (RFC 8288) that names a URL under `api_base`, such as GitHub's
`rel="next"` page, comes back naming the same path and query under this connection's proxy
URL (`ROUTER_PUBLIC_URL` + `/v1/agents/connections/{id}/proxy`), so a client that follows it,
Octokit's paginate included, stays on the proxy. URLs in a body (`url`, `comments_url`) still
name `https://api.github.com`: never send the router's credential there; call their path
through the proxy. With `ROUTER_PUBLIC_URL` unset the router has no proxy URL to name, so it drops every
`Link` (fail closed): a connection then loses GitHub's pagination until the URL is set.

Every other built-in, `linear` included, is MCP-only: a direct call answers 400 «connector
"linear" has no api_base endpoint». Why Linear has none is in `linear.yaml`.

For Linear's GraphQL API, connect `linear_app` («Linear (own OAuth app)») instead. It signs in
with your own Linear OAuth app, and its token serves both the GraphQL API and Linear's MCP
tools:

1. Read the callback URL: `GET /v1/agents/connectors/linear_app`, field `redirect_uri`.
2. In Linear, create an OAuth app at https://linear.app/settings/api/applications/new with
   that callback URL.
3. Give the router its client id and secret: `PUT /v1/agents/connectors/linear_app/oauth-client`.
4. Create a `linear_app` connection and run its OAuth consent as for any connector.

Gong needs its tech admin first. In Gong: **Admin center › Settings › MCP** (under Ecosystem) **› MCP
servers › New MCP server integration**
([Gong's guide](https://help.gong.io/docs/create-an-integration-to-connect-to-the-mcp-server)).
Set the redirect URI to the connector's `redirect_uri`, and the registration type to
**Automatic** for `dcr` (Manual issues your own client id and secret; the type cannot be changed later). Until then Gong refuses every consent with
`unauthorized_client`, «This MCP client is not authorized for your company». The connection
stays pending, and its last validation says why.

A `linear` connection stays as it is; it does not move to `linear_app`. A connection keeps
the revision it was made on, so a `github` connection made before revision 4 takes direct calls
only after its next consent or token save.

## 3. Give an agent the tools

Dashboard: open the agent › **Tools** › **Connectors** › **Add connector**.

1. Pick the connector.
2. Under **Whose account**, choose **One app connection** (`fixed`) or **Each user’s own** (`session`). The list then shows «App connection <name>» or «Each user’s own account».
3. **Connect** lists the connection's tools. Tick the ones the agent may call. There is no
   wildcard: a tool that is not ticked is never offered.
4. Save.

The agent sees each tool as `<binding name>__<tool>`, for example `github__get_me`.

`github` (revision 5) offers GitHub's Actions tools beside its default ones: `actions_list`,
`actions_get`, `actions_run_trigger` and `get_job_logs`. The manifest asks for them with the
`X-MCP-Toolsets: default,actions` header. A binding's `tools` still narrows them: a tool that is
not granted is never offered. A connection made before revision 5 lists them after its next
consent or token save.

With the API, the binding goes in `connectors[]` of the agent config
(`AgentConnectorBinding`):

```json
{
  "name": "linear",
  "connector_id": "linear",
  "connection": {"type": "session"},
  "tools": [{"name": "list_issues"}]
}
```

A `fixed` binding names `connection.connection_id` and pins each tool's `schema_digest`.
A `session` binding may grant a tool by name alone.

Test it in **Playground**. For a `session` binding the end user may have no connection yet.
The call then waits for them to sign in on its own `ai_tool_call` step, which is
`awaiting_authorization` and carries an `authorization` with the `provider`, `title`, `url`,
`handoff_token` and `expires_at`. The reply also carries a `connector_authorization` card, which
the dashboard renders. **Connect** opens the consent popup, and once they consent the same call
runs in the same reply. A `tool_approval` with only the `tool_call_id` and `allowed: false`
declines it, and a consent that is refused, fails or is not finished in ten minutes ends it.
Either way the model is told, and nothing runs. A native app opens
`url#handoff_token=<handoff_token>` in its web authentication sheet, with its own scheme as the
session's `return_url`. On iOS that is StreamChatAI's `AIToolAuthorizationView`, which
`examples/voice_agents/swift_assistant` uses for Gmail and Linear. A spoken turn on a call has
no reply to show it on, so by voice the binding answers that it is not available.

`require_approval: ["create_issue", "delete_*"]` on a binding holds each call of a tool it names
until the session's user allows it. The call's step is `awaiting_approval`, addressed to them, and
nothing reaches the provider before they answer with `tool_approval` (`tool_call_id`, the reply's
`request_id`, `allowed`), on their socket or their backend's. They answer as the kind of caller
that opened the session, as they reach it (`session.Owner.Reaches`): a guest token with a signed-in
user's id is not them. Declined, or not answered in ten
minutes, the call is not sent and the model is told. A session with nobody to ask (incognito, a
run, a shared chat, an MCP event's) refuses the call at once. In a channel of a type
`chat_channels` names, the call asks the writer of the message the reply answers, who answers
with their own user token through `POST /v1/agents/conversations/{cid}/tool_approvals` while a
member of the channel. The hook names the writer by id alone, so any verified token of that id
answers for them, unless they are the session's own user (a session opened through the API
answering in the channel), who is asked as the kind of caller that opened it; the backend may
answer any (`api/conversations.go`, AI-3154). There the
writer has two minutes, not ten, when the Router opened the session for the message, as it does
unless a session opened through the API answers in the channel: it answers one message for at
most two minutes (`askTimeout`, `api/messagehooks.go`) and then closes that session, which stops
the call, and an answer after that is a 404 (`answerHosted`, `api/threadhooks.go`). The model gets
no round to say why, so the reply ends with a line that the approval expired, that the step
waiting did not run (an earlier call of the reply may have), and that the person can ask again, and the step says "Not allowed in time" (`ExpireApprovals`, `conversation/parts.go`, AI-3302). An entry must match a tool the
binding grants, and `sandbox: true` is refused beside it (`session/connector_approval.go`).
Beside a sensitive connector (Nessy), a binding's write tool needs `require_approval`: the
config is refused unless each tool it grants only reads (`read_only_tools`, or an http tool's
`read_only` at the digest the grant pins: one granted by name or at another revision's digest
does not) or is held, and a `tool_patterns` binding needs an entry such as `*` that matches each pattern as written
(`connectors/sensitive`, `ConfigComplaint`; across a parent and its child agents, `GraphComplaint`). In agent.yaml it is `require_approval:` on
the connector entry. Tools a caller declares at createSession are not checked. The caller runs
them, or a person's device does (`executor: client`). The router sends a client tool's
arguments to the caller on the events socket (`api/sessionws.go`). Every channel member can
also read them in the conversation's tool part, but only when they are 512 bytes or fewer
(`conversation/parts.go`, `maxClientArguments`) (AI-1642). If one of them
sends data on to anyone else, declare it with `approval`. On a voice call the router then asks
the user and sends the call only on yes. In text the router does not ask: the caller's client
must wait for `tool_approval` before it runs the tool.

For a session your backend creates, pass the end user's connection in
`connector_bindings: [{"name": "linear", "connection_id": "…"}]`. Leave it out and the
router uses the user's only connected connection to that connector, if there is exactly one.

`agent.yaml`: the sync API accepts `connectors`, and the Go SDK folder reader reads the block
(`sdks/go/agents/config.go`, `connectorBindings`). An entry whose `connection:` the app does not have
is left out with a warning, and the rest of the agent syncs; `required: true` makes it an error. `sandbox: true` lets code in the session's sandbox call the connector's API with the binding's connection.
The left-out entries go to the router as `left_out_connectors` and are served on the agent config.

  the placeholder stops at once; it costs one agent config read per request. The Daytona broker
  withdraws a grant by putting `va_withdrawn` in its secret, which it deletes at Close: deleted,
  the placeholder left in the env var got 502 «could not reach upstream host», which code cannot
  tell from the host failing; now the request reaches the host without a token, and GitHub
  answers 401 (live probe, 2026-10-29, AI-1876). Daytona refuses a request that carries a placeholder it
  does not substitute (another host, the query, another session's): 502 «could not reach upstream

  granted host when the value is not Base64-encoded (live Basic-auth check, staging 2026-10-21).

  staging E2E, 2026-10-22, session `01a16514-923c-7843-9214-40a94453f194`: `git ls-remote` of a public repo with

  granted host and writes through the connector's tools. A request to a granted host that is not a
  GET or a HEAD gets 403 «… refused: code in the sandbox only reads through a connector; write with

  bare `apt-get install` finds no package. With it, `git lfs pull` of a public repository read its
  objects through the proxy (staging, 2026-11-05, AI-2066).
  Connections pinned to an earlier revision get the reads without a reconnect. Allowed domains
  take any method. Under the Daytona broker nothing checks methods: code can write with the token
  (`internal/sandbox/egress/AGENTS.md`, «Read-only»).
  GitHub refuses the token as `Authorization: Bearer` from git (401 to `git-receive-pack`, probe
  2026-10-22T03:53:09Z; Basic `x-access-token:<token>` was taken), so `run_code`'s description
  gives git the URL form. GitHub revision 7 grants github.com (AI-1576); a connection on
  revision 6 keeps its two API hosts until it is reconnected.

  grants, the connector limiter and the audit. That is intended; under the proxy broker the code
  only reads (above).
- Known limit (A5, accepted for GitHub): Daytona scrubs only the token's literal value. A granted
  host that echoes the token escaped or encoded would hand it to the sandbox. Wave 14's proxy
  broker closes it.
- Known limit (any header, AI-1976, accepted): Daytona substitutes the placeholder in any request
  header to a granted host, not only `Authorization` (https://www.daytona.io/docs/en/secrets.md,
  «Substitution scope»; the live suite sends it in `X-Probe`). The proxy broker substitutes only in
  `Authorization` (`internal/sandbox/egress/AGENTS.md`, step 5). A granted host that echoes that header would hand the token to the sandbox.
- Known limit (Daytona lag): after the router withdraws a secret (connection deleted or needs a
  reconnect), Daytona keeps substituting it for a while. The withdrawal is an update, which takes
  effect within 15 seconds (https://www.daytona.io/docs/en/secrets.md); a live probe on
  2026-10-29 saw the token gone within 8 s (a delete, before AI-1876, took 16 to 24 s). Wave 14's proxy broker resolves per
  request and stops substituting at once.
- Known limit: a router crash, or a Close that Daytona refuses, leaves the secret (a live
  token) and maybe the sandbox at Daytona until the sweep (w15-sweep, AI-1577) removes it. A
  Close that times out behind a running run deletes the secret (or the proxy's record) at
  once; the sandbox stays.
- A provider's error text never reaches a log or an error: both brokers log the error's class

---
name: dashboard
description: How to work on the Volt dashboard (/Users/thierry/workspace/volt-dashboard), Stream's admin SPA, and its Agents section that talks to the acceleration router. Read before touching Volt or wiring a router change into it.
---

# Volt dashboard

Checkout: `/Users/thierry/workspace/volt-dashboard`. Not the same as this repo's `dashboard/`
(Next.js); Volt is Stream's production dashboard and the Agents section is being added to it.

Volt has its own rules. Read its `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/rules/*.md` before editing, and
use its `.claude/skills/` (`new-route`, `new-api-hook`, `gen-api`, ...) for routine work.

## Stack

React 19, TypeScript 7, Vite, TanStack Router (file-based) + React Query, Tailwind 4,
Radix/shadcn. **Bun only**, never npm. Tests: Vitest + Testing Library (MSW for HTTP),
Playwright for e2e.

The shell defaults to Node 19, which breaks `bun lint`, `bun dev` and Vitest. Prefix every
Volt command with `nvm use 24 &&` (or `export PATH=~/.nvm/versions/node/v24.11.1/bin:$PATH`).

## Run it against a local router

Full guide: `docs/local-agents/README.md`. Short version:

```bash
# in Vision-Agents
export VOLT_CHECKOUT=/Users/thierry/workspace/volt-dashboard
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f "$VOLT_CHECKOUT/docs/local-agents/compose.volt.yaml" up -d --build router
# in volt-dashboard (.env.local: HOST=local.getstream.io PORT=3011 AGENTS_ROUTER_URL=http://localhost:8080)
bun dev
```

Open `https://local.getstream.io:3011/organization/<orgId>/<appId>/agents/` (not
`localhost`, or CORS/auth break). The override puts the router in `proxy` mode, so it reads the app and organization
the dev proxy sets, with Volt's
CORS origin. Rebuild the router after pulling router changes.

Set `ROUTER_DEV_KEK` (single-quoted) and `ROUTER_PUBLIC_URL=http://localhost:8080` in the
repo-root `.env`, which compose hands the router. Without the KEK no plugin client secret can be
saved, and changing it leaves the stored ones unreadable. Local dev keeps the plain KEK in
`ROUTER_DEV_KEK`: Cloud KMS (`ROUTER_AUTH_KMS_KEY`) is for hosted deployments, and the router
refuses the two together. An `.env` that still sets `ROUTER_AUTH_KEK` is refused: rename it.

## How Agents is wired

- Dev-only. `src/api/agents.ts` throws outside `import.meta.env.DEV`.
- Browser calls `/__agents/<orgId>/<appId>/v1/...`; `scripts/agents-dev-proxy.ts` (mounted in
  `vite.config.ts`) strips credentials, sets `X-Customer-Id` = app id, and forwards to
  `AGENTS_ROUTER_URL`. Configs under `examples` in the router won't show up; they live under
  the numeric app id.
- Requests go through `agentRequest` / `agentQueryOptions` (`src/queries/agents/`). Don't
  call `fetch` directly.
- Types: `src/types/agents.ts` re-exports from `src/gen/agents/` (generated). Never edit `src/gen/`.
- Routes: `src/routes/organization/$orgId/$appId/agents/`. Components:
  `src/components/custom/agents/`. Helpers: `src/utils/agents/`. Nav: `src/constants/sidebars.tsx`.

## Picking a model

Any field that picks an STT, TTS, LLM or other model uses the model picker, never a
`<select>` or free-text input. It renders a summary card: the label above, the current
choice in bold ("gemini / gemini-3.8-flash"), a muted detail line ("Pinned model.",
"The router's default.", "Now provider / model" for a route), and a **Change** button.
Change opens a dialog with two sections: **Routers** (route cards from
`/v1/<modality>/routes`, default first) and **Models** (a table of pinnable models from
`/v1/<modality>/providers`). The columns follow the modality: LLM shows popularity,
intelligence index, tokens per second and input and output price per million tokens, TTS
Elo and characters per second, STT WER and latency, search the search index and cost
per task (Artificial Analysis numbers from
`benchmark`, refreshed with the `refresh_model_stats` skill), anything else the live
popularity, latency, error rate, languages and speed.

- In a react-hook-form form: `AgentModelSelect` (`agent-model-select.tsx`) with `name`,
  `label`, `modality`, `purpose` (dialog description), `defaultRoute`, optional `hint`.
  It stores the bare target (a route id or `provider/model`); empty means the default route.
- When one choice spans several modalities (e.g. a text LLM or a realtime speech-to-speech
  model) or doesn't map to a single form field: `AgentModelPicker`
  (`agent-model-picker.tsx`) with `sources` and a `modality:target` value. See
  `agent-conversation-model.tsx`.

## Ordering a list of choices

`AgentModelChain` (`agent-model-chain.tsx`) is the reordering primitive: a form field
holding `string[]`, shown as one `AgentModelPicker` per entry in the order they are tried.
The first row takes the `label`, the rest are "Fallback 1", "Fallback 2". Each row has a
drag grip and, for keyboard and tests, **Move up** / **Move down** / **Remove** buttons
(`aria-label`s read "Move Fallback 1 up"). **Add fallback** appends `defaultRoute`.

Volt has no drag-and-drop dependency and this uses native HTML5 drag on the grip: the drag
image is set to the grip's row so the whole row follows the cursor, and `dragover` on a
neighbour reorders as it goes, so the list on screen is what dropping would leave behind.
Follow the same shape — grip plus move buttons — anywhere else rows are user-ordered,
rather than reaching for `dnd-kit`.

Use it for anything routing tries in order. A modality block's `providers` is a priority
list that wins over `target`, so write one entry back as `target` and several as
`providers`, clearing whichever is unused. Every type reads a list. LLM falls back down it
per failed response; search retries a failed search elsewhere only when a list is written,
a single target reports the failure instead.

## Changing the router API

`api/agents/openapi.yaml` is a copy of `acceleration/api/openapi.yaml`. After a spec change:
copy it over, run `bun run gen:agents`, and fix type errors. Route changes: `bun routes:generate`.

## Before calling it done

```bash
bun lint                 # must pass
bun run build
bun run vitest run tests/unit/agents
```

UI copy is sentence case; sidebar group titles are one word and labels don't repeat them
(see Volt's `CLAUDE.md`). Only use `<Icon>` from `components/ui/icon.tsx` in sidebars.

skills.name: decision_model
skills.desc: What a decision model is in this repo, the contract one implements, the System One protocol most vendors here speak, and how to add a vendor or a model to the decision_model router. Read before adding a decision model, a decision model vendor or a guardrail backend.
skills.body:
---
name: decision_model
description: What a decision model is in this repo, the contract one implements, the System One protocol most vendors here speak, and how to add a vendor or a model to the decision_model router. Read before adding a decision model, a decision model vendor or a guardrail backend.
---

# Decision models

A decision model answers named questions about a piece of state with typed values and the
probabilities behind them. It writes no prose. What used to be called an LCM (large classifier
model) here is this; the industry settled on "decision model", and so did we.

The per-modality half of [router-interface](../router-interface/SKILL.md):

| What | Where |
| --- | --- |
| The contract | [`internal/decisionmodel`](../../../acceleration/internal/decisionmodel/decisionmodel.go) |
| The wire protocol | [`internal/decisionmodel/systemone`](../../../acceleration/internal/decisionmodel/systemone/systemone.go) |
| One package per vendor | `internal/decisionmodel/<vendor>/` |
| The router | [`internal/decisionrouter`](../../../acceleration/internal/decisionrouter/router.go) |
| The models | the `decision_model` section of [`router.yaml`](../../../acceleration/internal/routing/router.yaml) |
| The modality | `routing.DecisionModel`, `"decision_model"` in the API and in stats |
| Callers | `/v1/classify`, `type: decision_model` guardrails, prompt injection screening |

## Our definition

Something is a decision model here when all four hold. If one does not, it belongs somewhere
else.

1. **The caller writes the criteria.** It is asked questions the caller wrote, about a state the
   caller chose. A moderation endpoint with a fixed taxonomy (OpenAI moderations, Stream
   Moderation) answers its own categories rather than the question asked, so it is not one.
2. **The answer is a distribution.** `violates: 0.93` is something a threshold acts on. A chat
   model's "Yes, this violates the policy" is something a parser acts on, and a parser that fails
   has no number to fall back to.
3. **The number is meant to be calibrated.** A decision model's 0.9 is meant to be 90%, which is
   what makes a threshold in config mean the same thing across policies. A prompted chat
   model's "0.9" is a token it learned to emit.
4. **It is one request and one answer.** There is no stream, no generated text, no token budget,
   no tools and no history. That is why it routes like `search`, not like `llm`, and why
   failover happens at start only. The caller is mid-turn, and a second provider's latency on
   top of the first one's failure is a longer silence than saying the judgement did not arrive.

A chat model with a JSON schema or logprobs passes the first test and fails the third. It
stays in `llmrouter`. The two run side by side: `internal/guardrail` has a decision model
backend and an LLM-judge backend, and the policy file picks one.

## The three questions

| Constructor | Asks | Answer lands in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Noul(instructions, yes, no)` | yes or no | `Answer.Yes`, a probability from 0 to 1 |
| `Choice(instructions, options)` | which of these | `Answer.Chosen`, plus `Probabilities` and `Confidence` |
| `Score(instructions, levels)` | where on this ordered scale | `Answer.Level`, which can fall between two levels, plus `Legend`, `Probabilities` and `Confidence` |

These three are what every vendor below takes. Do not add a fourth unless every vendor's API
has it: a question type that only one provider supports can't be routed. A hazard battery
is several `Noul`s in one request, not a new type. OpenAI's own API calls the noul a
`predicate` and Vercel's AI SDK calls it `boolean`; translate that at the edge, never in the
contract.

Getting the most out of them:

- **A model can only answer with an option it was given.** Include a "none of these" option
  whenever the options may not cover an input. `Choice` keeps an option whose description is
  empty (it goes on the wire as `null`), because the name can be all an option needs.
- **Ask everything at once.** The questions in one request are answered independently and
  share the cost of the state's tokens, so a question whose answer turns out to be irrelevant
  is close to free. Ask for everything you might need and let Go decide what applies. That
  keeps policy in code rather than in a prompt.
- **Use `Score` for a spectrum.** A noul at 0.5 means an even split between yes and no, not
  "medium".
- **`Confidence` says how peaked a distribution is, not whether acting on it is safe.** A
  guardrail should threshold on the probability it cares about, not on confidence.

## The contract

`decisionmodel.Provider` is `Classify`, `Start`, `Close`, `Provider` and `Model`. The rules:

- **Validate first.** Call `Request.Validate()` before anything reaches the wire. A question with
  no instructions, or a type nobody knows, is refused locally rather than spending a round trip
  to come back as a 422.
- **An unanswered question is an error, never a zero value.** A missing `violates` read as `0.0`
  is a guardrail that allows everything, and nothing about the turn would say so.
- **`Result.Model` is the version that answered, not the alias that was asked.** Aliases move
  when a release ships, and a threshold tuned against one version needs to know.
- **Report usage and let the price list price it.** Report input and output tokens. The price
  list (`acceleration/prices/vendor.json`, then the database) turns them into cost; never
  compute cost in the provider.
- **Map failures onto the contract's errors.** A rate limit (429) wraps `ErrRateLimited`. An
  overloaded service (503, 529) or a network failure wraps `ErrUnavailable`. Anything else is
  the request's own fault. `/v1/classify` turns those into its status codes.
- **No options, ever.** `options.Classifier.Terms()` returns nothing, and that is not a gap to
  close later. Everything a caller asks for travels in the questions, so there is no parameter
  for a provider to accept and quietly drop. A provider that cannot express a question should
  fail the request rather than answer a different one. The caller cannot tell from a
  probability that it was answered about something else.

## The protocol: System One

TypeSafe published System One for Jev. OpenRouter, Perplexity, Alibaba Model Studio and
AnyRouter adopted it unchanged:

```json
{"model": "...", "state": "text, or a JSON object whose parts a question names in backticks",
 "questions": {
   "is_bug":  {"type": "noul",   "instructions": "...", "criteria": {"true": "...", "false": "..."}},
   "team":    {"type": "choice", "instructions": "...", "criteria": {"payments": "...", "none": null}},
   "urgency": {"type": "score",  "instructions": "...", "criteria": ["lowest level", "...", "highest"]}}}
```

The answers come back keyed the same way, as `{"type", "noul" | "choice" | "score", "probabilities",
"confidence", "legend"}`, beside `model` and `usage.input_tokens` and `usage.output_tokens`.
`systemone.Client` speaks this and nothing else. Perplexity refuses any field it does not
know, so the request carries `model`, `state` and `questions` and nothing more.

Google's Decisions API is the one vendor here off System One, in
[`internal/decisionmodel/gemini`](../../../acceleration/internal/decisionmodel/gemini/gemini.go).
Its answers use System One's fields, but the state is `input` (a state with parts goes as
its JSON text), a noul's criteria are `true_description` and `false_description`, the key is
`x-goog-api-key`, usage is `total_input_tokens`, and the answer names no model. A yes or
no probability is never below 0.01 or above 0.99, so a threshold outside that range never
fires.

OpenAI's own Decisions API (`POST /v1/decisions`, limited preview) is another shape that
differs: `input` instead of `state`, questions and answers as arrays carrying `name`,
`predicate` with `probability`, and `choices` and `levels` as objects. Reach GPT-6 Luna
Decisions through OpenRouter, which translates it into System One. Write an `openai` vendor
only when there is a reason to skip OpenRouter, and do the translation inside that package.

## The vendors and models

| Vendor | Endpoint | Key | Models declared |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `typesafe` | `api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` | `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` | `jev-latest` (the default route's pin) |
| `openrouter` | `openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions` | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | `typesafe/jev-1.13`, `openai/gpt-6-luna-decisions`, `cloudflare/clef-flash`, `cloudflare/clef`, `respan/span-01-lite`, `liquid/d1`, `jaredpalmer/kev-4b`, `perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.1-27b`, `inception/mercury-decide`, `inception/mercury-decide:free` |
| `perplexity` | `api.perplexity.ai/v1/decisions` | `PERPLEXITY_API_KEY` | `pplx-decider-v1.1-27b`, `pplx-decider-v1-27b` |
| `gemini` | `generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/decisions` (not System One) | `GOOGLE_API_KEY` | `gemini-decision-1` |

To see what OpenRouter currently serves, run
`curl "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models?output_modalities=decisions"`. A model can be listed
there with no endpoint behind it, which is why Decider V1 goes to Perplexity directly.

How they are routed:

- **`classify-fast`** is what a guardrail or prompt injection screening gets when it names
  nothing. It prefers `typesafe/jev-latest`, because every threshold in use was tuned against
  Jev. Without the pin, health ranking would hand guardrails to whichever of the ten answered
  fastest last.
- **Clef** is the only `high-quality` model, so it is what the two `*-high-accuracy` shortcuts
  resolve to.
- **Free endpoints** (`:free`) are capped at a few requests a minute and a few dozen a day. They
  are declared `realtime: false`, so a live route never lands on one, and they are priced with
  `free: true` in `prices/vendor.json` rather than no price. `TestEveryRoutedModelIsPriced`
  still catches a price that was forgotten.
- **Data policy.** Only TypeSafe and Gemini declare one (Gemini's retention is unspecified,
  so a request asking for no retention skips it). What happens to an OpenRouter request depends on
  where OpenRouter forwards it, so its models declare none, and a customer who asks for a data
  policy is kept away from them.

## Adding a model

On a vendor that already exists, it is a `router.yaml` entry and its price:

1. Add `provider`, `model` (exactly the vendor's model id), a one-sentence `description`,
   `languages`, `realtime` and `tier` to `router.yaml`, and its `input_tokens` rate to
   `acceleration/prices/vendor.json`, read from the vendor's price list and dated in the
   `router.yaml` comment.
2. Choose a tier on purpose. `low-latency` is for the live path. `high-quality` is a slower
   model that is more accurate.
3. Run the integration suite below against it. A model that cannot tell an SDK question from a
   pizza question must not be a candidate for a guardrail.

## Adding a vendor

On System One, a vendor is an `Endpoint` and nothing else:

1. Create `internal/decisionmodel/<vendor>/<vendor>.go` with `ProviderName`, an `Endpoint`
   (key and base-URL env vars, base URL, path, default model) and
   `New(systemone.Options) (*systemone.Client, error)`. Copy `perplexity` as the template.
2. Register it in [`registry.go`](../../../acceleration/internal/decisionrouter/registry.go),
   and add a row to `TestEachVendorIsAskedAtItsOwnEndpointWithItsOwnKey` and a key to the
   `keys` map in `integration_test.go`.
3. Declare its models in `router.yaml`. `TestTheDefaultRegistryHasEveryProviderTheConfigDeclares`
   fails until step 2 is done, which is the point.
4. Make sure to register usage and include pricing information, see the `pricing` skill from this repo on how to do this.

Off System One, the package implements `decisionmodel.Provider` itself. It translates the
neutral request into the vendor's wire shape and back inside that package, and follows every
rule under "The contract". The contract carries no vendor's JSON tags, and keeping it that
way is what makes the next vendor cheap.

## Testing

- **Wire behaviour** (validation, criteria shape, unanswered questions, status mapping) is tested
  once, in `systemone_test.go`, against an `httptest` server with a made-up endpoint.
- **A vendor** is covered by the registry test above: right path, right key, right model.
- **`integration_test.go` in `decisionrouter`** (`//go:build integration`) asks every model
  declared in `router.yaml` an obvious yes and an obvious no, and skips a vendor whose key is not
  set. Run it with
  `go test -tags integration ./internal/decisionrouter/ -run DecisionModelIntegration`.
  An OpenRouter account with no credits answers 402 on every paid model, while the
  `:free` one still works.

# Decision models

A decision model answers named questions about a piece of state with typed values and the
probabilities behind them. It writes no prose. What used to be called an LCM (large classifier
model) here is this; the industry settled on "decision model", and so did we.

The per-modality half of [router-interface](../router-interface/SKILL.md):

| What | Where |
| --- | --- |
| The contract | [`internal/decisionmodel`](../../../acceleration/internal/decisionmodel/decisionmodel.go) |
| The wire protocol | [`internal/decisionmodel/systemone`](../../../acceleration/internal/decisionmodel/systemone/systemone.go) |
| One package per vendor | `internal/decisionmodel/<vendor>/` |
| The router | [`internal/decisionrouter`](../../../acceleration/internal/decisionrouter/router.go) |
| The models | the `decision_model` section of [`router.yaml`](../../../acceleration/internal/routing/router.yaml) |
| The modality | `routing.DecisionModel`, `"decision_model"` in the API and in stats |
| Callers | `/v1/classify`, `type: decision_model` guardrails, prompt injection screening |

## Our definition

Something is a decision model here when all four hold. If one does not, it belongs somewhere
else.

1. **The caller writes the criteria.** It is asked questions the caller wrote, about a state the
   caller chose. A moderation endpoint with a fixed taxonomy (OpenAI moderations, Stream
   Moderation) answers its own categories rather than the question asked, so it is not one.
2. **The answer is a distribution.** `violates: 0.93` is something a threshold acts on. A chat
   model's "Yes, this violates the policy" is something a parser acts on, and a parser that fails
   has no number to fall back to.
3. **The number is meant to be calibrated.** A decision model's 0.9 is meant to be 90%, which is
   what makes a threshold in config mean the same thing across policies. A prompted chat
   model's "0.9" is a token it learned to emit.
4. **It is one request and one answer.** There is no stream, no generated text, no token budget,
   no tools and no history. That is why it routes like `search`, not like `llm`, and why
   failover happens at start only. The caller is mid-turn, and a second provider's latency on
   top of the first one's failure is a longer silence than saying the judgement did not arrive.

A chat model with a JSON schema or logprobs passes the first test and fails the third. It
stays in `llmrouter`. The two run side by side: `internal/guardrail` has a decision model
backend and an LLM-judge backend, and the policy file picks one.

## The three questions

| Constructor | Asks | Answer lands in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Noul(instructions, yes, no)` | yes or no | `Answer.Yes`, a probability from 0 to 1 |
| `Choice(instructions, options)` | which of these | `Answer.Chosen`, plus `Probabilities` and `Confidence` |
| `Score(instructions, levels)` | where on this ordered scale | `Answer.Level`, which can fall between two levels, plus `Legend`, `Probabilities` and `Confidence` |

These three are what every vendor below takes. Do not add a fourth unless every vendor's API
has it: a question type that only one provider supports can't be routed. A hazard battery
is several `Noul`s in one request, not a new type. OpenAI's own API calls the noul a
`predicate` and Vercel's AI SDK calls it `boolean`; translate that at the edge, never in the
contract.

Getting the most out of them:

- **A model can only answer with an option it was given.** Include a "none of these" option
  whenever the options may not cover an input. `Choice` keeps an option whose description is
  empty (it goes on the wire as `null`), because the name can be all an option needs.
- **Ask everything at once.** The questions in one request are answered independently and
  share the cost of the state's tokens, so a question whose answer turns out to be irrelevant
  is close to free. Ask for everything you might need and let Go decide what applies. That
  keeps policy in code rather than in a prompt.
- **Use `Score` for a spectrum.** A noul at 0.5 means an even split between yes and no, not
  "medium".
- **`Confidence` says how peaked a distribution is, not whether acting on it is safe.** A
  guardrail should threshold on the probability it cares about, not on confidence.

## The contract

`decisionmodel.Provider` is `Classify`, `Start`, `Close`, `Provider` and `Model`. The rules:

- **Validate first.** Call `Request.Validate()` before anything reaches the wire. A question with
  no instructions, or a type nobody knows, is refused locally rather than spending a round trip
  to come back as a 422.
- **An unanswered question is an error, never a zero value.** A missing `violates` read as `0.0`
  is a guardrail that allows everything, and nothing about the turn would say so.
- **`Result.Model` is the version that answered, not the alias that was asked.** Aliases move
  when a release ships, and a threshold tuned against one version needs to know.
- **Report usage and let the price list price it.** Report input and output tokens. The price
  list (`acceleration/prices/vendor.json`, then the database) turns them into cost; never
  compute cost in the provider.
- **Map failures onto the contract's errors.** A rate limit (429) wraps `ErrRateLimited`. An
  overloaded service (503, 529) or a network failure wraps `ErrUnavailable`. Anything else is
  the request's own fault. `/v1/classify` turns those into its status codes.
- **No options, ever.** `options.Classifier.Terms()` returns nothing, and that is not a gap to
  close later. Everything a caller asks for travels in the questions, so there is no parameter
  for a provider to accept and quietly drop. A provider that cannot express a question should
  fail the request rather than answer a different one. The caller cannot tell from a
  probability that it was answered about something else.

## The protocol: System One

TypeSafe published System One for Jev. OpenRouter, Perplexity, Alibaba Model Studio and
AnyRouter adopted it unchanged:

```json
{"model": "...", "state": "text, or a JSON object whose parts a question names in backticks",
 "questions": {
   "is_bug":  {"type": "noul",   "instructions": "...", "criteria": {"true": "...", "false": "..."}},
   "team":    {"type": "choice", "instructions": "...", "criteria": {"payments": "...", "none": null}},
   "urgency": {"type": "score",  "instructions": "...", "criteria": ["lowest level", "...", "highest"]}}}
```

The answers come back keyed the same way, as `{"type", "noul" | "choice" | "score", "probabilities",
"confidence", "legend"}`, beside `model` and `usage.input_tokens` and `usage.output_tokens`.
`systemone.Client` speaks this and nothing else. Perplexity refuses any field it does not
know, so the request carries `model`, `state` and `questions` and nothing more.

Google's Decisions API is the one vendor here off System One, in
[`internal/decisionmodel/gemini`](../../../acceleration/internal/decisionmodel/gemini/gemini.go).
Its answers use System One's fields, but the state is `input` (a state with parts goes as
its JSON text), a noul's criteria are `true_description` and `false_description`, the key is
`x-goog-api-key`, usage is `total_input_tokens`, and the answer names no model. A yes or
no probability is never below 0.01 or above 0.99, so a threshold outside that range never
fires.

OpenAI's own Decisions API (`POST /v1/decisions`, limited preview) is another shape that
differs: `input` instead of `state`, questions and answers as arrays carrying `name`,
`predicate` with `probability`, and `choices` and `levels` as objects. Reach GPT-6 Luna
Decisions through OpenRouter, which translates it into System One. Write an `openai` vendor
only when there is a reason to skip OpenRouter, and do the translation inside that package.

## The vendors and models

| Vendor | Endpoint | Key | Models declared |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| `perplexity` | `api.perplexity.ai/v1/decisions` | `PERPLEXITY_API_KEY` | `pplx-decider-v1.1-27b`, `pplx-decider-v1-27b` |
| `gemini` | `generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/decisions` (not System One) | `GOOGLE_API_KEY` | `gemini-decision-1` |

---
name: deploy
description: Ship acceleration/cmd/router to Stream's hosted environments. Read before deploying the router or asking why the hosted one behaves differently.
---

# Deploy the router

The hosted router behind `accelerate-<region>.gcp.stream-io-api.com` (production) and
`accelerate-staging.gcp.stream-io-api.com` is `acceleration/cmd/router`
built from this repo. **The deploy lives in Stream's private infra repo** (`GetStream/chat`):
`infra/docs/accelerate_launch.md` is the runbook, `infra/charts/accelerate/README.md` the
chart, and the CLI, cluster names and credentials are all there. This repo is public — name
the runbook, not the infrastructure.

Kubernetes owns the image, a version registry owns the binary: a pod fetches
`router-linux-<arch>` at start, so shipping a router is publishing a binary, moving that
pointer and restarting. Not an image build, not a chart deploy.

## Build

The router is cgo (opus, opusfile, soxr), so each architecture builds on its own
architecture, and both must be published or the deploy rejects the version. Tag the commit
`accelerate-vX.Y.Z` here and push the tag. The private repo's build workflow builds from that
tag, but it publishes to an S3 release bucket, not to the bucket pods fetch from; a
release reaches pods by building it by hand, then `rocky launch upload` once per architecture
and `rocky launch deploy`, which moves the pointer and restarts the pods (runbook step 8).

By hand, one container per architecture, from the repo root:

```bash
VERSION=vX.Y.Z
mkdir -p /tmp/router-release
docker run --rm --platform linux/arm64 \
  -v "$PWD":/src:ro -v "$(go env GOMODCACHE)":/go/pkg/mod -v /tmp/router-release:/out \
  -e GOWORK=off -e GOPROXY=off -e GOTOOLCHAIN=local -e VERSION="$VERSION" \
  -w /src/acceleration golang:1.27-bookworm bash -c '
    apt-get -qq update && apt-get -qq install -y --no-install-recommends \
      pkg-config libopus-dev libopusfile-dev libsoxr-dev >/dev/null
    CGO_ENABLED=1 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w -X main.release=$VERSION" \
      -o /out/router-linux-arm64 ./cmd/router'
```

`GOWORK=off` because `go.work` otherwise puts the module in workspace mode, which the build
refuses; `GOPROXY=off` builds from the host module cache, so the container uses exactly the
modules the host resolved. `main.release` is the version Sentry files events under, as the
workflow sets it. Repeat with
`--platform linux/amd64`, which works under emulation.

`GOPROXY=off` also means a module the host has not downloaded fails the build: after a
`go.mod` change, run `go mod download` in `acceleration/` on the host first.

Versions are `vX.Y.Z` or `vX.Y.Z-<prerelease>`, an unreleased build is named after its
commit (`v0.6.9-dev-<short sha>`), and a published one is immutable. The build is
reproducible, so the checksum a pod reports traces back to a commit.

## Overlap deploys (staging and the benchmark release)

Staging and the benchmark release (`perfbench -target benchmark`, nobody else's traffic) ship
a router without dropping a call. The runbook is `infra/docs/accelerate_overlap_deploy.md` in
the private repo; `rocky fastdeploy --service accelerate-staging` (or `accelerate-benchmark`)
builds this checkout and swaps it in, in 11-20 s warm.

- It needs `source ~/.config/rocky/gcp.env`, Docker, Go and gcloud, and an arm64 machine:
  the build runs natively and these releases' pods run arm64 only. It builds the working tree,
  uncommitted changes included, so the clean-tree rule below is for tagged releases.
- `--status` prints what each pod runs. The fetch initContainer's log only says what a pod
  started on, which a swap has since replaced.
- On staging a fastdeploy and a tagged release move the same pointer, and a restarted pod
  comes back on whichever was last. Pull before a fastdeploy, or it rolls back a teammate's
  release. Load-test on benchmark, not staging.

- A supervisor (devrun) owns the public socket and hands it to each router as fd 3
  (`listen_fd`), with a peer port of its own (`node.listen`). A swap starts the new router on
  the same socket, waits for `/health`, then SIGTERMs the old one.
- The old router stops accepting, keeps every call until it ends, bounded by
  `shutdown.drain` (1 h), still answering its peers, then exits. A second signal ends its
  calls now. At most three generations run at once.
- A draining router exits on `session.Manager.Len()` reaching zero, which counts a session
  until its `Close` returns. Anything new that holds a call open must be counted there, or
  the old router exits under it.
- A call only ends when the client's `close` reaches the router. A client that stops reading
  its session socket, or closes the connection straight after `close`, leaves the session
  running and holds the old router for the whole drain. `Pipeline.Leave` in the Go SDK waits
  for the router to hang up.
- To check a deploy, run perfbench against the benchmark release during the swap and confirm
  every call held, nothing answered 5xx, and devrun logged `pid N (sha) drained in ...,
  exit 0` for each old router once its last call ended.

## Sandbox proxy

Staging and every prod shard run the router with `broker: proxy`: code in a sandbox reaches a
connector's API through the router's egress proxy (`acceleration/internal/sandbox/egress/AGENTS.md`),
not through Daytona Secrets.

| Where | On since | GetStream/chat PR |
|---|---|---|
| staging | AI-2035 | |
| prod us-east4 | AI-2461 | #20044 |
| prod us-west1, europe-west4 | AI-2464 | #20103 |

AI-2462 proved it live on prod us-east4: `run_code` `GET api.github.com/user` through the proxy
answered 200, and the token never reached the sandbox.

- The values are in GetStream/chat on `master`. Staging's file
  is `infra/shards/us-east1-acceleration/accelerate-staging.yaml`. Each prod shard has its own
  file, `infra/shards/<region>-acceleration/accelerate-prod.yaml`.
- `router.sandboxProxy` holds `enabled`, `broker: proxy`, the public URL (it holds the proxy port)
  and the LoadBalancer's reserved address. The accelerate chart (`infra/charts/accelerate`, same
  repo) renders the Service from them.
- `router.overlapDeploy.holdSandboxProxy: true` makes devrun hold the proxy port :8091.
  `router.overlapDeploy.devrunImage` pins the devrun that can hold it (chat #19840).
- The CA certificate and key are two secrets, `ROUTER_CODE_SANDBOX_PROXY_CA_CERT` and
  `ROUTER_CODE_SANDBOX_PROXY_CA_KEY`. They reach the pods through `accelerate-secrets`, which is
  synced from Secret Manager. Staging has its own CA. Each prod shard has its own P-256 CA
  (AI-2460). The comment above `sandboxProxy` in each values file names the CA's expiry.
- Rotate each CA before it expires. Staging: the steps are in Linear AI-2069. Prod: AI-2663
  (us-east4), AI-2664 (us-west1) and AI-2665 (europe-west4), each due 2027-10-02.
- This repo is public. Read addresses and secret paths in the values file, and do not copy them here.

Verify after an apply, on each shard (AI-2461, AI-2464):

1. The rollout finishes, and each router logs `serving the sandbox egress proxy` with `tls=true`.
2. TLS verifies against that shard's CA: `openssl s_client -connect <address>:8091 -CAfile
   <shard CA cert> -verify_ip <address> -verify_return_error` prints `Verification: OK`.
3. A CONNECT without a credential gets `407 Proxy Authentication Required`.
4. One `run_code` `GET api.github.com/user` through a binding with `sandbox: true` answers 200.

Every prod region has a public hostname, `https://accelerate-<region>.gcp.stream-io-api.com`: all
three are behind the global load balancer (`accelerate_prod_regions` in
`infra/dns/gcp-stream-io-api-com/accelerate_global_lb.tf`). To test a region, call its hostname as
the app. Prod runs `authMode: proxy` with `proxyDeclaresKind: true`, so send `X-Stream-App-Id:
<app>` and `Stream-Auth-Type: server` (`acceleration/internal/auth/auth.go`,
`proxied.Authenticate`). Also send `X-Stream-Api-Key-Id: <the app's public key>` (`APIKeyIDHeader`,
`auth.go:112-118`) and `X-Stream-Actor-Name: <your name>`. Without the key header, the router
records the run's usage with no API key and raises the `unattributed` usage alert. This happened on
prod us-west1 and europe-west4 on 2026-11-03 21:28Z (AI-2464 E2E). The sandbox still reaches the
shard's proxy on its public address.

Datadog (AI-2463, chat #20097, `infra/shards/us-east4-acceleration/datadog/sandbox_egress.tf`):

- The dashboard "Accelerate sandbox egress proxy" shows the proxy's requests per cluster, decision
  and host.
- The monitor `sandbox_egress_5xx` fires on 3 or more 5xx in 30 minutes in `accelerate-prod`, all
  clusters together. A refused Upgrade (`denied_request`, 501) does not count. It notifies
  `@oncall-agents` and pages nobody.
- Datadog scrapes the router in us-west1 and europe-west4 since #20103 (`monitoring.datadog.enabled`).

To turn the proxy off on one shard:

1. In that shard's values file, set `router.overlapDeploy.holdSandboxProxy: false` and
   `router.sandboxProxy.enabled: false`.
2. Run `rocky accelerate up --region <region>-acceleration --env prod`.
3. Wait for the rollout to finish. An edit alone changes nothing.

With the proxy off, prod refuses a session that binds a sandbox again. The steps come from the
AI-2461 and AI-2464 apply plan. The chart renders the hold only while `sandboxProxy.enabled` is on.

## Production

Production is three shards, us-east4, us-west1 and europe-west4. Each region has its own hostname,
`accelerate-<region>.gcp.stream-io-api.com`, that reaches only that shard. All three are published
(`local.accelerate_prod_regions`); us-east4's is the SDKs' default (`DefaultURL`,
`sdks/go/stream/backend.go:57`). Any shard serves any app. Each runs the router with its own
Postgres and Redis beside the global ones in us-east4 (`acceleration/README.md`, "Shards"). The
runbook is `infra/docs/accelerate_shards_rollout.md` in the private repo.

A release is a tagged build, published once, then deployed per shard:

- `rocky launch upload` both architectures once; the binary is shared by every shard.

# Deploy the router

The hosted router behind `accelerate-<region>.gcp.stream-io-api.com` (production) and
`accelerate-staging.gcp.stream-io-api.com` is `acceleration/cmd/router`
built from this repo. **The deploy lives in Stream's private infra repo** (`GetStream/chat`):
`infra/docs/accelerate_launch.md` is the runbook, `infra/charts/accelerate/README.md` the
chart, and the CLI, cluster names and credentials are all there. This repo is public — name
the runbook, not the infrastructure.

Kubernetes owns the image, a version registry owns the binary: a pod fetches
`router-linux-<arch>` at start, so shipping a router is publishing a binary, moving that
pointer and restarting. Not an image build, not a chart deploy.

## Build

The router is cgo (opus, opusfile, soxr), so each architecture builds on its own
architecture, and both must be published or the deploy rejects the version. Tag the commit
`accelerate-vX.Y.Z` here and push the tag. The private repo's build workflow builds from that
tag, but it publishes to an S3 release bucket, not to the bucket pods fetch from; a
release reaches pods by building it by hand, then `rocky launch upload` once per architecture
and `rocky launch deploy`, which moves the pointer and restarts the pods (runbook step 8).

By hand, one container per architecture, from the repo root:

```bash
VERSION=vX.Y.Z
mkdir -p /tmp/router-release
docker run --rm --platform linux/arm64 \
  -v "$PWD":/src:ro -v "$(go env GOMODCACHE)":/go/pkg/mod -v /tmp/router-release:/out \
  -e GOWORK=off -e GOPROXY=off -e GOTOOLCHAIN=local -e VERSION="$VERSION" \
  -w /src/acceleration golang:1.27-bookworm bash -c '
    apt-get -qq update && apt-get -qq install -y --no-install-recommends \
      pkg-config libopus-dev libopusfile-dev libsoxr-dev >/dev/null
    CGO_ENABLED=1 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w -X main.release=$VERSION" \
      -o /out/router-linux-arm64 ./cmd/router'
```

`GOWORK=off` because `go.work` otherwise puts the module in workspace mode, which the build
refuses; `GOPROXY=off` builds from the host module cache, so the container uses exactly the
modules the host resolved. `main.release` is the version Sentry files events under, as the
workflow sets it. Repeat with
`--platform linux/amd64`, which works under emulation.

`GOPROXY=off` also means a module the host has not downloaded fails the build: after a
`go.mod` change, run `go mod download` in `acceleration/` on the host first.

Versions are `vX.Y.Z` or `vX.Y.Z-<prerelease>`, an unreleased build is named after its
commit (`v0.6.9-dev-<short sha>`), and a published one is immutable. The build is
reproducible, so the checksum a pod reports traces back to a commit.

## Overlap deploys (staging and the benchmark release)

Staging and the benchmark release (`perfbench -target benchmark`, nobody else's traffic) ship
a router without dropping a call. The runbook is `infra/docs/accelerate_overlap_deploy.md` in
the private repo; `rocky fastdeploy --service accelerate-staging` (or `accelerate-benchmark`)
builds this checkout and swaps it in, in 11-20 s warm.

- It needs `source ~/.config/rocky/gcp.env`, Docker, Go and gcloud, and an arm64 machine:
  the build runs natively and these releases' pods run arm64 only. It builds the working tree,
  uncommitted changes included, so the clean-tree rule below is for tagged releases.
- `--status` prints what each pod runs. The fetch initContainer's log only says what a pod
  started on, which a swap has since replaced.
- On staging a fastdeploy and a tagged release move the same pointer, and a restarted pod
  comes back on whichever was last. Pull before a fastdeploy, or it rolls back a teammate's
  release. Load-test on benchmark, not staging.

- A supervisor (devrun) owns the public socket and hands it to each router as fd 3
  (`listen_fd`), with a peer port of its own (`node.listen`). A swap starts the new router on
  the same socket, waits for `/health`, then SIGTERMs the old one.
- The old router stops accepting, keeps every call until it ends, bounded by
  `shutdown.drain` (1 h), still answering its peers, then exits. A second signal ends its
  calls now. At most three generations run at once.
- A draining router exits on `session.Manager.Len()` reaching zero, which counts a session
  until its `Close` returns. Anything new that holds a call open must be counted there, or
  the old router exits under it.
- A call only ends when the client's `close` reaches the router. A client that stops reading
  its session socket, or closes the connection straight after `close`, leaves the session
  running and holds the old router for the whole drain. `Pipeline.Leave` in the Go SDK waits
  for the router to hang up.
- To check a deploy, run perfbench against the benchmark release during the swap and confirm
  every call held, nothing answered 5xx, and devrun logged `pid N (sha) drained in ...,
  exit 0` for each old router once its last call ended.

Staging and every prod shard run the router with `broker: proxy`: code in a sandbox reaches a
connector's API through the router's egress proxy (`acceleration/internal/sandbox/egress/AGENTS.md`),
