skills.body:
---
name: docs
description: How to edit the agents docs on getstream.io. Use when writing or updating agents documentation pages, sidebars or the SDK switcher.
---

Docs live in the main site repo, typically located at workspace/getstream.io, under `content/docs`

Some general docs tips

- Keep it short
- Show examples before explaining details
- Write from the code, not from memory. Check the SDK (`sdks/<lang>`) and `acceleration/api/openapi.yaml` before documenting an API, key or default

## How a page reads

Write it so it needs no deslop pass. `agents/_default/02-agents/creating-an-agent.md` is the reference for how a page opens and flows, and Thierry's deslop commits in getstream.io (7ee27d28eb, 21c69fd256, edf81f51f2, 1d93015abe) show the cuts.

- Open with why the reader wants it and one real example, not a definition: "Your support agent shouldn't answer: Please solve the Navier-Stokes problem", not "A guardrail screens what a caller asks"
- Example first: the `agent.yaml` or the call, then the command to try it (`getstream agents test support --sync`) and a question to ask. Pick an example the reader can run as is, such as a connector the app owns rather than one each user signs in to. Then explain only what the example doesn't show
- Real example values (`dentist_ai`, "Northwind Pizza, what can I get you?", "What is your return policy?"), never `foo` or `my-thing`
- One or two sentences per paragraph, written like a person: "It returns the connection", not "The answer is the connection". Contractions are fine. State facts, not "should": "is configurable", not "should be configurable"
- Where there are options, recommend one and say when to pick the other: "We recommend each user's own account for personal data, and a shared account for company tools"
- One H2 per thing the reader wants to do. A fact lives on one page: detail that has its own page is cut to a link. End with `## Going further` and `<Cards>`
- Say what a feature can't do in a plain sentence, under `## Limitations` when there are several. A limit the reader can hit stays; a cap on a field goes
- A table that sums up the page is fine when its last column links each row to its page (`| Path | What it holds | Learn more |`)

Leave out:

- Validation rules, field caps and error codes ("refused with a 400", length caps, "refused rather than ignored"). An error the reader sees while trying the example is shown as printed, and a troubleshooting page lists the errors people really hit, by their message
- Internal mechanics the reader never touches: channel names, sync fingerprints, our staging clusters and test apps
- Raw HTTP paths when an SDK or the CLI does it. A call with no SDK method gets one curl block
- Client setup boilerplate in snippets: show the call
- Sentences that restate the code above them, and signposting ("The next section explains")
- Which SDK supports what "for now". When only some SDKs have a feature, one `<Admonition>` names them
- Bold lead-ins in bullets or prose (bold is for step titles), and hype ("amazed", "effortlessly")

## Only what works

- A page says only what a user can install and run today, and you saw work end to end: run every snippet, curl and command, against staging if needed. Reading the code confirms a name, not a behaviour
- "Which SDKs support X" means released packages (npm, PyPI, Maven Central, pub.dev, the released CLI), not source on `main`
- Not proven yet? Leave it out and ticket it. Don't caveat it ("not tested yet")

## Where things live

- Content: `getstream.io/content/docs`, a plain directory of the getstream.io repo (it was GetStream/docs-content). Its authoring conventions are in `content/docs/AGENTS.md`
- Pages: `agents/<framework>/*.md`; pages shared by every SDK go in `agents/_default/`
- Sidebars: `_sidebars/[agents][<framework>].json` (`baseURL`, `defaultLanguages`, `items` of `{ title, slug, markdown }`). `[agents][default].json` is the `/agents/docs/` home
- Framework slugs: `javascript`, `ios` (shown as Swift), `android` (Kotlin), `flutter` (Dart), `python`, `go-golang`, `dotnet-csharp`, `ruby`, `rust`, `php`. A new slug needs a label in `routing.ts` and a logo in `public/docs-assets/icons/`
- SDK switcher and product menu: `getstream.io/src/docs/utils/routing.ts` and `productMenu.ts`. A new sidebar must be reachable from them

## Writing

- The page H1 comes from the sidebar `title`, so don't put a `#` heading in the markdown
- Use `$framework` in links (`/agents/docs/$framework/quickstart/`) so shared pages work under every SDK
- Components: `<Cards>`, `<Card icon title description href>`, `<Admonition type="info">`, `<Tabs>`, `<Steps>`, mermaid fences. `icon` takes Remixicon names (an unknown name fails the build); `logo="go"` takes SDK logos
- Only ASCII, and no em dashes. Links are root-relative, and slugs are lowercase with hyphens

## Gotchas

- Every server SDK reads `agent.yaml` and syncs the directory in one request, skipping it when `.agent_sync` matches. They sync only when you call `sync` (Python `agent.sync()`, .NET `SyncAsync`); a session never syncs. Say which SDK a behaviour applies to
- Client SDKs (JavaScript in the browser, Swift, Android, Flutter) never sync or configure agents. Swift and browser JavaScript are handed a config id by the backend; Android and Flutter open an agent by its stored name
- `SyncRouters` rejects unknown keys in `routers/*.yaml` (including `description`)

## Preview and ship

- `npm run dev` in getstream.io (Node 24), then open `http://localhost:3000/agents/docs/<framework>/`. Don't run builds or checks unless asked

Docs live in the main site repo, typically located at workspace/getstream.io, under `content/docs`

Some general docs tips

- Keep it short
- Show examples before explaining details
- Write from the code, not from memory. Check the SDK (`sdks/<lang>`) and `acceleration/api/openapi.yaml` before documenting an API, key or default

## How a page reads

Write it so it needs no deslop pass. `agents/_default/02-agents/creating-an-agent.md` is the reference for how a page opens and flows, and Thierry's deslop commits in getstream.io (7ee27d28eb, 21c69fd256, edf81f51f2, 1d93015abe) show the cuts.

- Open with why the reader wants it and one real example, not a definition: "Your support agent shouldn't answer: Please solve the Navier-Stokes problem", not "A guardrail screens what a caller asks"
- Example first: the `agent.yaml` or the call, then the command to try it (`getstream agents test support --sync`) and a question to ask. Pick an example the reader can run as is, such as a connector the app owns rather than one each user signs in to. Then explain only what the example doesn't show
- Real example values (`dentist_ai`, "Northwind Pizza, what can I get you?", "What is your return policy?"), never `foo` or `my-thing`
- One or two sentences per paragraph, written like a person: "It returns the connection", not "The answer is the connection". Contractions are fine. State facts, not "should": "is configurable", not "should be configurable"
- Where there are options, recommend one and say when to pick the other: "We recommend each user's own account for personal data, and a shared account for company tools"
- One H2 per thing the reader wants to do. A fact lives on one page: detail that has its own page is cut to a link. End with `## Going further` and `<Cards>`
- Say what a feature can't do in a plain sentence, under `## Limitations` when there are several. A limit the reader can hit stays; a cap on a field goes
- A table that sums up the page is fine when its last column links each row to its page (`| Path | What it holds | Learn more |`)

- Validation rules, field caps and error codes ("refused with a 400", length caps, "refused rather than ignored"). An error the reader sees while trying the example is shown as printed, and a troubleshooting page lists the errors people really hit, by their message
- Internal mechanics the reader never touches: channel names, sync fingerprints, our staging clusters and test apps
- Raw HTTP paths when an SDK or the CLI does it. A call with no SDK method gets one curl block
- Client setup boilerplate in snippets: show the call
- Sentences that restate the code above them, and signposting ("The next section explains")
- Which SDK supports what "for now". When only some SDKs have a feature, one `<Admonition>` names them
- Bold lead-ins in bullets or prose (bold is for step titles), and hype ("amazed", "effortlessly")

- A page says only what a user can install and run today, and you saw work end to end: run every snippet, curl and command, against staging if needed. Reading the code confirms a name, not a behaviour

skills.body:
---
name: generative-ui
description: How an agent's interactive UI (OpenUI, A2UI) travels from the model to the apps - the agent.yaml `ui:` key and the prompt it compiles, the router's streaming splitter, the `ui_delta`/`ui_completed` socket frames, what is kept in Stream Chat, and LiveUI in the client SDKs. Read before changing any of them or debugging a card that is missing, stuck or jumps.
---

# Generative UI

An agent can answer with a card instead of text: a restaurant with its tables, a trip with a map.
The model writes the card as a program in a fenced block, the router splits it off its words as it
streams, and the apps render it with their own renderer (`stream-chat-react`'s `AIUIHost`,
`stream_chat_flutter_ai`, StreamChatAI). The router knows no UI format beyond OpenUI patches; it
carries the program as text.

```
model tokens
  -> agent: ui_stream.go splits UI from prose (before stage directions and TTS)
       -> prose: spoken on a call, written in chat
       -> UIDelta / UICompleted events
            -> session socket: ui_delta / ui_completed frames (no buffering)
            -> conversation: Stream Chat message custom.ai_ui (partial updates, then settled)
            -> chatlog: custom.ai_ui on a call's transcript message
  -> agent history keeps the UI block, so the model can patch it next turn
```

## The agent.yaml `ui:` key

`ui:` tells the model what it may draw. The SDK that loads the folder compiles it into a
`## Interactive UI Generation` section and syncs it as the config's `ui_instructions`, apart from
`instructions.md`, so the router sees only text. The output is deterministic, so the prompt
prefix stays cacheable across turns. The prompt is mixed mode: the model answers in prose and
adds a card only when it helps.

The router tells the model `ui_instructions` after the instructions (`session.Spec.prompt`),
unless the session was opened with `ui: false`, which a device may send. The router then omits
`ui_instructions`, so an app that shows no UI leaves the catalog out of every turn and can expect
prose; this does not prevent the model from producing UI blocks, which are still split off the
reply. The session row keeps the choice (`agent_sessions.no_ui`), so a reopened or forked
conversation is not told them either. Go and JavaScript write
`ui_instructions`. A renderer's own prompt pasted into `instructions.md` (`stream-chat-react`'s
`openUIInstructions` is OpenUI's, 53 KB, and says the entire reply must be openui-lang) can't be
turned off either and contradicts prose plus one block: use `ui:` instead.

```yaml
# agents/concierge/agent.yaml
name: concierge
llm: llm-fast
ui:
  format: openui            # the default, or a2ui
  keep: [CardHeader, Form, Chips, FollowUpBlock]   # built-ins to offer; their children come along
  components: ui/components.json   # default path; read when the file exists
  blueprints: ui/blueprints.yaml   # default path; read when the file exists
  patch_mode: true          # teach openui-patch for refining the previous card
  voice_ui: true            # a card on calls too, after one spoken sentence
  rules:
    - Always pair RestaurantCard with AvailabilityGauge when the wait is known.
```

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `format` | `openui`, the default, or `a2ui`. Anything else is refused. |
| `keep` | OpenUI: restricts the built-in catalog (`uiBuiltins` in `sdks/go/agents/ui.go`) to these names plus their required children (`Form` brings `FormControl`, `Buttons`, `Button`); `Card` is always in. A2UI: names the basic catalog's components and functions to offer, and nothing else comes along, as stream-chat-swift's own prompt generator does. Empty offers all of them. A name that is neither built in nor a custom component is refused. |
| `components` | The app's own components in the portable format every app reads (`UIComponents.json`): `name` (snake_case), `description`, `parameters` (JSON schema with `x-order`, the positional order), `events`, optional `slots`. Each becomes a PascalCase signature: `restaurant_card` -> `RestaurantCard(name: string, ...)`. |
| `blueprints` | A YAML list of `name`, `when`, `order`, `rules`, `example`. Each is a line telling the model which components, in which order, for which kind of ask. An `example` is a program in the format, checked at load so it renders as written: OpenUI for unknown components, too many arguments and undefined or orphan references, with the line of the problem; A2UI as stream-chat-swift's `A2UIProgram` checks it, for messages it can't read, components and properties the catalog doesn't have, missing required properties, children never defined, components nothing holds, cycles and nesting past 50. |
| `patch_mode` | OpenUI only: adds the rule to answer a refinement of the previous card with an `openui-patch` block of only the changed statements. Refused with `a2ui`, since only OpenUI patches are merged and an A2UI reply writes a new surface. |
| `voice_ui` | Changes the opening rule from "no UI block on a voice call" to "one spoken sentence, then the card". |
| `rules` | Appended as `### Brand & Design Rules`. |

Paths are relative to the agent directory and may not leave it (symlinks included); each file is
capped at 512 KiB.

Loaded by: Go (`sdks/go/agents/ui.go`, from `Load`, into `Folder.UIInstructions`) and JavaScript (`sdks/js/src/ui-catalog.ts`,
from `loadFolder` in `folder.ts`). Python, .NET, Ruby, Rust and PHP don't read `ui:` yet (see the
note at the end of the `sdk` skill), and the `getstream` CLI refuses it as an unknown key
(`cli/internal/agentrc/agentrc.go`, `KnownFields`), so `getstream agents sync` fails on it. The two compilers must produce the same bytes for the same
folder: `sdks/testdata/ui/concierge/` is compiled by a Go test and a JavaScript test, both held to
`sdks/testdata/ui/concierge.instructions.txt`, which Go writes: what the model is told, the
instructions and the UI joined by a blank line, as the router joins them. An SDK that adds `ui:` checks itself
against the same pair. `a2ui` is compiled by Go (`sdks/go/agents/ui_a2ui.go`) and JavaScript
(`sdks/js/src/ui-a2ui.ts`), both held to `sdks/testdata/ui/concierge-a2ui/` and
`concierge-a2ui.instructions.txt`. JavaScript parses this YAML by hand; it still differs from yaml.v3 on
escapes inside quoted strings (`'it''s'`), empty list items, and `ui:` written as a flow mapping.

## How the model writes UI

The compiled prompt asks for one short sentence, then the card in a ```` ```openui-lang ```` block,
`root = Card([...])` first so the shell streams at once. With `format: a2ui` the card is A2UI 1.0
messages in a ```` ```ui:a2ui@1.0 ```` block, one JSON object per line: a `createSurface` naming the
catalog `getstream.io:app-catalog`, the id the apps' A2UI renderers give the basic catalog with their
own components, then `updateComponents`, `root` first. The prompt is the one stream-chat-swift's
renderer writes for itself (`A2UIInstructions`): its protocol and guidelines, then the catalog as
JSON Schema, the basic catalog's components and functions that `keep` names beside the app's own,
each app component as the renderer has it (`PortableComponent`: its parameters as properties, its
events joining its description). `sdks/go/agents/a2ui/` holds the basic catalog and the protocol as
the renderer has them, which `a2ui/generate.sh` writes again from a stream-chat-swift checkout; a Go
test holds the catalog to the one in `swift_assistant/a2ui/instructions.md`, which the renderer
wrote, so regenerate both together. JavaScript carries the same three files as a module,
`sdks/js/src/generated/a2ui.ts`, which `npm run a2ui` in `sdks/js` writes from Go's copies; run it
after `generate.sh`, or a JavaScript test fails. The router's splitter
(`acceleration/internal/agent/ui_stream.go`) reads:

- ```` ```openui-lang ```` and ```` ```openui-patch ```` (OpenUI, replace or patch)
- ```` ```ui:<format>[@<version>][+patch] ````, such as `ui:a2ui@1.0`

A block opens only on a fence at the start of a line. The splitter runs on every agent's reply,
UI or not, so prose that mentions UI (`wrap the list in a <ui> element`) stays prose. Only the
first UI block of a reply is its UI. A fence split across tokens is held back until it is known,
never shown as prose for a moment.

A patch is statements that replace those with the same identifier, add new ones at the end, or
remove one with `name = null` (a `$variable` set to `null` stays). `MergeOpenUIStatements`
(`conversation/ui.go`) and its copies in `sdks/js/src/conversation.ts` and
`sdks/dart/.../core/conversation.dart` do the merge.

## In the router

- `agent.go` runs every chunk through `uiStream.Add` before stage directions and the TTS
  chunker, so `[header, map]` isn't stripped as a direction and a call never reads UI code
  aloud. It sends `UIDelta` as UI arrives and `UICompleted` when the block closes, and keeps the
  block in the assistant's history (`HistoryBlock`) so the model can patch it.
- `api/sessionws.go` writes them to the session socket with no timer:
  - `{"type":"ui_delta","turn_id","format","version"?,"mode"?,"delta"}`
  - `{"type":"ui_completed","turn_id","format","version"?,"mode"?,"content"}`

  `mode` is left out for `replace`. A delta is the next piece of the raw block; a patch's delta is
  the patch, not the merged program.
- `conversation/conversation.go` folds them into the reply's `custom.ai_ui`
  (`{v, format, version?, status: "streaming"|"complete", content}`), merging a patch onto the
  last completed UI of the conversation (seeded from history when it reopens). Stream Chat gets
  partial updates every `answerEvery` (150ms) while the reply is written and the settled UI when
  it finishes. `conversation_updated` broadcasts for text deltas are coalesced to the same 150ms;
  one held back is sent from the live loop's tick (`publishHeld`), so the last words before a
  pause reach watchers without waiting for the next event.
- A UI that would take the message's custom data over 48 KiB is left out of that write
  (`fitUI`): the reply keeps its words and has no card.
- `chatlog/chatlog.go` keeps `custom.ai_ui` on a call's transcript message, so a card drawn on a
  call is in the chat afterwards.

## In the client SDKs

- `Turn.ui` (JavaScript, Dart, Swift and Kotlin `TurnUI`) is the turn's UI from the socket:
  `format`, `version`, `status` (Swift's and Kotlin's `isStreaming`), `content`, with patches merged onto the transcript's previous
  card. A patch with no card before it in this transcript, as after a reload, sets no `ui`:
  Stream Chat's copy, which the router merged, is the one to show.
- `LiveUI` lays the socket's UI over the Stream Chat reply while it is written, so the card draws
  at socket speed instead of at Chat's 150ms. JavaScript's `AgentChat` applies it to every
  message it hands out; in Dart, the app calls `liveUI.observe` and `liveUI.overlay` itself
  (`flutter_assistant/lib/agent_chat.dart`), and in Swift too (`swift_assistant`'s
  `AgentChat.swift`, which publishes each change inside an animation) and Kotlin
  (`android_assistant`'s `AgentTransport.kt`, which redraws the conversation when `observe` says
  what shows changed). Swift's, JavaScript's, Kotlin's and Dart's `TurnUI.content` also hold back
  the OpenUI statement no newline has ended yet while it streams, so a card grows a part at a time
  rather than reflowing with every delta, and `LiveUI` leaves a reply its text until one
  statement is finished. The rules, which keep a card from jumping:
  - A reply that names its turn (`support_runtime.turn_id`) shows only that turn's UI.
  - Before its turn id is in Chat, the newest generating reply shows `latest()`: the newest
    turn's UI, only when that turn is the agent's. The person's question (`said`) and a new
    `responding` turn clear it, so a new reply never shows the card before it.
  - Once Chat says the reply is written (`generating` false) or its `ai_ui` is complete, what
    Chat stored shows.

## Debugging

- Card never shows: is it in the reply's `custom.ai_ui` in Stream Chat? If not, did the model
  write a fence the splitter reads (router logs, or the `ui_delta` frames on the socket)? Was it
  over 48 KiB?
- Card shows UI code as text, or a call reads it aloud: the block didn't open as UI, usually a
  fence info string the splitter doesn't know.
- Card blanks or jumps between turns: check the `LiveUI` rules above against the message's
  `support_runtime.turn_id`, `generating` and `ai_ui.status`.
- A component the model places but the app can't render: compare the agent's `ui/components.json`
  and `keep` with what the app's renderer registers. Flutter's `OpenUIRenderer` doesn't render
  every built-in yet.

## Known gaps

- The agent, the conversation and the chatlog each keep their own "previous UI" for patches; a
  patch after a tool round can be merged onto a different base in each.
- An interrupted call reply can leave a half-written `ai_ui` with `status: "streaming"` in the
  transcript, and a refused one is saved with its UI.
- The UI block is in the assistant's history `Content`, which `lastAssistantSaid`, the echo
  filter and the flow controller read as speech.
- `ui_delta` and `ui_completed` aren't declared in `internal/api/handwritten.go` yet.

  chunker, so `[header, map]` isn't stripped as a direction and a call never reads UI code
  aloud. It sends `UIDelta` as UI arrives and `UICompleted` when the block closes, and keeps the
  block in the assistant's history (`HistoryBlock`) so the model can patch it.
- `api/sessionws.go` writes them to the session socket with no timer:
  - `{"type":"ui_delta","turn_id","format","version"?,"mode"?,"delta"}`
  - `{"type":"ui_completed","turn_id","format","version"?,"mode"?,"content"}`

  `mode` is left out for `replace`. A delta is the next piece of the raw block; a patch's delta is
  the patch, not the merged program.
- `conversation/conversation.go` folds them into the reply's `custom.ai_ui`
  (`{v, format, version?, status: "streaming"|"complete", content}`), merging a patch onto the
  last completed UI of the conversation (seeded from history when it reopens). Stream Chat gets
  partial updates every `answerEvery` (150ms) while the reply is written and the settled UI when
  it finishes. `conversation_updated` broadcasts for text deltas are coalesced to the same 150ms;
  one held back is sent from the live loop's tick (`publishHeld`), so the last words before a
  pause reach watchers without waiting for the next event.
- A UI that would take the message's custom data over 48 KiB is left out of that write
  (`fitUI`): the reply keeps its words and has no card.
- `chatlog/chatlog.go` keeps `custom.ai_ui` on a call's transcript message, so a card drawn on a
  call is in the chat afterwards.

## In the client SDKs

- `Turn.ui` (JavaScript, Dart, Swift and Kotlin `TurnUI`) is the turn's UI from the socket:
  `format`, `version`, `status` (Swift's and Kotlin's `isStreaming`), `content`, with patches merged onto the transcript's previous
  card. A patch with no card before it in this transcript, as after a reload, sets no `ui`:
  Stream Chat's copy, which the router merged, is the one to show.
- `LiveUI` lays the socket's UI over the Stream Chat reply while it is written, so the card draws
  at socket speed instead of at Chat's 150ms. JavaScript's `AgentChat` applies it to every
  message it hands out; in Dart, the app calls `liveUI.observe` and `liveUI.overlay` itself
  (`flutter_assistant/lib/agent_chat.dart`), and in Swift too (`swift_assistant`'s
  `AgentChat.swift`, which publishes each change inside an animation) and Kotlin
  (`android_assistant`'s `AgentTransport.kt`, which redraws the conversation when `observe` says
  what shows changed). Swift's, JavaScript's, Kotlin's and Dart's `TurnUI.content` also hold back
  the OpenUI statement no newline has ended yet while it streams, so a card grows a part at a time
  rather than reflowing with every delta, and `LiveUI` leaves a reply its text until one
  statement is finished. The rules, which keep a card from jumping:
  - A reply that names its turn (`support_runtime.turn_id`) shows only that turn's UI.
  - Before its turn id is in Chat, the newest generating reply shows `latest()`: the newest
    turn's UI, only when that turn is the agent's. The person's question (`said`) and a new
    `responding` turn clear it, so a new reply never shows the card before it.
  - Once Chat says the reply is written (`generating` false) or its `ai_ui` is complete, what
    Chat stored shows.

## Debugging

- Card never shows: is it in the reply's `custom.ai_ui` in Stream Chat? If not, did the model
  write a fence the splitter reads (router logs, or the `ui_delta` frames on the socket)? Was it
  over 48 KiB?
- Card shows UI code as text, or a call reads it aloud: the block didn't open as UI, usually a
  fence info string the splitter doesn't know.
- Card blanks or jumps between turns: check the `LiveUI` rules above against the message's
  `support_runtime.turn_id`, `generating` and `ai_ui.status`.
- A component the model places but the app can't render: compare the agent's `ui/components.json`
  and `keep` with what the app's renderer registers. Flutter's `OpenUIRenderer` doesn't render
  every built-in yet.

## Known gaps

- The agent, the conversation and the chatlog each keep their own "previous UI" for patches; a
  patch after a tool round can be merged onto a different base in each.
- An interrupted call reply can leave a half-written `ai_ui` with `status: "streaming"` in the
  transcript, and a refused one is saved with its UI.
- The UI block is in the assistant's history `Content`, which `lastAssistantSaid`, the echo
  filter and the flow controller read as speech.
- `ui_delta` and `ui_completed` aren't declared in `internal/api/handwritten.go` yet.

---
name: go-testing
description: How Go tests are written in acceleration/ and sdks/go. Read before adding a test or a test suite.
---

# Go testing

## Rules

- Group tests in a testify suite (`suite.Suite`). Shared setup lives in the suite, in one place.
- Never mock. A provider is a stub registered in its router's registry, or the real one behind an integration build tag; everything else is real.
- Test behaviour through the outside. Assert on outputs and state, never on which method was called.
- Name a test as the sentence it proves: `TestAnIdAnotherSessionHasIsRefused`.
- Avoid table tests, common as they are in Go. Write one test per behaviour, each named for what it proves, and put what they share in the suite or a helper.
- Anything that needs Postgres, Redis or a provider's API starts with `//go:build integration` and skips, rather than fails, when what it needs is not configured.
- Outside a suite, check with `require`, never `testify/assert`: a failed check stops the test there.
- A unit test that waits on a real timer runs in a `testing/synctest` bubble, where the timer fires at once (`AgentSuite.onFakeClock` in `internal/agent`). Make the goroutines and channels the test waits on inside the bubble: a goroutine that waits on something from outside stops the fake clock. A test that waits on network I/O stays on the real clock, with or without a build tag (an integration test, or a unit test on a local socket): a wait on network I/O stops the fake clock. A test that needs real time between two events also stays on the real clock: on the fake clock, work that does not wait takes no time.
- Every skip says what keeps the test from running: the env var or tool that is missing, or what the provider cannot do. A skip with no such reason ("pending fixture") is a test to fix or delete.

## Which kind of test

Read the file for what you are testing:

- [controllers.md](controllers.md): HTTP operations in `internal/api`, run against the whole router with `RouterSuite`. Who may call an endpoint, whose a resource is, fixtures, parallel suites.
- [store.md](store.md): the models and queries in `internal/store`, run against Postgres with `StoreSuite`.
- [ai-routing.md](ai-routing.md): STT, TTS, STS, LLM, search and the other AI providers and their routers. One shared suite per kind of AI that every provider embeds.

## Before you push

Checks a reviewer runs and an author often skips:

- Mutate every rule you added, at every call site, in a scratch copy: delete the clause, make the condition `true`, empty a migration's Down. A mutant no test fails is a missing test.
- Run the touched suites on the merge with current `origin/main`. CI's green is from the `main` it ran on.
- An entry added to a shared list (`dataTables`, `importedModels`, `usageIndexes`) changes every reader of that list: read each one.
- Round-trip an id that moves, is derived or is replayed: A to B to A, and a second run, each end as one row.
- A shipped migration never runs again: change it in a new one.
- A new migration is expand-only: it drops or renames nothing the release before still reads or writes.
- A migration's lock timeout is in the `go` skill's `store.md` ("Which database"). Its version slot is in the `parallel-agents` skill ("Migration versions").
- Work moved onto `context.WithoutCancel` takes its follow-on calls (billing, the cache drop) with it.
- A fix covers every path to the same data: each writer, and each copy of it (a cache, `data_changes`).

skills.desc: How Go is written in this repo - errors (errors.md), state (store.md), logging (logging.md), spans, context, goroutines, comments. Read before writing or changing Go code.
skills.body:
---
name: go
description: How Go is written in this repo - errors (errors.md), state (store.md), logging (logging.md), spans, context, goroutines, comments. Read before writing or changing Go code.
paths:
  - "**/*.go"
---

# Go

These rules are the choices this repo makes. General Go style is not repeated here.

## Rules

- Check the `go` directive of the nearest `go.mod` before you use a newer feature. The 8 modules pin different versions: `acceleration` is on 1.27, `tui` on 1.26, `sdks/go` on 1.25.
- Errors: read `errors.md` beside this file before you make, wrap, log or answer one. In short: `stack.Wrap` once where it enters, handle it once, and never send its text to a caller.
- Log with `log/slog`. Put the data in key-value fields, not in the message: `logger.Warn("could not store an MCP event subscription", "subscription", sub.ID, "error", err)`.
- An HTTP handler returns its error and does not log it. `withRequestLog` (`internal/api/server.go`) logs the error with its stack, and a 5xx at error level (see `errors.md` and "HTTP API" in AGENTS.md).
- Name a span in lowercase dotted words, the area then the step: `appconfig.read`, `quota.allow`, `turn.llm`.
- Pass `ctx context.Context` as the first parameter. A service may hold a lifetime context made in `New`, with its cancel function, as `channels.Service` does.
- Pass the caller's context on; never start from `context.Background()` where one is reachable. A new root drops the trace span and the attribution, so the work shows up in no trace and bills no one. Work that outlives the caller (a goroutine, a deferred cleanup) takes `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` and its own timeout. An object that outlives the request that made it keeps `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` in a `ctx` field, as `agent.Agent` and `session.Session` do; never the request's context itself, which is cancelled. `Background` is right only at a root: `main`, a lifetime context in `New` or `Start`, a queue worker. Tests use `t.Context()`; a `Cleanup` runs after it is cancelled, so it uses `context.WithoutCancel(t.Context())`.
- Start no goroutine in `init()` or in a constructor. Start it in `Start(ctx)` or `Run(ctx)`, as `chatlog.Log.Start` does.
- In the code of a call (the agent, the floor control, the harness, the speech and model providers and their routers), start a goroutine with `goroutine.Go(ctx, fn)` (`internal/goroutine`), not with `go`. Give it the context of the call. Then a panic in the goroutine stops only that call, not the router and all its calls. `TestEveryGoroutineOfACallStartsThroughGo` (`internal/goroutine/guard_test.go`) fails on a `go` statement in these packages.
- Only the goroutine that owns a channel closes it, and it closes it once. A goroutine that can still send after the owner stops does not send on that channel: it selects on the owner's done channel or `ctx.Done()`. A send on a closed channel and a second close both panic. The backend tests run with `-race`, which finds the races that lead to these panics.
- Return a nil slice for "none". A JSON response is the exception: it sends `[]`, not `null`.
- Query Postgres through bun's builders (`NewSelect`, `NewInsert ... On("CONFLICT ...")`, `NewUpdate`, `NewDelete`) on a model, not `NewRaw` or `ExecContext` with a SQL string. A table without a model gets a small unexported one. An insert lists `.Column(...)` so database defaults still apply. Keep SQL raw only where the builder cannot write it or would change what it does: advisory locks, `SET LOCAL`, DDL and catalog reads, `INSERT ... SELECT`, `WITH RECURSIVE`, window and `GROUPING SETS` queries, a statement whose SQL text a test matches, and jsonb that must refuse `\u0000` (bun stores it as text).
- Defensive code (a retry, a fallback, a second check) gets a comment that names the concrete threat: concurrent writers, a network failure the caller retries, malformed input. If you cannot name one, do not add it (see "Code style" in AGENTS.md).

## Comments

- A comment says why, once, in the fewest words. Do not narrate what the code does.
- Write no new ticket, PR or plan reference in a comment: it belongs in the commit and the PR. Leave the ones already there.
- A link to a public, stable source (an RFC, an engine's documented limits) is fine. The comment still states the fact.

## Other skills

- Errors, wrapping, logging and what reaches a caller: `errors.md` beside this file.
- Postgres and Redis state, models, repositories and validation: `store.md` beside this file.
- When to log and at which level, field names, redaction, and a value a tool reads back from a log: `logging.md` beside this file.
- Tests: the `go-testing` skill (`.claude/skills/go-testing/SKILL.md`).
- Timeouts on outbound calls and streams: the `security` skill (`.claude/skills/security/go.md`, "Abuse limits").
- N+1 queries and batch sizes: the `loop_performance_bench` skill (`.claude/skills/loop_performance_bench/SKILL.md`).

---
name: good_morning
description: Pull and merge the latest code across the workspace repos (chat, Vision-Agents, artemis-impl, getstream.io, volt-dashboard). Use when the user says good morning or asks to sync their repos. Checks the team Slack channel and summarises new messages from the last day. 
---

# Good morning

Bring every repo below up to date. Run them in parallel; each is independent.

| Repo | Branch | Then merge |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `~/workspace/chat` | `master` | |
| `~/workspace/Vision-Agents` | `main` | |
| `~/workspace/artemis-impl` | current | |
| `~/workspace/getstream.io` | `main` | |
| `~/workspace/volt-dashboard` | `main` | |
| `~/workspace/cli` | `main` | |

For each repo:

```bash
cd ~/workspace/<repo>
git fetch origin --prune
git checkout <branch>                         # only when the table names one
git pull --no-rebase --autostash              # skip if the branch has no upstream
git merge --autostash --no-edit origin/<base> # only when the table names one
```

## Rules

- Merge, never rebase, and never force anything.
- Uncommitted work stays put: `--autostash` stashes and reapplies it. If `checkout` refuses
  because of local changes, stop for that repo and report it rather than stashing by hand.
- On a merge conflict, run `git merge --abort` and report the conflicting files. Don't resolve
  them unless the user asks. Once resolved, `git commit` reapplies the autostash itself; never
  `git stash pop` afterwards, which would pop an unrelated older stash.
- If reapplying the autostash conflicts, git keeps it in `git stash list`. Leave the conflicted
  files as they are and report them.
- In `getstream.io`, `content/docs` is now a plain directory of the repo. If an old nested
  checkout of docs-content is still there, the pull refuses to overwrite it: stop and ask, since
  that checkout may hold unmerged work.
- Don't push.

## Report

One line per repo: branch, how many commits came in (`git rev-list --count ORIG_HEAD..HEAD`
or compare `HEAD` before and after), and any conflict or skipped step.

As part of your report, check the team's #video-ai channel to summarise messages in the last 12 hours, keep it simple and a bulletpoint format of important topics such as new examples, customer issues to check on, etc. If slack is not connected, prompt the user to set it up.

skills.name: integrate_new_models
skills.desc: Find the models worth adding with the new_models skill, then build support for each one in its own branch and open a draft PR per model.
skills.body:
---
name: integrate_new_models
description: Find the models worth adding with the new_models skill, then build support for each one in its own branch and open a draft PR per model.
---

# From "we should have this" to a PR per model

[new_models](../new_models/SKILL.md) says what is missing. This does the work, one model at a
time, one branch at a time, so each lands as a PR that can be judged on its own.

## 1. Get the list

Run [new_models](../new_models/SKILL.md) and keep its report. It has already dropped anything
in [`router.yaml`](../../../acceleration/internal/routing/router.yaml), so what is left is the
work. Drop anything else the report cannot give an API id and a docs page for — an integration
cannot be written against a blog post.

## 2. Decide how big each one is

Two very different jobs wear the same words. Before dispatching anything, check whether the
vendor already has a package for that modality — `internal/tts/<vendor>`, `internal/stt/<vendor>`,
`internal/llm/<vendor>`, `internal/sts/<vendor>`:

- **The package exists.** A new model from a vendor we already speak is usually a `router.yaml`
  entry plus whatever the new model does that the old one could not. Small.
- **The package does not exist.** A new vendor, or a modality we have never asked that vendor
  for, is a provider package, its registry entry, three test files and the config. Gemini TTS is
  this even though we already talk to Gemini for STT and speech-to-speech.

Say which of the two each model is in the report at the end. It is the difference between an
afternoon and a week, and it is the first thing a reviewer wants to know.

## 3. One subagent per vendor per modality

Dispatch a subagent per unit of work, in parallel, each with the model `claude-opus-5-5-medium`.
Cloud subagents based on the working branch are the way to do it: each takes its own branch and
VM, and the cloud environment carries the vendor API keys as secrets, so the integration tests
can actually run. Locally, `best-of-n-runner` gives the same isolation through a worktree.

The unit is one vendor's models in one modality, not one model. Three OpenAI LLMs are one PR,
because three PRs editing the same lines of the `llm:` block conflict with each other and none
of them can be merged on its own. Two vendors are always two PRs even in the same modality.

skills.desc: Consider changes to the llm standardization/interface
skills.body:
---
name: llm-interface
description: Consider changes to the llm standardization/interface
---

# LLM Interface

Start by reviewing the latest changes here:
- OpenAI: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latest-model
- Claude: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/working-with-messages
- Gemini: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/latest-model
- Grok: https://docs.x.ai/developers/model-capabilities/text/generate-text

## What to standardize

The feature set for voice AI definitely needs to be standardized. 
- Text input into streaming response
- Usage / cost tracking
- Cache control
- Conversation persistence (use store:true or similar systems when available)
- Tool calling

This requires text response creation to be standardized

But in general it's good to standardize more. This makes it easier to switch between models

## What not to standardize

- Reasoning levels are different per model. They also don't map cleanly to each other. So lets just keep track for each LLM what's valid

## Cache Standards



## Guidelines

You can find the llm.go LLM interface
We mostly want to follow OpenAI's naming conventions where possible since they are the biggest in non-coding AI usage.

For openAI (but probably not for others) there are performance benefits to the websocket mode
https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/websocket-mode


### History



### Cache control

CachePolicy:
- TTL (0 for no caching)

Breakpoints: 
- For models that support this we should automatically handle the setting of a break point after the instructions
- With a shared per agent config cache (so instructions are reused)
- While having it set to implicit mode so the customer conversation grows

skills.name: loop_performance_bench
skills.desc: Run the router performance loop - profile locally, fix the top cost, cut needless API, SQL and Redis calls, deploy to the benchmark cluster, ramp, record agents held and $/voice-minute, repeat ten times. Use when asked to run the performance loop, to improve how many agents one router holds, or to lower the hosting cost per voice minute.
skills.body:
---
name: loop_performance_bench
description: Run the router performance loop - profile locally, fix the top cost, cut needless API, SQL and Redis calls, deploy to the benchmark cluster, ramp, record agents held and $/voice-minute, repeat ten times. Use when asked to run the performance loop, to improve how many agents one router holds, or to lower the hosting cost per voice minute.
---

# The performance loop

Ten rounds of: find what the router spends its CPU and round trips on, fix the biggest one,
prove it on the benchmark cluster, and write down what moved. Read the
`performance_benchmark` skill first: this one assumes its setup, its break rules and its
report. `performance_benchmark/findings.md` holds what earlier loops found and fixed; read
it so you do not chase a cost that is already gone.

Follow the [benchmark rules](../../../AGENTS.md#benchmark-rules). Ten rounds are a budget,
not a quota: keep negative results and revert changes that do not pay for themselves.

What each round reports: **agents held** on the fixed two-node benchmark router, **reply
p50/p95** at that step, **router mCPU per agent**, and **hosting $ per voice minute**:

```
$/voice-min = 2 nodes × $0.154/h ÷ agents held ÷ 60
```

Only Go hosting counts: the mocks bill nothing, and model cost is not the router's.

## 0. Once, before round 1

- Work on a branch off `main` (`thierry/router-perf-loop` style). One commit per fix,
  `perf(<scope>): ...`.
- The benchmark router must stay at **2 pods on 2 n4a-standard-4 nodes** (HPA 2/2 in
  `shards/us-east1-acceleration/accelerate-benchmark.yaml` in the private infra repo, with
  `router.mockProviders: true` and `router.pprofAddr`). Never let it autoscale past two
  nodes: the cost per minute is only comparable on fixed hardware.
- Bring up the callers: `kubectl apply -f performance_benchmark/cluster/perfbench.yaml`, then
  `performance_benchmark/cluster/setup.sh`.
- Round 0 is the baseline: deploy the branch as it is and ramp (step 4) before changing
  anything.

## 1. Profile locally

```bash
performance_benchmark/loop/local.sh round-3 32 90s
```

It builds the router, runs it on `:8081` with the mocks and pprof against the compose
Postgres and Redis, holds 32 conversations, and writes CPU, allocs, mutex, block and
goroutine profiles to `performance_benchmark/out/round-3/`. Then:

```bash
go tool pprof -top -nodecount=40 performance_benchmark/out/round-3/cpu.pb.gz
go tool pprof -top -sample_index=alloc_space performance_benchmark/out/round-3/allocs.pb.gz
```

Bucket the CPU before choosing: Opus encode and decode, SRTP and UDP syscalls, GC, the
scheduler, HTTP and websocket, TLS, the SDK's stats, the voice logic, Postgres and Redis.
GC high means allocations: fix the top `alloc_space` entry, not GC. Count goroutines per
agent in `goroutine.txt`: a few hundred extra timers or loops per agent is a cost too.

Prefer the cluster profile from the last round (step 4) when there is one: 32 agents on a
laptop hides what only shows at 512.

## 2. Review the calls each request makes

Every round, also look at the round trips, not only the CPU. A query or Redis command
saved runs on every turn of every agent, and Postgres and Redis are shared by every pod.

Count them on the local router. `local.sh` names its Postgres connections `perfloop`, so
turn on statement logging, watch Redis, and run it with one agent:

```bash
docker exec vision-agents-postgres-1 psql -U postgres -c "ALTER SYSTEM SET log_statement='all'" \
  -c "ALTER SYSTEM SET log_line_prefix='%m [%a] %p '" -c "SELECT pg_reload_conf()"
docker exec vision-agents-redis-1 redis-cli monitor > /tmp/redis-monitor.log &
performance_benchmark/loop/local.sh calls 1 60s
docker logs --since 2m vision-agents-postgres-1 2>&1 | grep '\[perfloop\].*statement:'
```

Take an idle minute first so background work (health pings, asynq, sweeps) can be
subtracted, and split the log by the request that made each statement. Postgres prints the
backend pid after the application name, which separates a sweep's transaction from a
request's. `MONITOR` shows each client's address: the native router connects through the
Docker gateway, so filter on that address to drop a dockerised router's traffic. It also
lists pipelined commands one by one, so read the code to tell a pipeline from separate round
trips. Put both settings back afterwards
(`ALTER SYSTEM RESET log_statement; ALTER SYSTEM RESET log_line_prefix; SELECT pg_reload_conf()`)
and stop the monitor.

Count at least: `createSession`, `createResponse` (a whole turn), `startSessionVoice`, and
one voice turn. Then, for each, ask:

- **Repeated reads.** The same row read twice in one request, or on every turn when it
  changes once a session: read it once and pass it down, or cache it in the session.
- **N+1.** A query per item in a loop: one query with `= ANY($1)` or a join. A batch split
  into chunks takes its chunk size from evidence: the engine's limit (PostgreSQL takes at
  most 65,535 bind parameters in one statement: the Bind message counts them in an Int16,
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/protocol-message-formats.html) and the input range
  the request validation allows. Not from gut feel or another constant. State the reasoning
  in the constant's doc comment and in the PR.
- **Transactions that need not be.** A single insert wrapped in its own transaction, or an
  advisory lock taken per row: batch the rows, or take the lock once.
- **Writes on the hot path.** A log or usage row written synchronously on every turn: buffer
  it and flush in batches off the turn.
- **Redis round trips.** Several commands one after another on the same request: one
  `Pipeline()`/`TxPipelined()`, or a Lua script when a later command depends on an earlier
  result. `HGETALL` per item in a loop: pipeline them or keep one hash.
- **Polling.** A `PING` or health read per request or per second per agent: share one
  checker per process.
- **Outbound API calls.** The same call to Stream or a provider on every turn: reuse the
  connection (TLS session cache, keep-alive) and cache what does not change during a call.

Record the counts before and after in the round's findings. A test that the request still
writes and returns the same thing is the evidence it still works; the count is the evidence
it mattered.

## 3. Fix one thing

The largest cost from step 1 or step 2, one per round. Prove it locally: a
`go test -bench` on the hot function (`-benchmem`, `-count 6`) for CPU and allocations, and
the package's tests, including its integration tests where they exist (`go-testing`
skill). Fixes in the WebRTC SDK go to `getstream-go-webrtc` first; bump `acceleration`,
`benchmark` and `performance_benchmark` to it afterwards.

## 4. Deploy and ramp

Deploy the branch to the benchmark release (`deploy` skill):

```bash
cd ../chat/infra && source ~/.config/rocky/gcp.env
./cli/rocky fastdeploy --service accelerate-benchmark
./cli/rocky fastdeploy --service accelerate-benchmark --status
```

Then ramp and profile the top step in parallel:

```bash
cd performance_benchmark
cluster/run.sh round-3 4 1024 60s | tee out/round-3.log
loop/profile.sh round-3 512 20      # in a second shell
```

`run.sh` ends the previous generation's calls and waits a minute first; never ramp onto a
router still draining the last run, its CPU lands in yours. Rerun `cluster/setup.sh` first
if `performance_benchmark/` or `sdks/go` changed.

## 5. Record

From `out/round-<n>/report.json`: agents held, what broke the next step, reply p50/p95,
router cores at the held step and mCPU per agent, $/voice-minute, and the audio score at the
held step (`audio`: SNR and the share broken). A fix that holds more agents while the SNR
falls or glitches climb is trading quality for capacity; say so. Compare with the
previous round:

```bash
go run -tags webrtc ./cmd/perfbench compare out/round-2 out/round-3
```

One run moves by up to 10%. When a round sits at the edge (p95 just over the 3 s bar),
run it again before calling it a regression. If a fix made things worse, revert it and
say so; a round with no gain is still a round.

## 6. After ten rounds

- Add a section to `performance_benchmark/findings.md`: a row per round (fix, held, p95,
  mCPU per agent, $/voice-minute) and what is still the largest cost.
- A chart of agents held, latency and cost across rounds, and a draft PR (`pr` skill).
- `kubectl delete -f performance_benchmark/cluster/perfbench.yaml`: the caller pod holds its
  own node until it is gone.

  mCPU per agent, $/voice-minute) and what is still the largest cost.

skills.desc: Migrate a voice or text agent from LiveKit, Retell, Vapi, Pipecat, Decagon, Sierra AI, GPT Live, or Deepgram Agents to a Stream accelerate agent. Use when the user asks to migrate, port, convert, or rewrite an agent from one of those platforms, or hands over a competitor agent's code, dashboard export, or API object.
skills.body:
---
name: migrate-to-accelerate
description: Migrate a voice or text agent from LiveKit, Retell, Vapi, Pipecat, Decagon, Sierra AI, GPT Live, or Deepgram Agents to a Stream accelerate agent. Use when the user asks to migrate, port, convert, or rewrite an agent from one of those platforms, or hands over a competitor agent's code, dashboard export, or API object.
---

# Migrate to accelerate

An accelerate agent is a folder, not a vendor object:

```
<name>/
  agent.yaml        # name, description, mode, stt/tts/sts/llm/voice, greeting, channels
  instructions.md   # the system prompt
  guardrail.md      # optional: what the agent will and will not answer
  knowledge/        # documents and urls.yaml the agent looks things up in
  skills/<name>.md  # work handed to a slower, smarter model (frontmatter: description, deadline)
  simulations/      # optional: test conversations
  <name>.py         # Agent(config="<name>", llm=stream.Accelerated(config="<name>", ...))
```

`agent.yaml` refuses unknown keys. Only send keys from the mapping tables here and in the
reference for the source platform; never carry a competitor field name across hoping it works.
The folder name, the directory, and `name:` in `agent.yaml` are the same name, and it must
be unique in the app: syncing a second agent under an existing name overwrites that config.

## First: read the right reference

Read exactly one of these before mapping anything, plus this file:

- LiveKit: [references/livekit.md](references/livekit.md)
- Retell: [references/retell.md](references/retell.md)
- Vapi: [references/vapi.md](references/vapi.md)
- Pipecat: [references/pipecat.md](references/pipecat.md)
- Decagon: [references/decagon.md](references/decagon.md)
- Sierra AI: [references/sierra.md](references/sierra.md)
- GPT Live: [references/gpt-live.md](references/gpt-live.md)
- Deepgram Agents: [references/deepgram-agents.md](references/deepgram-agents.md)

Then set up with the CLI skill at https://getstream.io/SKILL-agents.md (`getstream init`,
`getstream agents init --template voice|text`, `getstream docs` for anything not covered
here). For Stream Chat, Video, or Moderation work the migration touches, use the Stream
skills at https://www.skills.sh/getstream/agent-skills/stream.

## Workflow

1. **Inventory the source.** Get the whole agent, not the screenshot: code repo, dashboard
   export, or API object; every tool definition; knowledge sources; phone/SIP setup;
   webhooks; dynamic variables; guardrails and eval suites. Ask for what is missing.
   Vendor ids, secrets, and webhook signing keys are never copied into the output.
2. **Map config** with the shared table below and the platform reference. Write the folder:
   `getstream agents init <name> --template voice` (or `text`) creates `agents/<name>/`
   (with editor schemas alongside in `agents/`), then replace its files. Sync and test
   accept a path to that folder; if you move it, drop the `$schema` comment line from
   `agent.yaml`.
3. **Map tools** (rules below), **knowledge** (documents into `knowledge/`, URL sources
   into `knowledge/urls.yaml`), and **integrations** (catalog and custom connectors under
   `connectors:` in `agent.yaml`; phone numbers and messaging lines under `channels:`).
4. **Sync and test.** `getstream agents sync <path>` then
   `echo "Where is order NW-1001?" | getstream agents test <name>` (stdin lines in a
   non-interactive terminal). Fix what the sync refuses; do not silence it by dropping
   fields silently. A session that refuses to start with `unknown target` means a model
   field names something unserved: go back to `ListRoutes`, do not retry spellings.
   `agents test` runs the stored config only: Python `register_function` tools in the
   entry point do not execute there. Validate tools by running the Python agent joined
   to a router (`STREAM_ACCELERATION_URL`), or report them as untested code. A tool that
   must work without Python running needs a connector (catalog or custom) instead.
5. **Report.** End with three lists: migrated, approximated (and how it differs), and
   no equivalent. A silent drop is a failed migration.

## Shared mapping

| Source concept | Accelerate target |
| --- | --- |
| Agent name, description | `agent.yaml` `name`, `description` |
| System prompt / instructions / general prompt | `instructions.md` |
| Who speaks first, first message | `greeting: {text: ..., mode: exact}` in `agent.yaml`; model-varied greeting is `mode: variation` |
| Cascaded pipeline: STT model | `stt: <provider>/<model>` in `agent.yaml`, or `Accelerated(stt=...)` |
| Cascaded pipeline: LLM | `llm: <provider>/<model>` or a capability shortcut such as `llm-fast`; or `Accelerated(model=...)` |
| Cascaded pipeline: TTS model + voice | `tts: <provider>/<model>`, `voice: <provider voice id>` |
| Speech-to-speech / realtime model | `sts: <provider>/<model>` (empty `sts: ""` takes the backend default); no separate STT/TTS |
| Function tool that runs your code | `@agent.llm.register_function(description=...)` in the Python entry point; the backend calls it back mid-conversation |
| Hosted/built-in tool (end call, transfer) | No tool needed for end/hangup; transfers and other platform actions go in `instructions.md` or a skill. See the platform reference |
| Procedure / workflow / AOP / state machine | A `skills/<name>.md` (description + instructions for the subagent), referenced from `instructions.md` |
| Tool that is an HTTPS call to a third-party system | A catalog connector (`connectors:` in `agent.yaml`, app or per-user connection); a plain webhook-style tool becomes a Python function that makes the call |
| MCP server given by URL (inline in the source config) | A custom connector plus a binding, never `mcp_servers:` or `plugins:` (the SDKs refuse both). See "MCP servers by URL" below |
| Knowledge base documents | Files in `knowledge/` |
| Knowledge base from URLs | `knowledge/urls.yaml` entries `{url, title?, description?, refresh_hours?}` |
| Retrieval tuning (top_k, chunk size) | No equivalent knob. Drop it and say so in the report |
| Knowledge in the prompt (inline docs) | Stays in `instructions.md` only if short; long text moves to `knowledge/` |
| Guardrails / content policy | `guardrail.md` |
| Phone number, SIP trunk | The router's phone setup (`acceleration/cmd/phone`; Twilio, Telnyx and other vendors in `acceleration/internal/phone`), not `agent.yaml` |
| WhatsApp / SMS / iMessage line | `channels: {whatsapp: {number: "+1..."}, identity: phone|link}` in `agent.yaml` |
| Memory / dynamic variables / user data | Session memory is keyed by user; per-user values arrive as session tags, not prompt variables. Map `{{var}}` prompt slots to instructions that ask or to tool results |
| Post-call analysis, summaries, webhooks on call end | Transcripts and episode cards on the router; a custom post-call webhook has no direct equivalent. Report it |
| Evals / simulations | `simulations/*.yaml`, run with `getstream agents simulate <name>` |
| Multilingual language setting | `Accelerated(language=...)`; keyterms lists map to `keyterms:` in `agent.yaml` |
| Sandbox / code execution | `sandbox: daytona` plus `sandbox_options:`; skills run code there |

### MCP servers by URL

A source's inline MCP server (LiveKit `MCPServerHTTP`, Vapi `mcp`, a GPT Live backend MCP
tool) is a custom connector. The app's backend creates it once, with
`POST /v1/agents/connectors`: `id` starts with `custom_`, `endpoint` is the server's public
`https` URL, `schemes` says how a connection signs in. The folder gets a binding in
`agent.yaml`: `{name, connector: custom_<id>, connection: <label>}`, and the source's tool
filter becomes `tools:`. Pick the shape by how the server signs in:

| The source server | `schemes` | Connection |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public, no credential | `["none"]` | The app's, saved with empty credentials. Keep `connection` in the binding: without it the binding gets no tools |
| An API key in a header | `["api_key"]` | The app's, with the key and the header name (never `Authorization`). The key is never copied into the folder |
| Each user signs in (OAuth) | `["oauth2_code"]` with `client: {registration: ["cimd", "dcr"]}` | Each user's own: leave `connection` out. The server must publish its OAuth protected resource metadata |

Creating the connector and its connection takes the app's server token, so unless you were
given one, report each server under "migrated" with the one-time setup call the app's backend
still has to make. Never write the source's header values or tokens into the output. The calls in full are in
[Custom connectors](https://getstream.io/agents/docs/python/connectors/mcp/).

Provider/model spellings: a competitor's model name is almost never a valid target.
`openai/gpt-4.1-mini`, `deepgram/nova-3`, and `cartesia/sonic-3` all fail session start
with `routing: unknown target`. Before writing any `stt`/`tts`/`sts`/`llm` value, list
what the deployment serves:

```bash
getstream agents api ListRoutes --modality llm   # also stt, tts, sts
```

Each route (`llm-fast`, `stt-fast`, `tts-fast`, `sts-fast`, `sts-duplex`, ...) lists its
candidate `provider/model` spellings. Use either a capability route or an exact candidate
spelling (for example `openai/gpt-live-1` under `sts-duplex`), and report every
substitution ("gpt-4.1-mini is not served; llm-fast used"). When nothing fits, leave the
field out (backend default) rather than inventing a name, but only on a new config: a
field left out of a re-sync keeps the value already stored under that name, so migrating
over an existing config means setting every model field explicitly. Even that has
limits: `sts: ""` clears speech-to-speech, but `voice: ""` and `keyterms: []` do not
clear a stored voice or keyterms. When migrating over an existing name, check
`getstream agents api ListAgentConfigs` after syncing and say in the report what the
stored config actually ended up with.

## Tool rules

- A Python function keeps its name, parameter names, and return text. JSON-schema tools
  (Vapi, Deepgram, Retell custom tools) become typed Python functions with the same
  schema in the type hints and docstring.
- Server-side tools with a URL: if the system has a connector, prefer it; otherwise the
  Python function performs the HTTPS call. The URL is configuration, not a secret; any
  credential it needed stays out of the folder and is named in the report as setup work.
- Client-side tools (browser/device actions) have no equivalent; the agent runs
  server-side. Report them.
- Handoffs between agents (LiveKit handoffs, Vapi squads, Retell transfer agents) become
  skills, not agents: one folder, one `skills/<name>.md` per specialist.
- Irreversible-action flags (`defer_until_eot`, strict/confirm modes) become an
  instruction to confirm before acting, plus a note in the report.

## Rules

- Never copy competitor code, keys, dashboard JSON verbatim, or signing secrets into the
  migrated folder. Re-express behaviour in the target shapes above.
- If a feature has no equivalent, say so in the report. Inventing an `agent.yaml` key,
  a model name, or a vendor API is a failed migration.
- Prefer the backend default over a guessed model. Prefer a skill over prompt stuffing
  for anything procedural. Prefer a connector over a hand-rolled HTTPS tool when the
  system is in the catalog.
- Keep the greeting, instructions tone, and tool behaviour identical unless the user
  asked to change them. Migration is not a rewrite.

skills.name: new_models
skills.desc: Find LLM, TTS, STT and STS models worth adding to the router by searching X and Artificial Analysis, then diffing against what we already route.
skills.body:
---
name: new_models
description: Find LLM, TTS, STT and STS models worth adding to the router by searching X and Artificial Analysis, then diffing against what we already route.
---

# What should we be integrating?

The router only wants the frontier and the models everybody is asking for. A weekly
fine-tune, a research checkpoint with no API, a seventh open-weights 3B — none of those are
worth a provider package. The job here is to come back with a short list, not a survey.

## 1. Ask X what shipped

[`cmd/xsearch`](../../../acceleration/cmd/xsearch/main.go) puts a question to Grok with the
`x_search` tool behind it, scoped to a set of handles and a date window. It takes
`XAI_API_KEY` from the environment, or from the nearest `.env` above the working directory,
so it runs the same locally and in a cloud agent.

```bash
cd acceleration
go run ./cmd/xsearch -days 45 -handles OpenAI,OpenAIDevs,AnthropicAI,GoogleDeepMind,xai \
  -query "Which new AI models were launched? For each give the model name, whether it is an LLM, TTS, STT or speech-to-speech model, and the launch date."
```

A call takes a minute or two. Run the batches in parallel, one per shell:

- `OpenAI, OpenAIDevs`
- `AnthropicAI, claudeai`
- `GoogleDeepMind, GoogleAI`
- `xai, AIatMeta, nvidia, NVIDIAAIDev, MSFTResearch`
- `ElevenLabs, DeepgramAI, inworld_ai, cartesia_ai, AssemblyAI`
- `ArtificialAnlys` on its own, which is where a launch gets ranked rather than announced

Keep the batches small. The tool takes twenty handles, but Grok summarises what it read, and
one answer covering eleven accounts silently drops whole vendors — a run with `AnthropicAI` in
a batch of eleven returned no Claude models at all, while the same handles on their own
returned three. One vendor family per batch is the rule; the fourth batch above is the tail
that rarely ships voice or frontier models in the same week.

Write the query so it stands alone. The tool passes the handles separately, so a question
saying "these accounts" makes Grok complain there are none. Widen `-days` when a batch
comes back thin, and drop a handle that returns nothing rather than guessing at its
spelling — accounts get renamed.

## 2. Check it is actually good

X is where a launch is claimed; [Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai) is
where it is measured. Fetch the board for the modality and see whether the model is near
the top or missing entirely:

- <https://artificialanalysis.ai/leaderboards/models>
- <https://artificialanalysis.ai/text-to-speech>
- <https://artificialanalysis.ai/speech-to-text>
- <https://artificialanalysis.ai/speech-to-speech>

Then open the vendor's own docs or changelog for the API model id and the launch date. A
model with a demo and no endpoint is not integrable; say so and drop it.

## 3. Subtract what we have

Everything we route is in
[`router.yaml`](../../../acceleration/internal/routing/router.yaml), one `model:` line per
entry, grouped `stt`, `tts`, `sts`, `llm`. Grep the id before reporting anything:

```bash
rg -n "^      model:" acceleration/internal/routing/router.yaml
```

A model already listed is done. A model that is plainly the next version of one we list is
still worth reporting, as an upgrade rather than a new integration — say which entry it
replaces.

Routing a vendor and having code for it are different questions. Check
`internal/{llm,tts,stt,sts}/<vendor>` too: a vendor with a package but no `router.yaml` entry
is the cheapest thing on the list, because the client already exists and the work is config.
Anthropic was in exactly that state — `internal/llm/anthropic` with nothing routed to it.

When you report a price, report the cached-input rate too if the vendor has one: an entry in
`acceleration/prices/vendor.json` with no `cached_input_tokens` rate bills cached tokens at its
input rate. Report the other dimensions a vendor prices by as well, as `vendor.json` writes

# What should we be integrating?

The router only wants the frontier and the models everybody is asking for. A weekly
fine-tune, a research checkpoint with no API, a seventh open-weights 3B — none of those are
worth a provider package. The job here is to come back with a short list, not a survey.

## 1. Ask X what shipped

[`cmd/xsearch`](../../../acceleration/cmd/xsearch/main.go) puts a question to Grok with the
`x_search` tool behind it, scoped to a set of handles and a date window. It takes
`XAI_API_KEY` from the environment, or from the nearest `.env` above the working directory,
so it runs the same locally and in a cloud agent.

```bash
cd acceleration
go run ./cmd/xsearch -days 45 -handles OpenAI,OpenAIDevs,AnthropicAI,GoogleDeepMind,xai \
  -query "Which new AI models were launched? For each give the model name, whether it is an LLM, TTS, STT or speech-to-speech model, and the launch date."
```

- `OpenAI, OpenAIDevs`
- `AnthropicAI, claudeai`
- `GoogleDeepMind, GoogleAI`
- `xai, AIatMeta, nvidia, NVIDIAAIDev, MSFTResearch`
- `ElevenLabs, DeepgramAI, inworld_ai, cartesia_ai, AssemblyAI`
- `ArtificialAnlys` on its own, which is where a launch gets ranked rather than announced

skills.name: pagination
skills.desc: How list endpoints page through results. Read before adding a list endpoint or a limit parameter.
skills.body:
---
name: pagination
description: How list endpoints page through results. Read before adding a list endpoint or a limit parameter.
---

# Pagination

Never use limit/offset. Lists take `limit` + `cursor`.

- Offset is slow: Postgres reads and discards every skipped row. A cursor is an indexed `WHERE`.
- Offset is wrong when data changes: an insert repeats a row on the next page, a delete skips one.

## Rules

- Response is `{items, has_more, next_cursor}`, like `SessionPage`. Never a bare array.
- Cursors are opaque base64url. Clients never build or parse them.
- Sort ends with `id` so the order is total. The cursor holds every sort key.
- Fetch `limit + 1` to set `has_more`. No counts.
- Filters are resent with every page; the cursor holds a position. It may also record the filters it was handed out for, and is then refused under others (a 400).
- A bad cursor is a 400.
- Index the sort keys behind the filter, e.g. `(customer_id, updated_at DESC, id DESC)`.
- A list that filters and sorts takes a body instead of query parameters: see the `query` skill.

## Example: querySessions

Spec: `SessionQuery` carries `limit` and `cursor` in the body, and `SessionPage` is the 200.

Position, in `internal/store/models.go`:

```go
type SessionPosition struct {
	UpdatedAt time.Time `json:"u"`
	ID        string    `json:"id"`
	Rank      float32   `json:"r,omitempty"`
}
```

Store, in `Sessions.Select`:

```go
if after := filter.Cursor; after != nil {
	query = query.Where("(updated_at, id) < (?, ?)", after.UpdatedAt, after.ID)
}
query = query.Limit(SessionLimit(filter.Limit) + 1)
```

Handler: `decodeCursor` and `encodeCursor` in `internal/api/cursor.go`; `page` trims the
extra row and says whether it was there. The session cursor also records which sort it
came from, so a cursor from one sort is refused by another.

Live sessions that nothing records get the same cut and sort in `Manager.find`, on their
`created`, which is truncated to microseconds (what Postgres keeps) so that a cursor from
one half does not repeat the other. A recorded live session is listed through its row.

A text search sorts by relevance, and its cursor adds the rank:
`(rank, updated_at, id) < (?, ?, ?)`.

Go SDK: list methods return the page and take a cursor; `Items.Unwind` follows it.

## Lists without a cursor yet

`listCalls`, `listSimulationRuns` and `getCallEvents` take a `limit` and no way to continue.
`listSimulationRuns` refuses a limit over 500, and `getCallEvents` one over the 10,000 decisions
a call keeps. `listCalls` answers 500 at most.
