skills.name: parallel-agents
skills.desc: Rules for running several coding agents on this repo at once (PR authors, reviewers, fixers, rebases), so they do not break each other's runs and do not burn tokens on repeated work. Read before you start more than one agent that writes code, runs integration tests or opens PRs.
skills.body:
---
name: parallel-agents
description: Rules for running several coding agents on this repo at once (PR authors, reviewers, fixers, rebases), so they do not break each other's runs and do not burn tokens on repeated work. Read before you start more than one agent that writes code, runs integration tests or opens PRs.
---

# Parallel agents

These rules come from running seven connector PRs with agents on `accelerate`. Each one names
a mistake that actually happened.

## Keep agents out of each other's way

- **Test database.** `acceleration/internal/config/testing.yaml` wins over `ROUTER_POSTGRES_DSN`
  (`TestTheTestingFileWinsOverTheEnvironment`). Setting the env alone does not isolate a run.
  - Each agent points `testing.yaml` at a database of its own, such as `model_router_test_<slug>_test`.
    Do it through a `go test -overlay` copy or in the agent's own worktree.
  - It also sets `ROUTER_POSTGRES_DSN` to the DSN of its `testing.yaml` copy (database
    `model_router_test_<slug>_test`) and `ROUTER_REDIS_ADDR` to its own Redis. It sets the Redis
    address in its `testing.yaml` copy as well (see below).
  - `internal/testenv` replaces both variables with the `testing.yaml` values in every package that
    imports it. With `-tags integration`, `internal/imagerouter` and `internal/testenv/redisready`
    do not import it, so they read the shell's values. Without the tag, `cmd/router`
    (`sandboxproxy_test.go:65`, `main_test.go:58`) and `internal/session` (`timeout_test.go:108`)
    also read `ROUTER_REDIS_ADDR` from the shell: set your own Redis there.
  - `imagerouter` does not create its database. On a fresh slug it fails with
    `database "model_router_test_<slug>_test" does not exist`. Run a package that imports
    `internal/testenv` first, on the same `testing.yaml`: it creates the database.
  - It restores `testing.yaml` before it commits. Never commit it.
  - Two agents on `model_router_test` drop each other's schema in the middle of a run.
- **One Postgres server for all agents.** Agents share one test Postgres and each uses its own
  database on it. Do not start a Postgres container per agent. Eight of them, with fsync on, put
  the Docker VM into swap. Run the shared server with `fsync=off`, `synchronous_commit=off` and
  `full_page_writes=off`: the suites truncate their tables before every test, and each `TRUNCATE`
  waits on fsync. `testing.yaml` points at `localhost:55432`, which is the compose router's
  Postgres (fsync on). Start the shared server on its own port once, and put that port in each
  agent's `testing.yaml` copy:
  ```bash
  docker run -d --name va-test-pg --restart unless-stopped --shm-size=2g -p 127.0.0.1:55433:5432 \
    -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres -v va-test-pg19data:/var/lib/postgresql postgres:19-alpine \
    -c fsync=off -c synchronous_commit=off -c full_page_writes=off -c max_connections=1000
  ```
  - Keep its data on disk, not on tmpfs. One server held 765 MB over 59 test databases.
  - Give it `--shm-size=2g`. Postgres keeps every table's statistics in shared memory, which never
    shrinks: with Docker's default 64 MB, 450 test databases made every query fail with "could not
    resize shared memory segment".
  - Give each agent its own Redis. The router's Redis config has no database number or key
    prefix, so two agents on one Redis share counters, health and session keys.
  - Set the agent's Redis address as `redis: addr:` in its `testing.yaml` copy, next to its `dsn`.
    `ROUTER_REDIS_ADDR` alone is not enough: the embedded `testing.yaml` wins over the
    environment (`config.go:691-697`), so the suites would still use `localhost:56379`.
  - The suites that wipe tables use their own database, named
    `model_router_<suite>_test_<slug>_test`. Find an agent's databases with
    `datname LIKE '%\_<slug>\_test'`.
  - When the agent is done, drop its databases (`DROP DATABASE … WITH (FORCE)`) and remove its
    Redis.
- **One package at a time.** Run integration tests with `-p 1`. Packages that run in parallel try to
  create the same new database and fail with a duplicate key.
- **Migration versions.** goose is strict. A migration older than the newest version a database
  has applied stops the router at start ("found N missing migrations before current version").
  - The two sets, `acceleration/migrations/global` and `acceleration/migrations/shard`, keep
    their versions apart (`goose_global_version`, `goose_shard_version`), so slots are per set.
  - Give each PR its own version slot before the agents start, spaced apart. Never let two agents
    pick "the current time".
  - Merge in version order. Before each merge, check the newest file under both sets on
    `origin/main`.
  - Two PRs that change the store both edit `internal/store/repos.go`, where the repositories
    are wired. Keep both sides.
  - A database that ran an earlier build of a PR can hold a version that a later merge lands below.
    Recreate that database.
- **No shared append files.** An SDK note is a file of its own in `.claude/skills/sdk/notes/`, and
  the root `CHANGELOG.md` is written only at a release, except one breaking-change line under
  `# Unreleased`. A branch from before that rule that still adds to the end of
  `.claude/skills/sdk/SKILL.md` or other lines to the root `CHANGELOG.md` moves its note to a file and
  drops those changelog lines.
- **Conflict markers.** Before every `git rebase --continue`, run `git diff --check` and grep for
  `<<<<<<<`, `=======` and `>>>>>>>`. Markers were committed twice by agents that skipped this.
- **Generated files.** Do not hand-merge `acceleration/api/openapi.yaml` or the generated clients.
  Take either side, regenerate them (see `acceleration/README.md`), and check the result with
  `.agents/skills/pr-review/scripts/generated.sh <repo root> origin/main`.
- **CI runs the integration suites.** `Integration (router)` (`.github/workflows/integration.yml`)
  runs each package in its matrix in its own job, on a PR that changes `acceleration/**` (not
  only `.md`), `go.work`, `go.work.sum` or the workflow, once the PR is ready: a draft runs no
  CI workflow, and `gh pr ready` starts it. Do not repeat those packages locally: run the suites
  you touched, and read CI for the rest after the PR is marked ready.
  - CI leaves out the vendor suites that need API keys (tts, stt, llm, sts, search, imagegen,
    detection). CI also leaves out `imagerouter` and `dlc` (AI-2040), and the Postgres packages
    `internal/campaign`, `internal/phone/outcome`, `internal/searchrouter` and
    `internal/simulation`. Run those by hand when you touch them, and list the runs in the PR.
  - The check is not required on `main`. When it ran, wait for it to pass before you merge.
    A check that did not run leaves nothing to wait for. A check `skipping` on a draft is not a
    pass: it did not run.
  - Push, wait until the push's runs are listed, then `gh pr ready`. Both events share one
    concurrency group, so a draft run created after the ready run would cancel it.

## Review and merge one PR at a time

Authors may write in parallel. Reviews and merges run one PR at a time.

- **Why.** Each merge makes the other open PRs conflict. When four PRs were reviewed at once, each
  review had to be redone on the merged tree, and some three or four times.
- **Order.** Merge one PR, then rebase the next one once onto the new base, then review it.
- **Review against the current base.** Build and test the PR merged onto `origin/main`, not
  the PR head alone. Two PRs built cleanly on their own and failed to compile together.
- **Findings live in agent messages, not on GitHub.** Put the full list of earlier findings into
  every re-review prompt.
- **Re-review the delta.** The same reviewer reads
  `git range-diff <old base>..<old head> origin/main..<new head>` and checks its own findings.
  A new finding in code the delta did not touch blocks the merge only if it is a Blocker.
- **A rebase after GO needs no new review** when the range-diff shows only `=` commits plus commits
  that change docs or tests. When Go code changed, the same reviewer checks the delta.
- **Nits go to a ticket**, never into the same PR. Each fix is new code, and new code brings new
  findings and another round.

## Spend fewer tokens

- **Fix with a fresh agent.** Give it the branch, the worktree and the list of findings. Do not
  resume the author: its context grew to 500k–700k tokens, and every tool call resends all of it.
- **Use a smaller model for mechanical work**: a rebase whose conflicts are only in docs, watching
  CI, editing a PR body.
- **Test only what changed while iterating.** Run the touched suites and the mutation checks. Before
  the final review, mark the PR ready, read CI's `Integration (router)` check and run by hand
  the suites it leaves out. The reviewer does not repeat either.
- **Ask the first reviewer to find everything.** Later rounds look only at the delta.
- **Wait for an agent's report.** Do not read its raw transcript file.

  review had to be redone on the merged tree, and some three or four times.
- **Order.** Merge one PR, then rebase the next one once onto the new base, then review it.
- **Review against the current base.** Build and test the PR merged onto `origin/main`, not
  the PR head alone. Two PRs built cleanly on their own and failed to compile together.
- **Findings live in agent messages, not on GitHub.** Put the full list of earlier findings into
  every re-review prompt.
- **Re-review the delta.** The same reviewer reads
  `git range-diff <old base>..<old head> origin/main..<new head>` and checks its own findings.
  A new finding in code the delta did not touch blocks the merge only if it is a Blocker.
- **A rebase after GO needs no new review** when the range-diff shows only `=` commits plus commits
  that change docs or tests. When Go code changed, the same reviewer checks the delta.
- **Nits go to a ticket**, never into the same PR. Each fix is new code, and new code brings new
  findings and another round.

## Spend fewer tokens

- **Fix with a fresh agent.** Give it the branch, the worktree and the list of findings. Do not
  resume the author: its context grew to 500k–700k tokens, and every tool call resends all of it.
- **Use a smaller model for mechanical work**: a rebase whose conflicts are only in docs, watching
  CI, editing a PR body.
- **Test only what changed while iterating.** Run the touched suites and the mutation checks. Before
  the final review, mark the PR ready, read CI's `Integration (router)` check and run by hand
  the suites it leaves out. The reviewer does not repeat either.
- **Ask the first reviewer to find everything.** Later rounds look only at the delta.
- **Wait for an agent's report.** Do not read its raw transcript file.

skills.desc: Run the voice-agent load benchmark in performance_benchmark/ to find how many cascaded agents one router holds, and read or compare its reports. Use when asked how many concurrent agents we support, to load-test or stress the router, to measure a performance change, or to explain a perfbench run.
skills.body:
---
name: performance_benchmark
description: Run the voice-agent load benchmark in performance_benchmark/ to find how many cascaded agents one router holds, and read or compare its reports. Use when asked how many concurrent agents we support, to load-test or stress the router, to measure a performance change, or to explain a perfbench run.
---

# The load benchmark

`performance_benchmark/` answers one question: how many cascaded voice agents does one
router hold at once, and what gives way first. Every agent in a run is a real
conversation — the Go SDK opens a session, the router joins the call and runs the whole
loop, and a caller in the benchmark joins the same call over WebRTC and talks to it. The
three models are the router's own `mock/*` providers, so a run reaches no vendor and bills
nothing. **What a run measures is the router**: its audio path, turn taking, sockets and
database. It says nothing about model quality; that is Voicebench, in
[GetStream/voice-ai-bench](https://github.com/GetStream/voice-ai-bench).

Follow the [benchmark rules](../../../AGENTS.md#benchmark-rules).

## 1. What a run needs

**Keys.** `STREAM_API_KEY` and `STREAM_API_SECRET`, from the repo-root `.env`. Nothing else:
there is no provider key in a run, by design.

**A router with the mocks on.** The mock providers are built only when
`ROUTER_MOCK_PROVIDERS=true`, so a default router has no `mock/mock-stt` to route to and
every session fails with an unknown model. Check before a run, not after:

```bash
curl -sS "$ROUTER/api/v1/models?capability=stt" | grep -c mock/mock-stt
```

The benchmark release carries `router.mockProviders: true` in `shards/us-east1-acceleration/accelerate-benchmark.yaml`
in the private infra repo. Locally, `ROUTER_MOCK_PROVIDERS=true` in the root `.env`.

**The webrtc tag.** The callers speak Opus over WebRTC, so every command needs `-tags webrtc`.
Without the tag it builds and then refuses to place a call.

**`kubectl` on the router's cluster**, for `-namespace` to report pod CPU and restarts. Without
it the run still works and the report just has no pod column.

## 2. Run one

From `performance_benchmark/`. The benchmark release is the default target and the one to use:
nobody else's traffic is on it, and a run saturates it for its duration.

```bash
go run -tags webrtc ./cmd/perfbench run \
  -target benchmark -label before -start 1 -factor 2 -max 64 -hold 90s -out out/before
```

The ramp doubles the agents each step, holds each step for `-hold` of real conversation, and
stops at the first step that broke. Wall time is about `-hold` per step plus joining, so the
default ramp to 64 is around ten minutes. Start with `-max 8 -hold 30s` to check the setup
works before asking for a long one.

| What you want | Change |
|---|---|
| Check the setup end to end | `-max 1 -hold 20s` |
| A number to quote | `-max 128 -hold 120s`, twice, and take the lower |
| A local router | `-target http://localhost:8080 -namespace ""` |
| The benchmark release, which nobody else uses (`accelerate-benchmark`, two pods, overlap deploys) | `-target benchmark` |
| Finer steps near the ceiling | `-start <last held> -factor 1` is refused; use `-start`/`-max` around it with `-factor 2` |

A step breaks when more than 5% of conversations never get the agent onto the call, more than
10% of turns go unanswered, a reply takes over three seconds at p95, more than 1% of the probe
callers' audio is broken, or a router pod restarts. The step before it is the answer, printed
as `Held N agents`.

## 3. Read it

A run writes `out/<run>/report.json` and prints the same thing as Markdown: a row per step
with sessions created, agents that joined, turns answered, and p50/p95/p99 for session
creation, time to the agent's track, reply latency and mid-reply audio gaps, plus the router
pods' CPU and restarts.

The four timings say where a ceiling is:

- **SessionMs** growing: the API and its database, not the media path.
- **TrackMs** growing: the router is slow to get an agent onto a call — dispatch, the SFU join.
- **ReplyMs** growing while the stage spans stay flat: queueing, not a model.
- **GapMs** appearing: the router is producing audio slower than real time. This is the one
  that users hear first.

**Audio quality.** The first four callers of every step record each answer and score it
against the 220 Hz tone the mock TTS sends (`internal/bench/quality.go`): `audio snr` is the
tone's power over everything else, per 100 ms of speech, typical and worst answer; clean Opus
reads 33 to 36 dB. `audio broken` counts glitches (100 ms windows under 20 dB: a click, a
skipped 20 ms frame, distortion) and dropouts (frames that went quiet mid-sentence; pauses
between sentences are not counted). A glitch now and then is a packet the network lost: the
router's own `turns.audio_dropped_ms` says whether it was the router.

**The caller can be the bottleneck.** Each conversation costs this machine an Opus encode and
decode. When a step reports `host CPU saturated`, that ceiling is the laptop's, not the
router's: the numbers above it are meaningless. Rerun that step from a bigger machine, or say
in the report that the ceiling was the harness.

## 3a. How we bench: callers in the benchmark cluster

Past about 64 agents a laptop's uplink queues the callers' audio (1.7 s under load), and the
report measures the uplink. A number to quote comes from callers in the benchmark cluster,
beside the router, against `accelerate-benchmark`:

```bash
kubectl apply -f performance_benchmark/cluster/perfbench.yaml   # 16-core pod, its own e2 node
performance_benchmark/cluster/setup.sh                          # build perfbench in it
performance_benchmark/cluster/run.sh after-x 4 1024 60s         # report in out/after-x
```

- The router is pinned to 2 pods on 2 n4a-standard-4 nodes; keep the HPA at 2/2 so the
  hardware, and the cost per voice minute, stays fixed between runs.
- `run.sh` ends draining router generations and waits a minute first: after a fastdeploy the
  old one still carries the last run's calls, and its CPU lands in the new run.
- Joins go at 20 a second (`-join-rate 20`); all at once trips Stream's connect limit.
- Profile a router pod during a step with pprof (`router.pprofAddr` serves it on the pods'
  loopback): `kubectl port-forward pod/<router> 16060:6060`, then
  `curl -o cpu.pb.gz "localhost:16060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30"`. At 512 a step's
  joins take about 25 s, so start 20 s in, not 40.
- Cost per voice minute is the two nodes ($0.154/h each, on demand) over agents held, over 60.
- When done, `kubectl delete -f performance_benchmark/cluster/perfbench.yaml`: the pod holds
  its node until it is gone.

## 4. Did a change help?

Two runs, same target, same ramp, same machine, back to back, and the router rebuilt and
redeployed between them (`deploy` skill). Then:

```bash
go run -tags webrtc ./cmd/perfbench compare out/before out/after
```

It prints the held ceiling before and after and, for every step both runs reached, reply p50
and p95 with the percentage moved. One run is noisy: a move under about 10% on one pair of
runs is not a result, and staging has other traffic. Say how many runs a claim rests on.

For a change meant to cut allocations, a `go test -bench` micro-benchmark on the hot function
is the evidence that it allocates less; this benchmark is the evidence that it mattered.

`performance_benchmark/findings.md` is what the runs so far found, what was fixed and what is
still slow. Read it before chasing a ceiling, and add to it after a run worth remembering.

## 5. Per-turn stages

The router emits a span per turn (`agent.turn`) with a child per stage — `turn.stt`,
`turn.cadence`, `turn.decision`, `turn.llm`, `turn.tts`, `turn.playout` — so a slow reply can
be attributed without guessing. They go nowhere unless the router has
`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` set. With the mocks the model stages are fixed costs
(mock STT settles a turn 600ms after speech stops, mock LLM answers in 250ms, mock TTS starts
audio in 150ms), so anything above that in `turn.decision` or `turn.playout` is the router's.

## 6. Report back

```
Ran: <target>, <start>→<max> agents x<factor>, hold <d>, commit <sha>
Held: <n> agents. Broke at <n>: <why>
At <held>: reply p50 <ms> p95 <ms>, track p95 <ms>, session p95 <ms>, gaps p95 <ms>
Router: <cpu>m across <n> pods, <restarts> restarts
Harness: host CPU <busy> of <cores> cores
Next: <the one thing to fix>
```

Never quote a ceiling from a run whose host was saturated, and never quote one from a router
without the mocks: that run measured a vendor.

skills.name: phonecheck
skills.desc: Test inbound or outbound phone calls through a local or remote router. Asks what to test, sets up numbers, hooks and the person side, places the calls with phonecheck, reports where each hop ran (agent SFU, router address, Stream SIP host, SFUs used, person side) and how long it took, then puts everything back. Use when asked to test phone calls, run a phone call check, see which servers a call used, test call latency sites, or explain a phonecheck run.
skills.body:
---
name: phonecheck
description: Test inbound or outbound phone calls through a local or remote router. Asks what to test, sets up numbers, hooks and the person side, places the calls with phonecheck, reports where each hop ran (agent SFU, router address, Stream SIP host, SFUs used, person side) and how long it took, then puts everything back. Use when asked to test phone calls, run a phone call check, see which servers a call used, test call latency sites, or explain a phonecheck run.
---

# Test phone calls with phonecheck

`acceleration/cmd/phonecheck` places a test call and logs where each hop ran. It only logs; no
pass or fail. `acceleration/cmd/phonecheck/README.md` has the flags and setup details. This
skill asks what to test, sets it up, runs, reports and puts things back.

## Rules for every step

- **Main session only.** The wizard (every question and the Approve) runs in the main session
  with the human, never in a sub-agent. If this skill is invoked inside a sub-agent, stop and
  say the wizard must run in the main session. Sub-agents only read logs and write the
  per-call report.
- **Long processes run in the background.** Start the router, the tunnel and each phonecheck run
  with the Bash tool's `run_in_background`, as
  `bash -c 'set -o pipefail; … 2>&1 | tee -a <scratchpad>/<name>.log'`, so the output shows in
  the Claude Code shell panel and is kept in its own log in the scratchpad:
  `<scratchpad>/router.log`, `<scratchpad>/tunnel.log`, `<scratchpad>/phonecheck-<n>.log`.
  `pipefail` keeps the process's own exit status, not `tee`'s. The background task's process is
  the `bash -c` wrapper, not the process inside it: record and stop the inner one as each step
  says. Right after starting one, print
  its log's full path, so the human can `tail -f` it or ask questions while the call runs. The
  main session stays free to answer.
- **Shell.** The user's shell is fish. Run every snippet as `bash -c '…'`. Shell variables do not
  last between tool calls: write literal values (env file path, router address, customer id,
  numbers, ids) into each command.
- **Env.** No code here loads a `.env`. Ask for its path (default: the repository root's
  `.env`) and load it in every command: `bash -c 'set -a; . <env file>; set +a; <command>'`.
  `go run` commands run from `acceleration/`.
- **Never print secrets.** Check env by name only. Keep credentials out of process args: pass
  them to curl on stdin with `-K -`, for example
  `printf 'user = "%s:%s"\n' "$TWILIO_PERSON_ACCOUNT_SID" "$TWILIO_PERSON_AUTH_TOKEN" | curl -sS -K - …`
  or `printf 'header = "Authorization: Bearer %s"\n' "$TELNYX_PERSON_API_KEY" | curl -sS -K - …`.
  Pipe every reply through `jq` and keep only the fields named here.
- **Voice URLs: classify, never print.** A vendor's voice URL or connection setting can embed a
  password: the voice URL of a router number attached before the router's call webhook existed
  holds the Stream SIP trunk's. Never print a voice URL; keep one only after the credential check in "Voice URLs" below passes.
- **Encode numbers.** A `+` in a query must be encoded: `curl -G --data-urlencode 'PhoneNumber=+15550100002'`,
  and the same for Telnyx `filter[…]` keys. In a router path it stays as is.
- **Ask with AskUserQuestion,** one step at a time, defaults first. Accept several answers at once.
- **State file.** `<scratchpad>/phonecheck-state.md`. Write a line right after each change, and
  before a change write the values needed to undo it: vendor, number, vendor id, old voice URL
  and method (person numbers only, and only as "Voice URLs" allows), old `connection_id`,
  tunnel URL, hooks added, router and tunnel process ids. A section "bought this run" lists
  numbers the skill bought. No secrets in it. Cleanup reads it.
- **Never touch a number the skill did not buy.** It attaches and releases only numbers listed
  under "bought this run". An existing number is used as it is.

## Voice URLs

Write `<scratchpad>/voice.jq` once:

```jq
def risky: (. // "") | ascii_downcase | test("sip(:|%3a)|dial|@|%40|\\?.*(token|key|secret|password|auth)");
def kind: (. // "") as $u | ($u | ascii_downcase) as $l
  | if $u == "" then "empty"
    elif ($l | test("sip(:|%3a)")) then "attached (points at Stream SIP)"
    elif ($l | test("twimlets\\.com/echo")) and ($u | risky | not)
      then "test script (echo twimlet without <Dial>)"
    else "other" end;
```

To look at a number, print only the class: `jq -L <scratchpad> 'include "voice"; … | (.voice_url | kind)'`.
Only before changing a person number, save its old value straight into the state file, never
to the screen. The check refuses a value with `sip:`, `<Dial>` or `@` in it, or a query string naming a
token, key, secret, password or auth:

```bash
… | jq -L <scratchpad> -r 'include "voice"; .incoming_phone_numbers[0] | if (.voice_url | risky) then error("holds SIP credentials or a <Dial>") else "twilio <n> sid=\(.sid) old_voice_url=\(.voice_url // "") old_method=\(.voice_method)" end' >> <scratchpad>/phonecheck-state.md
```

Telnyx: the same on `.data` of `GET /v2/texml_applications/<id>`. If the check fails, do not
change that number: tell the human why and skip its runs.

## Router numbers: the router's API

Every router number step goes through the router's HTTP API, the way a customer does it. Never
the `phone` CLI for numbers. Write `<scratchpad>/router-auth.py` once:

```python
import base64, hashlib, hmac, json, os, sys, time

if len(sys.argv) > 1:  # local router in noauth: the header names the customer
    print(f'header = "X-Customer-Id: {sys.argv[1]}"')
    sys.exit()
b64 = lambda raw: base64.urlsafe_b64encode(raw).rstrip(b"=").decode()
now = int(time.time())
head = b64(b'{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}')
claims = b64(json.dumps({"server": True, "iat": now, "exp": now + 600}).encode())
key = os.environ["STREAM_API_SECRET"].encode()
sig = b64(hmac.new(key, f"{head}.{claims}".encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest())
print(f'header = "api_key: {os.environ["STREAM_API_KEY"]}"')
print('header = "Stream-Auth-Type: jwt"')
print(f'header = "Authorization: Bearer {head}.{claims}.{sig}"')
```

It prints curl config, so nothing secret is in an arg. Local: pass the customer id. Remote
(Stream's hosted router, behind its proxy): no argument; it signs a 10-minute server token with
`STREAM_API_SECRET`, and the customer is the app `STREAM_API_KEY` belongs to. Every call, with
`<auth>` the customer id or nothing:

```bash
bash -c 'set -a; . <env file>; set +a; python3 -I <scratchpad>/router-auth.py <auth> | curl -sS --fail-with-body -K - http://localhost:8080/v1/phone/numbers | jq "if (.error? // null) then .error | {code, message} else [.[] | {e164, vendor, stream_trunk_id}] end"'
```

| Step | Request | Keep |
|---|---|---|
| list | `GET /v1/phone/numbers` | `[].e164`, `.vendor`, `.stream_trunk_id` (present = attached) |
| search | `GET /v1/phone/numbers/available?vendor=<twilio\|telnyx>&country=US&features=voice&limit=3` | `.numbers[].e164`, `.vendor`, `.monthly_cost_micros`; `.skipped` |
| buy | `POST /v1/phone/numbers` with `-H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"vendor":"<v>","e164":"<n>","country":"US","tags":{"purpose":"phonecheck"}}'` | `.e164`, `.vendor`, `.monthly_cost_micros` |
| attach | `-X POST /v1/phone/numbers/<n>/attach` with `-H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'` | `.trunk_id`, `.sip_uri` |

   release or keep. Releasing is irreversible and stops the monthly charge. Router number:
   release (see the table; it also unwires an attached one), while the router still runs.

   so.

   nothing is left: `pgrep -x phonecheck`, `pgrep -f 'cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8080'`

tell the human its path.
skills.bodyMd:
# Test phone calls with phonecheck

`acceleration/cmd/phonecheck` places a test call and logs where each hop ran. It only logs; no
pass or fail. `acceleration/cmd/phonecheck/README.md` has the flags and setup details. This
skill asks what to test, sets it up, runs, reports and puts things back.

## Rules for every step

- **Main session only.** The wizard (every question and the Approve) runs in the main session
  with the human, never in a sub-agent. If this skill is invoked inside a sub-agent, stop and
  say the wizard must run in the main session. Sub-agents only read logs and write the
  per-call report.
- **Long processes run in the background.** Start the router, the tunnel and each phonecheck run
  with the Bash tool's `run_in_background`, as
  `bash -c 'set -o pipefail; … 2>&1 | tee -a <scratchpad>/<name>.log'`, so the output shows in
  the Claude Code shell panel and is kept in its own log in the scratchpad:
  `<scratchpad>/router.log`, `<scratchpad>/tunnel.log`, `<scratchpad>/phonecheck-<n>.log`.
  `pipefail` keeps the process's own exit status, not `tee`'s. The background task's process is
  the `bash -c` wrapper, not the process inside it: record and stop the inner one as each step
  says. Right after starting one, print
  its log's full path, so the human can `tail -f` it or ask questions while the call runs. The
  main session stays free to answer.
- **Shell.** The user's shell is fish. Run every snippet as `bash -c '…'`. Shell variables do not
  last between tool calls: write literal values (env file path, router address, customer id,
  numbers, ids) into each command.
- **Env.** No code here loads a `.env`. Ask for its path (default: the repository root's
  `.env`) and load it in every command: `bash -c 'set -a; . <env file>; set +a; <command>'`.
  `go run` commands run from `acceleration/`.
- **Never print secrets.** Check env by name only. Keep credentials out of process args: pass
  them to curl on stdin with `-K -`, for example
  `printf 'user = "%s:%s"\n' "$TWILIO_PERSON_ACCOUNT_SID" "$TWILIO_PERSON_AUTH_TOKEN" | curl -sS -K - …`
  or `printf 'header = "Authorization: Bearer %s"\n' "$TELNYX_PERSON_API_KEY" | curl -sS -K - …`.
  Pipe every reply through `jq` and keep only the fields named here.
- **Voice URLs: classify, never print.** A vendor's voice URL or connection setting can embed a
  password: the voice URL of a router number attached before the router's call webhook existed
  holds the Stream SIP trunk's. Never print a voice URL; keep one only after the credential check in "Voice URLs" below passes.
- **Encode numbers.** A `+` in a query must be encoded: `curl -G --data-urlencode 'PhoneNumber=+15550100002'`,
  and the same for Telnyx `filter[…]` keys. In a router path it stays as is.
- **Ask with AskUserQuestion,** one step at a time, defaults first. Accept several answers at once.
- **State file.** `<scratchpad>/phonecheck-state.md`. Write a line right after each change, and
  before a change write the values needed to undo it: vendor, number, vendor id, old voice URL
  and method (person numbers only, and only as "Voice URLs" allows), old `connection_id`,
  tunnel URL, hooks added, router and tunnel process ids. A section "bought this run" lists
  numbers the skill bought. No secrets in it. Cleanup reads it.
- **Never touch a number the skill did not buy.** It attaches and releases only numbers listed
  under "bought this run". An existing number is used as it is.

## Voice URLs

Write `<scratchpad>/voice.jq` once:

```jq
def risky: (. // "") | ascii_downcase | test("sip(:|%3a)|dial|@|%40|\\?.*(token|key|secret|password|auth)");
def kind: (. // "") as $u | ($u | ascii_downcase) as $l
  | if $u == "" then "empty"
    elif ($l | test("sip(:|%3a)")) then "attached (points at Stream SIP)"
    elif ($l | test("twimlets\\.com/echo")) and ($u | risky | not)
      then "test script (echo twimlet without <Dial>)"
    else "other" end;
```

To look at a number, print only the class: `jq -L <scratchpad> 'include "voice"; … | (.voice_url | kind)'`.
Only before changing a person number, save its old value straight into the state file, never
to the screen. The check refuses a value with `sip:`, `<Dial>` or `@` in it, or a query string naming a
token, key, secret, password or auth:

```bash
… | jq -L <scratchpad> -r 'include "voice"; .incoming_phone_numbers[0] | if (.voice_url | risky) then error("holds SIP credentials or a <Dial>") else "twilio <n> sid=\(.sid) old_voice_url=\(.voice_url // "") old_method=\(.voice_method)" end' >> <scratchpad>/phonecheck-state.md
```

Telnyx: the same on `.data` of `GET /v2/texml_applications/<id>`. If the check fails, do not
change that number: tell the human why and skip its runs.

## Router numbers: the router's API

Every router number step goes through the router's HTTP API, the way a customer does it. Never
the `phone` CLI for numbers. Write `<scratchpad>/router-auth.py` once:

```python

    print(f'header = "X-Customer-Id: {sys.argv[1]}"')
    sys.exit()
b64 = lambda raw: base64.urlsafe_b64encode(raw).rstrip(b"=").decode()
now = int(time.time())
head = b64(b'{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}')
claims = b64(json.dumps({"server": True, "iat": now, "exp": now + 600}).encode())
key = os.environ["STREAM_API_SECRET"].encode()
sig = b64(hmac.new(key, f"{head}.{claims}".encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest())
print(f'header = "api_key: {os.environ["STREAM_API_KEY"]}"')
print('header = "Stream-Auth-Type: jwt"')
print(f'header = "Authorization: Bearer {head}.{claims}.{sig}"')

`<auth>` the customer id or nothing:

   `GET /v2/phone_numbers` with `filter[phone_number]=<n>` (keep `data[].id`,
   `data[].connection_id`), `GET /v2/texml_applications/<person app id>` (keep
   `data.voice_url | kind`, `data.voice_method`), and the numbers on that app,
   `GET /v2/phone_numbers` with `filter[connection_id]=<person app id>` (keep `data[].phone_number`).
9. **Local only: hooks.** Run the read-only `go run ./cmd/phone hooks` and show it. Note any
   stale tunnel URL to remove.
10. **Keep or release** the bought numbers: not asked now. Asked per number at cleanup.

## Approve

Show ONE summary and wait for an explicit yes:

- the calls, in order: each combination × runs, each about `-talk` plus 10 s plus 35 to 65 s for the `call_sites` row, so a minute or more, a few cents each;
- numbers to buy, vendor and monthly cost, and any mid-run release of a just-bought number;
- the router address and the customer id every request uses;
- account changes: hooks pointed at a tunnel URL (app-wide: while it is up the local router
  also gets the Stream app's other call events; it gets no new-message events, since the router
  writes no message hook and Stream Chat delivers messages to its shard's router); any stale hook URL
  to remove; numbers to attach; Twilio voice URLs to set; the Telnyx person app's voice URL,
  with the numbers on that app listed (it changes all of them);
- for each person number whose voice setting is `other` (it points at some other app or
  webhook), say plainly: while the test runs, real calls to that number reach the test script
  instead; it is put back afterwards. Recommend a number used only for tests. Never print the URL;
- cleanup: what goes back (hooks, voice URLs, `connection_id`s, tunnel, router), what stays (the
  bought numbers, until you say otherwise; a kept Twilio router number points at the closed
  tunnel), and that release is asked per number afterwards.

No yes: nothing is bought or changed; stop the router this skill started and end.

## 2. Do (after the yes)

In this order, each change into the state file:

1. **Tunnel and hooks** (local only). `command -v cloudflared`; if missing, ask the human. Start
   `bash -c 'set -o pipefail; cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8080 2>&1 | tee -a <scratchpad>/tunnel.log'`
   in the background (it needs no env file), write cloudflared's own process id
   (`pgrep -f 'cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8080'`) to the state file, take its
   `https://<random>.trycloudflare.com` URL, then `go run ./cmd/phone hooks -url <tunnel URL>`
   (the call hook only: a text to the agent's channel is not answered by this local router)
   (`-remove <stale URL>` only if approved; `-app <id>` only for a router in app mode). A local
   Telnyx router's own TeXML app (`TELNYX_CONNECTION_ID`) needs its voice URL on the tunnel; the
   human sets that. Before any Twilio router number is attached, restart the local router with
   `ROUTER_PUBLIC_URL=<tunnel URL>` added to its start command (section 1, step 3), as the
   Twilio number's voice URL is built from it: `kill` the router's id from the state file, wait
   until nothing listens on :8080, start it again, and write the new process id to the state
   file. The env file's `ROUTER_PUBLIC_URL` is a local address Twilio cannot reach.
2. **Router numbers.** Buy (see the table); add to "bought this run". For inbound, after its
   outbound runs: attach.
3. **Person numbers.** Twilio `POST …/IncomingPhoneNumbers.json` with `PhoneNumber=<n>` (keep
   `sid`, `phone_number`). Telnyx `POST /v2/number_orders` with
   `{"phone_numbers":[{"phone_number":"<n>"}],"connection_id":"<person app id>"}` (keep
   `data.id`, `data.status`). Add to "bought this run".
4. **Person setup.** First save each old value as "Voice URLs" says. The echo URL is README §4's: `https`, `Say` first, `Pause length` matching
   `-talk`. Twilio, outbound: `POST …/IncomingPhoneNumbers/<sid>.json` with `VoiceUrl`,
   `VoiceMethod=GET`. Telnyx: put the number on the person app (`PATCH /v2/phone_numbers/<id>`
   `{"connection_id":"<person app id>"}`); outbound also `PATCH /v2/texml_applications/<id>`
   `{"voice_url":"<echo URL>","voice_method":"get"}`.

## Run

List the customer's numbers again and check the rules in 1.5. If another attached number
blocks an inbound run, stop and tell the human. Then, per combination `<n>` (1, 2, …), in the
background, one at a time:

```bash
bash -c 'set -o pipefail; set -a; . <env file>; set +a; cd acceleration/cmd/phonecheck && go run . outbound -provider twilio -router http://localhost:8080 -customer <customer> -agent-number +15550100001 -person-number +15550100002 -talk 20s -runs 1 -region us-east 2>&1 | tee -a <scratchpad>/phonecheck-<n>.log'
```

`-provider` is the person's vendor; `inbound` for the other direction. Print the log's path. The
tool waits up to 90 s for the `call_sites` row and logs `call_sites row after N s` when it comes. Start the next run once this one's exit is
reported. To stop a run early, interrupt the tool itself, so it still hangs up and closes the
session: `pkill -INT -x phonecheck` (`go run` names the binary after its folder). Then check
`pgrep -x phonecheck` finds nothing.

## Report

After each run, dispatch one sub-agent (Agent tool) to read `<scratchpad>/phonecheck-<n>.log`
and, locally, the lines of `<scratchpad>/router.log` with that run's `session_id` (logged in
`the agent is on the call`). It returns the block below, so the large logs stay out of the
main session. Per call, one short block:

- **Hops:** agent SFU, caller SFU (and where Stream placed each side), router address, Stream
  SIP host (on a trunk call, Stream's media address from its SDP answer, `observed`), the
  customer's trunk when there is one, SFUs used, person side and `region_label`, each with `observed`, `inferred` or
  `reported`.
- **Timings:** `connect_ms`, `session_ms` (from the agent on the call until its session and the person's call ended), `person_call_s` (the call itself), `total_ms`, and when the `call_sites`
  row came.
- **Gaps:** anything missing, plainly: `person call not observed` (Telnyx outbound), no
  `call_sites` row, a host that did not resolve, a run skipped and why.

## Clean up, always

On every exit: success, failure, or the human stopping. Read the state file and undo only what
it lists, in reverse:

1. Put back each voice URL, method and Telnyx `connection_id`.
2. `go run ./cmd/phone hooks -remove <tunnel URL>`; check with `go run ./cmd/phone hooks` that it
   is gone.
3. For each number under "bought this run", ask separately (number, vendor, attached or not):
   release or keep. Releasing is irreversible and stops the monthly charge. Router number:
   release (see the table; it also unwires an attached one), while the router still runs.
   Person number: Twilio `DELETE …/IncomingPhoneNumbers/<sid>.json`, Telnyx
   `DELETE /v2/phone_numbers/<id>`. Say what is kept and what stays attached: an attached
   number blocks inbound tests on other numbers. A kept Twilio router number keeps its voice
   URL on the closed tunnel: its calls fail until the router is reachable there again, so say
   so.
4. Stop any phonecheck run left (`pkill -INT -x phonecheck`), then the tunnel, then the router:
   `kill <id>` for each process id in the state file, then their background tasks. Check that
   nothing is left: `pgrep -x phonecheck`, `pgrep -f 'cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8080'`
   and `lsof -tiTCP:8080 -sTCP:LISTEN` each print nothing.

If a run was killed hard, a call may still be up and the state file says what is left to undo;
tell the human its path.

skills.name: pr
skills.desc: Create a draft pull request for the Vision-Agents repo using gh CLI.
skills.body:
--- name: pr description: Create a draft pull request for the Vision-Agents repo using gh CLI. --- # Pull Request (Vision-Agents) ## Before creating - Run `git log main..HEAD --oneline`. If the branch contains more than one independent logical change, STOP and ask the user whether to split it before proceeding. - Run `uv run --no-sync dev.py check`. Skip if the diff does not touch Python code (`*.py`) or `pyproject.toml` — e.g. docs-only, `.gitignore`, `.github/`, or `.claude/` changes. - Do not run integration tests locally, CI handles them. - Do not edit the root `CHANGELOG.md`: it is written once per release (Changelog in `AGENTS.md`). The one exception is a line under `# Unreleased` → **Breaking Changes** for a PR that breaks a published SDK's API. Put what users need to know in the PR body. ## Creating - Always `gh pr create --draft`. Push the branch first. - A draft runs no CI workflow; CodeQL, the labeler and CodeRabbit still run. `gh pr ready` starts the workflows whose paths the PR touches, and every push after it runs them again, so mark it ready once the branch is done, not before. - Follow `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Read every commit on the branch, do not summarise from the latest commit alone. ## Title - Aim for 50 characters, never more than 65. The repo only squash-merges and uses the PR title as the commit subject on `main` once a PR has two or more commits, and GitHub appends ` (#NNN)`. 65 plus that suffix stays within the 72 GitHub's docs give as the commit title maximum; 50 is what `git help commit` and Pro Git recommend. - Say what changes, not how. The ticket id (`AI-833`) counts toward the limit; details go in the body. - Bad, 85 characters: `feat(connectors): connector definitions table seeded from built-in manifests (AI-833)`. Good, 44: `AI-833: connector definitions with revisions`. ## Body - Explain with pictures, not paragraphs. Near the top, a `## How it works` section shows the idea with a chart. Give small tables for "change → result → test that proves it" and for before/after. - **ASCII, in a fenced code block,** for branching logic (a tree) and data flow (boxes and arrows). Mermaid stacks these as tall columns of boxes; ASCII is shorter and reads the same in `gh pr view`. Draw with `├─ └─ │ ->` and keep each line within 80 columns, the default terminal width. - **A mermaid `sequenceDiagram`** for a protocol or concurrency. It spreads across, not down, so ASCII saves no height, and the actor columns leave too little width for the messages. No `;` inside a message (it splits statements). - Name each actor in full, or by a short form readers already know (`PG` for Postgres). No one-letter keys: the reader should not look anything up. - After creating the PR, open it and check that each chart renders and lines up. - Keep prose short: one or two sentences per point, and nothing a diagram or table already shows. A reviewer should get the idea in a minute without a wall of text. - Cite evidence: `file:line`, test names, commits. Mark anything not checked as unverified. - `## Why` is motivation + context. `## Changes`, if included, is high-level; never per-bullet justifications, those belong in `## Why`. - Link public GitHub issues inline within `## Why` (e.g. "users reported X (#478)"), not as a trailing `Fixes #N`. - Do not paste CI, lint, or tool output in the body. - Do not hard-wrap paragraphs. GitHub renders each newline inside a paragraph as a visible line break, so a 72-column-wrapped paragraph becomes a staircase. Write each paragraph or bullet as one unbroken line; rely on the browser to soft-wrap. Only use newlines to separate paragraphs, list items, or block elements. ## SQL changes When a PR changes the shape of a query, for performance or any other reason, the body shows the evidence. Query plans are the one tool output the body carries. - **Query, before and after, side by side.** Use an HTML table with one column per version. A markdown table cannot hold a code block. - **Plans, before and after, collapsed.** Run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on both versions against the same data, and put each in a `
` block. Compare buffers (`shared hit`, `read`), not only time: a warm cache can make a slow plan look fast. Say where you ran them and on how many rows. - **The outcome, in one line or a small table.** Show what got better and by how much, both for the query (buffers, rows scanned, time) and for whoever uses it (the endpoint, the page, the job). ````markdown
BeforeAfter
```sql SELECT ... ORDER BY revision DESC LIMIT 1 ``` ```sql SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id, id) ... ```
Plan before: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), staging, 1.2M rows ``` Seq Scan on connector_definitions ... Buffers: shared hit=120 read=8410 ```
Plan after ``` Index Scan using connector_definitions_pkey ... Buffers: shared hit=4 ```
| | Before | After | | --- | --- | --- | | Buffers (hit + read) | 8,530 | 4 | | Execution time | 412 ms | 0.08 ms | | `GET /v1/agents/connectors` p95 | 450 ms | 15 ms | ```` The numbers in the example are made up, to show the shape. A real PR uses only numbers from plans it ran.

skills.name: pricing
skills.desc: How to make new billable work (a model, vendor, modality or phone feature) report usage and get priced correctly. Read before adding anything the router bills, or when work shows up unpriced.
skills.body:
---
name: pricing
description: How to make new billable work (a model, vendor, modality or phone feature) report usage and get priced correctly. Read before adding anything the router bills, or when work shows up unpriced.
---

# Pricing and usage

Providers report quantities; the price list turns them into cost. Never compute cost in a provider.

- **Meters:** `internal/pricing/pricing.go`. **List prices:** `acceleration/prices/vendor.json` (rates only, `region` required).
- **The database is the source of truth.** On start a router adds items the database has never priced, at rates × 1.08. It never changes an existing price, so get the rates right before the first deploy. Later changes go through a price change per environment (management API) plus a `vendor.json` PR. See `check_prices`.
- **Unpriced work is recorded at $0.** It reserves no spend and raises `unpriced`, and configs naming it get a 400. `free: true` is a price; a missing entry is not.
- **Every meter the vendor bills needs a rate.** Missing cached or cache-write rates fall back to input. A missing `output_tokens` rate does not fall back: it is free.
- **Vendor cost:** if the vendor's response says what it charged, put it in `VendorCostMicros` so `router prices drift` can check the rate.

## Every change

1. Report usage from the provider, in meters the vendor bills.
2. Add the `vendor.json` entry from the vendor's pricing page, dated in the `router.yaml` comment. Self-hosted models get `local: true` instead.
3. Run `go test ./internal/routing/ -run TestEveryRoutedModelIsPriced`, `router prices check`, and the modality's integration suite.
4. After the deploy, in each environment: `router prices show --unpriced` is empty, the start log has no "billable work has no price", and one real request returns `X-Stream-Cost-Micros` equal to quantity × price.

## By type

- **LLM:** `input_tokens`, `cached_input_tokens`, `cache_write_input_tokens`, `output_tokens`. Write a long-prompt surcharge as `tiers` (`above_input_tokens`) and a service tier as `when: {service_tier}`. A customer-key (BYOK) twin is generated: never write one. See `router-llm`.
- **STS:** split by modality (`input_audio_tokens`, `output_text_tokens`, …), plus generic `input_tokens`/`output_tokens` at the audio rates as a fallback for vendors that report no split. See `router-sts`.
- **STT:** `audio_ms` (per minute is `per: 3600000`). See `router-stt`.
- **TTS:** `characters`, or `audio_ms` if the vendor bills by duration. See `router-tts`.
- **Decision model:** `input_tokens`, plus `output_tokens` if billed. A System One vendor reports usage for you; `:free` endpoints use `free: true`. See `decision_model`.
- **Search:** `requests`, or tokens for LLM-backed search. See `router-search`.
- **Image, detection, OCR:** `images`, `pages`, or tokens, whichever the vendor bills. See `router-detection`.
- **Memory, knowledge:** `requests`; knowledge also uses `bytes_written`, `bytes_queried`, `bytes_returned`, `results` and `byte_hours`. Add new billed work to `internal/billable` so `--unpriced` checks it.
- **Sandbox:** `vcpu_seconds`, `memory_gb_seconds` and `disk_gb_seconds`, with `when: {class}`, recorded by the usage jobs. Each new region or target needs entries.
- **Phone:** per vendor, `dial` and `call_minutes` (`call_seconds`); SMS uses `messages`, `message_segments` and `media_messages` with `when` by `country`, `direction` or `category`. A cost the vendor quotes outright (a number's month) goes through `Quoted`, with no entry. WhatsApp and iMessage are billed by the app's own account: don't price them. A new vendor goes in `billable.Items`. See `telnyx`, `phonecheck`.
- **Runtime:** `stream` `text`/`voice`/`video` by `seconds`, recorded in slices by `routing.NewRecorder`. These are the operator's own prices: set them by price change, not in `vendor.json`.

skills.name: prospect-competitor-research
skills.desc: Research a prospect's top 5 competitors and write a dated, sourced report: press releases, latest blog posts, changelogs, new features, where each competitor is ahead, and who is shipping AI features and how those features surface in the product. Use when someone asks for competitive research, a competitor analysis, a market scan, or call prep for a prospect or customer, given a company name and website, even if they never say competitors.
skills.body:
---
name: prospect-competitor-research
description: "Research a prospect's top 5 competitors and write a dated, sourced report: press releases, latest blog posts, changelogs, new features, where each competitor is ahead, and who is shipping AI features and how those features surface in the product. Use when someone asks for competitive research, a competitor analysis, a market scan, or call prep for a prospect or customer, given a company name and website, even if they never say competitors."
---

# Prospect competitor research

Write a report a seller can read before a call: who the prospect competes with, what those competitors shipped lately, where they are ahead, and how they are putting AI into their apps. Every claim has a date and a link.

## Collect the brief

Ask only for what is missing. Name and website are required.

| Input | Default |
| --- | --- |
| Prospect name | required |
| Website | required |
| Competitors | Research the top 5 |
| Focus | The prospect's core product |
| Window | News and posts from the last 6 months, AI features from the last 12 |

## Read the prospect first

Read their homepage, product pages, pricing, about page, and newsroom. Note what they sell, to whom, on which platforms (web, iOS, Android), and the words they use for the product. Then search news for the last 6 months: funding, launches, acquisitions, leadership changes. Note any AI features they already ship, so the gap analysis has a baseline.

## Pick the five competitors

A competitor is a product the same buyer would put on the same shortlist for the same job. Find candidates from G2 and Capterra categories, "alternatives to" and "vs" pages, the prospect's own comparison pages, and analyst lists. Pick five: usually the two or three incumbents plus the challengers growing fastest. Write one line per competitor saying why it made the list. If the user named competitors, use theirs and do not swap any out.

## Research each competitor

Research the five in parallel: launch one subagent per competitor with the brief below and the window, and ask each to return its notes in the shape of the per-competitor section of the report. Read the notes critically; drop anything without a source.

For each competitor, read:

- **Changelog and release notes**: the product's changelog, docs "what's new", and App Store and Play Store release notes.
- **Blog**: the five most recent posts, with dates and one line each.
- **Press**: their newsroom and press wire releases (PR Newswire, Business Wire) in the window.
- **Product and pricing**: new tiers, add-ons, and what moved behind a paywall.
- **Signals**: funding, acquisitions, partnerships, and job posts that name AI, LLM, or agent roles.

For every AI feature, record:

skills.name: provider_audit
skills.desc: Audit what is left on every vendor account the product pays for — prepaid balance, credits, character or minute quota, spend this month — read-only, and say which account is about to run out. Use when asked how much money is left, to audit providers, for a vendor's balance, credits or quota, or whether any account is about to run out.
skills.body:
---
name: provider_audit
description: Audit what is left on every vendor account the product pays for — prepaid balance, credits, character or minute quota, spend this month — read-only, and say which account is about to run out. Use when asked how much money is left, to audit providers, for a vendor's balance, credits or quota, or whether any account is about to run out.
---

# Audit vendor accounts

A prepaid vendor account at zero refuses requests: the Gemini API, for one, answers
HTTP 402 to every key of the billing account
([billing](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/billing)). The keypool alerts only fire
once calls fail. This skill reads what is left before that.

`vendors.md` is the inventory: every vendor the product depends on, what it is for, who
pays, which key the router reads, and how to see what is left. `audit.py` calls every
read-only balance API in it and prints one table.

Vendors are core or connector. Core vendors are the ones the platform needs to work
(models, memory, sandboxes, GPU hosts, infra); connector vendors (Telnyx, Twilio, Linq and
the other phone and channel vendors) are bring-your-own, used only by connectors.

## Run it

Everything is read-only: GETs to documented billing or usage endpoints. Never top up,
change a plan or a key from here.

The script reads keys only from the repo-root `.env`, run from the repo root:

```bash
uv run --no-project --env-file .env .claude/skills/provider_audit/audit.py --min USD=20
```

It prints `vendor | left | unit | source | checked_at | note`, one row per key (a pool
`NAME=k1,k2` gives two): the core rows, then the connector rows under their own heading.
Then `BELOW:` for each core balance under its `--min`, and `BELOW (connector):` for each
connector one. `--min` takes `UNIT=AMOUNT` and repeats (`--min USD=20 --min
characters=100000`); it compares only rows in that unit, so `USD spent this month` is
never a balance. Exit code 1 means a core balance is below its minimum. A connector
balance below it and an error row (a 401, a timeout, an odd body) are reported and never
fail the run.

For example:

```text
vendor | left | unit | source | checked_at | note
ExampleVendor | <amount> | USD | https://example.com/docs/balance | <time> |
OtherVendor | error | | https://example.com/docs/usage | <time> | error (OTHER_API_KEY): HTTP 401 ...
```

Read each row:

- a number: what is left, or spent this month for postpaid accounts;
- `error (ENV): HTTP 401 ...`: the key cannot read billing: a scope the API needs
  (`vendors.md` names it, with the doc) or a dead key;
- `skipped: ENV not set`: no such key in `.env`;
- `unknown (dashboard only)`: no API; open the URL in `source`.

Some balances need an admin or management key the router never holds:
`OPENAI_ADMIN_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_ADMIN_KEY`, `DEEPGRAM_ADMIN_KEY`,
`OPENROUTER_MANAGEMENT_KEY`, `XAI_MANAGEMENT_KEY`. Set one in `.env` to read that
account; without it the row says `skipped: <VAR> not set`.

## Keep the inventory current

Each time, from the repo root:

```bash
# Every key the router code reads. Skip our own (ROUTER_*, USAGE_*, STREAM_*, CLIENT_SECRET,
# OTHER_TOKEN) and the connector tokens (GITHUB_, GITLAB_, LINEAR_). A second credential of
# a listed vendor (SINCH_APPLICATION_*, VONAGE_API_SECRET, VONAGE_PRIVATE_KEY,
# TELNYX_PUBLIC_KEY) needs no row of its own; *_PERSON_* keys are in the Telnyx and Twilio rows.
git grep -hoE '"[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*_(API_KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|KEY)"' origin/main -- \
  'acceleration/*.go' ':!*_test.go' | sort -u
# Every provider routed, per modality.
awk '/^[a-z_]+:/{s=$1} /^    - provider:/{print s, $3}' acceleration/internal/routing/router.yaml | sort -u
# Every implemented phone vendor and its credentials; each needs a row in vendors.md.
awk '/- vendor:/{v=$3} /implemented: true/{i=v} /credentials:/&&i==v{print v, $0}' acceleration/internal/phone/phone.yaml
```

Then the hosts that hold no router key: `acceleration/deploy/*/README.md` (GPU hosts),
`compose.yaml`, `.github/workflows/`, the deploy skill, and the clients' own repos
(Volt, the docs site). A new vendor gets a row in `vendors.md`. One with a read-only
balance API also gets a check in `audit.py`: a function under `@check("Vendor", "ENV")`
whose docstring is the API's doc URL, and a test in `test_audit.py`. A connector
vendor's name also goes in `CONNECTORS`. Cite the doc or
the live answer for every claim; mark the rest `unverified`.

The tests run a real local HTTP server in place of each vendor:

```bash
uv run --no-project --with pytest pytest -c /dev/null \
  --confcutdir .claude/skills/provider_audit .claude/skills/provider_audit
```

skills.name: query
skills.desc: How list endpoints take filters and sorts, modelled on Stream's query syntax. Read before adding a filter, a sort, or a query endpoint.
skills.body:
---
name: query
description: How list endpoints take filters and sorts, modelled on Stream's query syntax. Read before adding a filter, a sort, or a query endpoint.
---

# Query

One filter language for every list, the one getstream.io uses for users, channels,
messages and calls. A caller who has written one Stream query can write ours.

Paging is the `pagination` skill (`.claude/skills/pagination/SKILL.md`). Read it first:
this skill decides which rows, that one decides where the page starts.

## Shape

A resource that needs more than a couple of equality filters gets
`POST /v1/<resource>/query`, operationId `query<Resources>`:

```json
{
  "filter": {"state": "closed", "created_at": {"$gte": "2026-09-01T00:00:00Z"}},
  "sort": [{"field": "created_at", "direction": -1}],
  "limit": 25,
  "cursor": "…"
}
```

The answer is a page, `{items, has_more, next_cursor}`, as in pagination.

- POST because a filter is a tree, and a tree in a query string is unreadable. It still reads
  and nothing changes.
- A simple `GET` list with a couple of query parameters stays as it is. Add `query<Resources>`
  beside it when it outgrows them; don't add a tenth query parameter.
- `filter` is optional. An empty filter is every row the caller may see.

Stream calls the field `filter_conditions`. We call it `filter`; the grammar is the same.

## Filter grammar

A filter is a JSON object. Keys are field names or logical operators, and all keys at one
level are ANDed.

| Operator | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `$eq` | equal; a bare value is shorthand | `{"state": "closed"}` |
| `$in` | equal to any of a list | `{"agent": {"$in": ["a", "b"]}}` |
| `$gt` `$gte` `$lt` `$lte` | range, on numbers and RFC3339 times | `{"created_at": {"$lt": "…"}}` |
| `$exists` | the field is set or not | `{"ended_at": {"$exists": false}}` |
| `$contains` | array holds the value; object holds every key and value | `{"custom": {"$contains": {"team": "x"}}}` |
| `$autocomplete` | prefix match on a name | `{"title": {"$autocomplete": "sup"}}` |
| `$q` | full-text match | `{"title": {"$q": "billing refund"}}` |
| `$and` `$or` | a list of filters | `{"$or": [{"state": "running"}, {"agent": "x"}]}` |

`custom.<key>` is shorthand for `$contains` on the custom object:
`{"custom.team": "x"}` is `{"custom": {"$contains": {"team": "x"}}}`.

Not supported, and a 400: `$ne`, `$nin`, `$nor`, `$not`, regexes. Negative filters walk
every row that does not match instead of seeking to the ones that do. Rewrite them as a
positive `$in`. Stream allows `$ne` only on `id` and booleans; we allow `$ne` only on booleans,
where it is just `$eq` with the other value.

## Rules

- Each endpoint declares an allow-list: field → operators, and the column each field reads.
  Anything else is a 400 that names the field and the operator. Never pass a caller's field
  name into SQL; it is looked up in the allow-list and the column comes from there.
- Only allow what an index serves. If `(customer_id, agent, created_at, id)` exists, `agent`
  gets `$eq` and `$in`; a field with no index gets nothing until it has one. Custom fields
  get `$eq`/`$contains` only, as containment (`@>`), which a `jsonb_path_ops` GIN index on
  the JSONB column answers. Never `$exists` on a custom key: key-exists (`?`, `?|`, `?&`)
  needs the default `jsonb_ops` index, which is several times larger.
- `$and`/`$or` nest one level deep at most, and `$in` takes at most 100 values. Deeper trees
  are a 400; they are how a list becomes a table scan.
- Scope is not a filter. The handler ANDs the customer, and for end users the user, onto
  whatever arrived, as `SessionFilter.UserID` does. A caller cannot widen it by writing
  `$or`.
- Values are typed by the field: a time must parse as RFC3339, a number as a number, an
  enum as one of its values. A wrong type is a 400, not an empty page.

## Sort

`sort` is a list of `{"field", "direction"}`, direction `1` ascending or `-1` descending, as
Stream does it. Fields come from a sort allow-list, usually two or three indexed columns.

- Omitted, the endpoint's default applies, e.g. `created_at` descending.
- The server appends `id` in the direction of the last key, so the order is total.
- The cursor holds every sort key and a fingerprint of the sort. A cursor sent with a
  different sort is a 400. See pagination for why the keys are in the cursor.
- One index per allowed sort, behind the filters it is used with.

## Paging

As in pagination: `limit` + `cursor`, never offset. Stream Chat's queries page by offset
with a 1,000 row ceiling; Stream Video's `queryCalls` hands back a `next` pointer. We do what
Video does.

- `filter` and `sort` are resent with every page. The cursor is only a position.
- The next page is the filter ANDed with `(sort keys, id) < (cursor values)`, flipped to `>`
  for ascending keys.
- Fetch `limit + 1` for `has_more`. No counts.

## Go

Put the grammar in one package and reuse it; an endpoint only supplies its allow-lists.

- A short allow-list needs no parser. `querySessions` (`internal/api/session_query.go`)
  declares its filter as closed Huma structs, with one struct per operator (`Equals`,
  `TextMatch`), so the schema validates the request and documents it too. Combinations
  the schema cannot express, such as a text search with `project_id`, are refused in
  `sessionQueryOf`. The cursor carries the sort, so a cursor from one sort is refused by
  another. Start here, and move to a tree only when `$and`, `$or` or `$in` are needed.
- Parse the body into a tree once, validating against the allow-list as you go. The
  handler gets a typed tree or an `invalidRequest` `APIError`.
- Compile the tree to bun `Where` clauses with bound values. Field names never reach SQL
  as text.
- Where a list merges rows held in memory with rows in Postgres, like live sessions in
  `Manager.find`, the same tree needs a `Match(item)` too, so both halves filter and sort
  alike.
- Document the allowed fields, operators and sorts in the operation's description; that is
  what a caller reads.
- Tests follow the `go-testing` skill: one per allowed operator, one for a rejected field
  and a rejected operator, one for a nested `$or`, and one that pages a filtered, sorted
  list to the end without repeating or skipping a row.

## SDKs

Go first, as AGENTS.md says. The filter is a plain map in every SDK (`map[string]any`, a
dict, an object), which is how Stream's SDKs take `filter_conditions`. Sort is a typed list.
List methods follow the cursor the way `Items.Unwind` does.

  gets `$eq` and `$in`; a field with no index gets nothing until it has one. Custom fields
  get `$eq`/`$contains` only, as containment (`@>`), which a `jsonb_path_ops` GIN index on
  the JSONB column answers. Never `$exists` on a custom key: key-exists (`?`, `?|`, `?&`)
  needs the default `jsonb_ops` index, which is several times larger.
- `$and`/`$or` nest one level deep at most, and `$in` takes at most 100 values. Deeper trees
  are a 400; they are how a list becomes a table scan.
- Scope is not a filter. The handler ANDs the customer, and for end users the user, onto
  whatever arrived, as `SessionFilter.UserID` does. A caller cannot widen it by writing
  `$or`.
- Values are typed by the field: a time must parse as RFC3339, a number as a number, an
  enum as one of its values. A wrong type is a 400, not an empty page.

## Sort

`sort` is a list of `{"field", "direction"}`, direction `1` ascending or `-1` descending, as
Stream does it. Fields come from a sort allow-list, usually two or three indexed columns.

- Omitted, the endpoint's default applies, e.g. `created_at` descending.
- The server appends `id` in the direction of the last key, so the order is total.
- The cursor holds every sort key and a fingerprint of the sort. A cursor sent with a
  different sort is a 400. See pagination for why the keys are in the cursor.
- One index per allowed sort, behind the filters it is used with.

## Paging

As in pagination: `limit` + `cursor`, never offset. Stream Chat's queries page by offset
with a 1,000 row ceiling; Stream Video's `queryCalls` hands back a `next` pointer. We do what
Video does.

- `filter` and `sort` are resent with every page. The cursor is only a position.
- The next page is the filter ANDed with `(sort keys, id) < (cursor values)`, flipped to `>`
  for ascending keys.
- Fetch `limit + 1` for `has_more`. No counts.

## Go

Put the grammar in one package and reuse it; an endpoint only supplies its allow-lists.

- A short allow-list needs no parser. `querySessions` (`internal/api/session_query.go`)
  declares its filter as closed Huma structs, with one struct per operator (`Equals`,
  `TextMatch`), so the schema validates the request and documents it too. Combinations
  the schema cannot express, such as a text search with `project_id`, are refused in
  `sessionQueryOf`. The cursor carries the sort, so a cursor from one sort is refused by
  another. Start here, and move to a tree only when `$and`, `$or` or `$in` are needed.
- Parse the body into a tree once, validating against the allow-list as you go. The
  handler gets a typed tree or an `invalidRequest` `APIError`.
- Compile the tree to bun `Where` clauses with bound values. Field names never reach SQL
  as text.
- Where a list merges rows held in memory with rows in Postgres, like live sessions in
  `Manager.find`, the same tree needs a `Match(item)` too, so both halves filter and sort
  alike.
- Document the allowed fields, operators and sorts in the operation's description; that is
  what a caller reads.
- Tests follow the `go-testing` skill: one per allowed operator, one for a rejected field
  and a rejected operator, one for a nested `$or`, and one that pages a filtered, sorted
  list to the end without repeating or skipping a row.

## SDKs

Go first, as AGENTS.md says. The filter is a plain map in every SDK (`map[string]any`, a
dict, an object), which is how Stream's SDKs take `filter_conditions`. Sort is a typed list.
List methods follow the cursor the way `Items.Unwind` does.

skills.name: refresh_model_stats
skills.desc: Refresh the Artificial Analysis numbers (TTS Elo and characters per second, streaming STT word error rate and latency) that the model picker shows. Use when the board has moved, a model was added to router.yaml, or someone asks for fresh model stats.
skills.body:
---
name: refresh_model_stats
description: Refresh the Artificial Analysis numbers (TTS Elo and characters per second, streaming STT word error rate and latency) that the model picker shows. Use when the board has moved, a model was added to router.yaml, or someone asks for fresh model stats.
---

# Refresh model stats

The model picker in Volt shows benchmark columns for voice and transcription models. They
come from `benchmark:` on each model in `acceleration/internal/routing/router.yaml`, which
`GET /v1/{modality}/providers` returns as `benchmark`. Nothing fetches them live; this skill
is how they change.

| Modality | Fields | Artificial Analysis source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| tts | `elo`, `characters_per_second` | [text-to-speech](https://artificialanalysis.ai/text-to-speech), arena Elo and median characters per second |
| stt | `word_error_rate` (0 to 1), `latency_ms` | [speech-to-text/streaming](https://artificialanalysis.ai/speech-to-text/streaming), AA-WER streaming index and time to final transcript |
| search | `search_index` (0 to 100), `cost_per_task` (USD) | [agents/search-api](https://artificialanalysis.ai/agents/search-api), Search Index and search plus model cost per task |
| llm | `intelligence_index`, `output_tokens_per_second` | [leaderboards/models](https://artificialanalysis.ai/leaderboards/models), Intelligence Index; speed per host from `models/<slug>/providers` |

The LLM table also shows input and output token prices. Those come from the price list
(`acceleration/prices/vendor.json`, then the database), not a benchmark, so this skill leaves
them alone: the `check_prices` skill checks them.

## 1. Pull the numbers

```bash
uv run --no-project .claude/skills/refresh_model_stats/aa_stats.py
```

It reads the data embedded in the pages and prints one tab-separated row per model and
host. For an LLM served by someone other than its maker, pass the AA slugs to get each
host's speed:

```bash
uv run --no-project .claude/skills/refresh_model_stats/aa_stats.py glm-5-3-flash kimi-k3
``` If it prints nothing, the page shape changed: fetch the page with `curl`, find the
field names (`qualityElo`, `medianCharactersPerSecond`, `aaWerStreamingIndex`,
`timeToFinalTranscriptSeconds`) and fix the script.

## 2. Match rows to our models

Match on what we actually call, not the closest name:

- A versionless model id takes the version the vendor serves today. `grok/grok-stt` is
  Grok Voice Transcribe 2.0; `cartesia/sonic-preview` is Sonic 3.6 (see its comment).
- Pick the variant our code runs. `cartesia/ink-2` is the socket that detects turns itself,
  so "semantic endpoints"; Nemotron on Together is the "Together AI" row.
- Arena Elo belongs to the weights, speed to the host. A model we self-host (`s2pro`,
  `breeze`) gets `elo` only, since AA measured someone else's servers.
- A search variant is the setting we send. Exa's `fast` and `auto` and Tavily's `basic`
  map by name. `perplexity/search` sends no `search_context_size`, and Perplexity's docs
  disagree on whether that means `low` or `high`, so it stays blank until we pin one.
- An LLM's intelligence is the row at the effort we send: OpenAI's `none` is
  "Non-reasoning", Astra, Gemini, Grok and Muse ask for `low`, Opus runs at medium, and an
  open-weight model runs with thinking off unless its entry sets `thinking`. No row at that
  effort means no `intelligence_index`. Speed is per host, and any effort of the same
  weights on the same host will do.
- A model AA has not measured gets no `benchmark` line. Do not borrow a sibling's numbers
  (`flux-general-multi` is not `Deepgram Flux`).

## 3. Write them

One line after the model's `description`, rounded the way the script prints them:

```yaml
      benchmark: { elo: 1273, characters_per_second: 115 }
      benchmark: { word_error_rate: 0.027, latency_ms: 490 }
      benchmark: { search_index: 74, cost_per_task: 0.127 }
      benchmark: { intelligence_index: 33, output_tokens_per_second: 330 }
```

Then, in `acceleration/`:

```bash
go test ./internal/api/ ./internal/routing/ -count=1
```

Restart the router so the picker sees the new numbers. Mention in the commit which models
moved and the date the board was read.
