---
name: router-tts
description: What the TTS router can be asked for, what each vendor calls it, and what it refuses to fake. Read before adding a TTS option or a voice provider.
---

# Routing text to speech

The per-modality half of [router-interface](../router-interface/SKILL.md). The vocabulary is
[`options.TTS`](../../../acceleration/internal/options/options.go); who can express what is
declared per model in [`router.yaml`](../../../acceleration/internal/routing/router.yaml).

Two paths again. A live voice is a socket at `/v1/tts/stream`, which streams PCM back a chunk
at a time and is judged on time-to-first-byte. A recording is a job at `/v1/tts/recordings`,
which returns one file — nobody is listening to an audiobook while it is being made, and that
is exactly what lets a codec and a bitrate be chosen instead of raw PCM.

## The three that carry the live path, and what each calls the same thing

`eleven_v3_conversational`, Sonic 3.6 and Realtime TTS-2 are the models the router leans on.
`eleven_flash_v2_5` is in the fourth column because it is where most of this vocabulary came
from, and it is the only one of the four that still has all of it.

| Option | ElevenLabs v3 conversational | Cartesia Sonic 3.6 | Inworld Realtime TTS-2 | ElevenLabs flash v2.5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| endpoint | `/v1/text-to-dialogue/stream-input` | `/tts/websocket` | `voice:streamBidirectional` | `.../multi-stream-input` |
| `voice` | `voices: [id]`, exactly one per socket | `voice.id` | `create.voiceId` | in the path |
| `languages` | `language_code` query, ISO 639-1 | `language` base code **or** `locale` (`en-GB`, 3.6+), never both, plus `accent` | `language` BCP-47, inferred from the text when absent | `language_code` query |
| `speed` | — | `generation_config.speed`, 0.6–1.5 | `audioConfig.speakingRate`, 0.5–1.5, above 0.8 recommended | `voice_settings.speed`, 0.7–1.2 |
| `volume` | — | `generation_config.volume`, 0.5–2.0 | — | — |
| `emotion`, `style` | audio tags in the text | `generation_config.emotion`, closed enum, English only, beta | `[bracket]` prose, or an `instruction` field on HTTP | — |
| `stability` | `voice_settings.stability`, first message only, 0–1 | — | `deliveryMode`: `STABLE`, `BALANCED`, `CREATIVE` | `voice_settings.stability`, continuous |
| `similarity` | — | — | — | `similarity_boost` |
| elevenlabs overwrite `voice_settings.style` | — (refused) | — | — | `voice_settings.style`, 0–1 |
| `format` | `output_format=pcm_<rate>` | `output_format.{container,encoding,sample_rate}`, `raw` only on the socket | `audioConfig.{audioEncoding,sampleRateHertz,bitRate}` | `output_format` |
| `pronunciations` | `pronunciation_dictionary_locators`, first message only | `pronunciation_dict_id` | — | same as v3 |
| `chunk_schedule` | — | `max_buffer_delay_ms`, 0–5000, default 3000 | `maxBufferDelayMs` and `bufferCharThreshold` (≤1000) | `generation_config.chunk_length_schedule` |

What the table is saying:

- **The best model has the fewest knobs.** `eleven_v3_conversational` takes one setting,
  `stability`, and takes it only on the first message. No speed, no similarity, no chunk
  schedule. Everything else it can do is said in the text, which is why it is the one that
  answers `Performs()` and ships [`AudioTagPrompt`](../../../acceleration/internal/tts/elevenlabs).
- **Speed ranges do not overlap, and one provider has none.** 0.6–1.5, 0.5–1.5, 0.7–1.2, and
  nothing at all. `speed` is not one number every voice accepts, and a provider asked for a
  speed outside its own range refuses.
- **`stability` is a dial at ElevenLabs and three modes at Inworld.** ElevenLabs documents
  0 to 1, and a live 0.3 spoke on v3 conversational, v4 and v4 Turbo (2026-10-15); a
  third-party claim that v3 takes only 0.0 / 0.5 / 1.0 is in no ElevenLabs doc. Inworld has
  `STABLE`, `BALANCED`, `CREATIVE` (its `delivery_mode` overwrite). `similarity` survives
  only on the v2 models.
- **"Sound urgent" has three incompatible shapes.** A closed enum of 58 words, English only
  (Cartesia). Free English prose that persists until `[reset]`, like a stage direction
  (Inworld). Tags the model acts as it reads them (ElevenLabs v3). Prose does not reduce to
  `angry`, and `angry` throws away everything a director would actually say. A single
  `emotion` string is expressible by Cartesia and nobody else; the other two want the
  direction in the text.
- **`volume` is Cartesia's alone**, and Inworld's nearest equivalent is `[very quiet]` — prose
  again, not a number.
- **`pronunciations` is not a per-request map anywhere.** ElevenLabs and Cartesia both want a
  dictionary uploaded first and referenced by id; Inworld has nothing. `map[string]string` on
  the options is the wrong shape, and the honest fix is the voice-catalogue treatment: prepare
  it once, reference it per session.
- **`chunk_schedule` is characters for one vendor and milliseconds for two.** It is really
  "how long to buffer before speaking". v3 conversational decides for itself — it waits for
  roughly 40 characters and 8 words — and gives you `flush` as the only lever, which is what
  `Final` already sends.
- **Format barely matters live.** Every socket here is PCM. It is the recorded path that needs
  it: `mp3_44100_128` for a file somebody downloads, `ulaw_8000` for telephony.

## Model ids drift, and two of these have

- Sonic 3.6 went generally available as `sonic-3.6`. `sonic-preview` — which
  [`cartesia.go`](../../../acceleration/internal/tts/cartesia/cartesia.go) still pins and its
  own comment predicted — now means the beta channel that tracks whatever is next, explicitly
  not for production.
- The router ships `inworld-tts-2-flash`, five times faster to first byte than `inworld-tts-2`
  and the cheapest of the four. It also ignores steering entirely: bracket instructions and
  the `instruction` field are dropped, though non-verbals like `[laugh]` still work. Steering is
  `inworld-tts-2` only, so declaring `emotion` on the flash entry would be a lie. `temperature`
  is ignored across the TTS-2 family; `deliveryMode` replaced it.
- `eleven_v3_conversational` registers exactly one voice per socket. `eleven_v3` allows ten,
  which is what makes it the scripted-dialogue model rather than the conversational one.

## What the router refuses to fake

A voice asked to sound urgent that speaks flatly is worse than one that says it cannot: the
caller cannot tell the difference from the audio, and the whole point of routing is that they
did not have to know which vendor answered. So options become `Terms()`, and only models whose
`supports:` lists every term asked for are candidates.

Today the batch entry `elevenlabs/eleven_v3` declares `[stability, similarity, format]`, which is the recorded path; it declares no `speed`, so a recording that asks for one is refused. `cartesia/sonic-3.6` is its batch entry (`realtime: false`, `[format]`), the one a priority list asked for a recording reaches, and `en-recorded` still prefers `eleven_v3`; the live `cartesia/sonic-preview` also declares `[format]`; its live factory refuses a format as `routing.ErrRequest`, since a live voice streams raw audio. Inworld is the same: `inworld/inworld-tts-2-batch` is its batch entry (`realtime: false`, `[format]`), and the live `inworld-tts-2` and `inworld-tts-2-flash` declare `[format]` and refuse it live. Of the live entries, `eleven_flash_v2_5` and `eleven_multilingual_v2`
declare `[speed, stability, similarity]`, sent as `voice_settings` when each context opens (stability 0.5,
similarity 0.8 when not asked); a speed outside 0.7–1.2 or a stability or similarity outside
0–1 is refused when the provider is built. The dialogue models (v3 conversational, v4, v4
Turbo) declare `[stability]` and have no speed, so a request naming one routes past them, and
`NewDialogue` refuses a speed or a similarity rather than drop it. A refused value, a speed
included, is the caller's mistake (`routing.ErrRequest`): no stat is recorded, so it cannot
mark the model unavailable for everyone. Every other live entry declares nothing, so it
serves requests that ask only for a target, a voice and a language. Cartesia
(`generation_config.speed`, 0.6–1.5) and Inworld (`audioConfig.speakingRate`, 0.5–1.5) can
express a speed but do not send one yet; wire it in their package, refuse outside their range,
then add `speed` to their `supports:`. Adding to that list means sending the field in that
provider's package under [`internal/tts`](../../../acceleration/internal/tts) first.

An agent's voice session passes no voice options: `startVoice` builds its request with a
target and a voice, and no voice options (`internal/agent/pipeline.go`), and the agent config has no `speed`
or other voice setting since it was taken out on purpose ("a voice speaks at its own pace").
A speed, stability, similarity or overwrite reaches a voice only through a request to
`/v1/tts/stream` or `/v1/tts/recordings`.

Batch v3 has no `speed` because it ignores one. Live on 2026-10-16 a speed of 0.7, 1.0, 1.2 and
1.5 all got a 200 from `eleven_v3`, in times that did not follow the speed, where Flash answered
1.5 with a 400. None of the ElevenLabs pages opened (best-practices, models,
text-to-speech/convert) says so either way, so re-probe before adding it back.

Voice ids are not a term. They are resolved by the voice catalogue in
[`internal/tts/voices`](../../../acceleration/internal/tts/voices), so a name that no provider
has is a 404 rather than a routing failure. `custom:` in front of one says it is the
customer's own and nothing else, so a name that is not theirs is refused rather than passed to
the provider's library.

A voice that is not the customer's own is checked when the voice opens (`Resolver.ResolveVoice`,
`Catalogue.Check`), for every caller: the socket, a session's agent and a recording.

- A voice in the provider's cached listing (`libraryTTL`, an hour) goes through with no
  round trip. Any other voice is looked up, and one that exists is remembered for an hour.
- Only the provider's own "no such voice" refuses. ElevenLabs answers that as
  `detail.code: voice_not_found`, with a 404 or a 400, so the code decides and not the status.
  The refusal is `routing.ErrRequest` and names the closest listed voice by edit distance over
  id and name. When none takes the voice the caller gets the refusal, not "every candidate failed".
- A refused voice is not handed to a vendor that cannot look voices up (Cartesia, Inworld,
  any vendor with no library): it would start and fail on the first line (`tts-quality` did,
  on Inworld and Cartesia, before AI-1395's second PR). `Select` asks the resolver once,
  before the first candidate (`routing.VoiceVetter`, `Resolver.Unvouched`,
  `Catalogue.Unvouched`), so the answer does not depend on which vendor health ranks first.
  Such a vendor still takes the voice when its own cached listing holds that id: a listed
  name does not count, since Cartesia and Inworld speak a voice by id. A listing that cannot
  be read holds nothing.
- That first ask is made only for a voice shaped like an ElevenLabs id: 20 letters and digits
  (`Finder.Shaped`; ElevenLabs does not document the format, every id seen live on 2026-10-16
  has it). A Cartesia UUID, an Inworld name such as `Ashley`, a mistyped name such as
  `Rachell`, `custom:` and no voice are not asked about and route as #989 left them: a name
  ElevenLabs refuses on a shortcut that also reaches Cartesia or Inworld still starts there
  and fails on the first line. Staging's Inworld key could not list voices (403, 2026-10-16, until
  its scopes were widened on 2026-10-19), so leaving Inworld out for a name its listing does
  not vouch for would refuse every Inworld voice on any key like it.
- ElevenLabs answers an id that cannot be one of its voices, such as a Cartesia UUID, with
  400 `detail.status: invalid_uid` (live 2026-10-16). `Exists` returns `errNotAVoiceID`, and
  `Check` lets the voice through without a warning and without turning the check off.
- Nothing is left out when no candidate can look the voice up, when the lookup failed, for a
  customer's own voice, for `custom:`, or for a candidate whose overwrites name a `voice_id`.
- A lookup that fails another way (a bad key, a 5xx, past `lookupTimeout`, 3s) lets the voice
  through as before. An unreadable listing still refuses, without a suggestion.
- ElevenLabs looks twice, `GET /v1/voices/{id}` and then `GET /v1/shared-voices?search={id}`,
  matched on the exact id. The first alone says `voice_not_found` for a Voice Library voice
  that speaks (ElevenLabs adds it to the account the first time it does). Do not probe a
  Voice Library voice with a synthesis: that adds it to the account.
- `/v1/voices?show_legacy=false` leaves legacy voices out of the listing, so
  `21m00Tcm4TlvDq8ikWAM` is looked up, found and spoken. "Not in the listing" is not a
  refusal.
- A "no such voice" answer is remembered for `rememberFor` (30s), and so is a failed listing
  or lookup per provider, so one `Start` that tries five ElevenLabs models asks once and the
  refusal is worded once; a failing or hanging vendor costs one lookup per window, not one per open.
- A candidate whose `overwrites.<vendor>.voice_id` is set is not checked: the overwrite is the
  voice spoken (`routing.VoiceOverwritten`, `ttsrouter/registry.go` `voiceOr`), so the
  request's `voice` is never asked of the provider.
- Not checked: Cartesia and Inworld voices on a target with no ElevenLabs candidate (their listers have no `Exists`), a router with no database (no resolver) and the standalone `cmd/agent` binary.

`GET /v1/agents/voices/library` lists the libraries `buildLibrary` wires (`cmd/router/main.go`):
ElevenLabs, Cartesia and Inworld, each only with a key here. Listings are cached for
`libraryTTL` (an hour), so a picker pays for a vendor's paging once an hour, not per request.

- Cartesia is read in full: pages of 100 until `has_more` is false or `next_page` is empty,
  with `next_page` sent back as `starting_after`
  ([docs](https://docs.cartesia.ai/api-reference/voices/list); 1,049 voices over 11 pages on
  2026-10-19). Past `cartesiaMaxPages` (100), or when a `next_page` comes back, the listing
  is an error and the catalogue keeps the list it had: a shortened list is never cached.
- Fish is not browsable. Its public `GET /model` stopped at 1,000 models (`window_limited`) at
  2.78-2.93s a page of 100 on 2026-10-19, so `provider=fish` answers how to use a Fish voice
  instead (`unbrowsable` in `library.go`): by its model id, which the router sends to Fish as
  `reference_id` ([docs](https://docs.fish.audio/developer-guide/core-features/text-to-speech)).
  Any other provider with no library still says it `publishes no voice library`.
- A listing the vendor answers with a 401 or 403 says the key cannot list voices
  (`listRefused`); a refused voice, a preview and a 5xx keep `refused`'s wording. That error
  reaches the caller only when it asked for one provider; with several, the provider is in
  `unavailable` and the error goes to a warn log (`internal/api/voices.go`).

## Three things that narrow candidates without being terms

- `providers` is a priority list tried in the order written, and this router's half of it is
  the streaming one: a vendor named live gets its socket model, not its file-returning one.
- `data_policy` is a requirement. Every entry in `router.yaml` declares what the vendor does
  with the text, `Config.Validate()` refuses one that does not, and an undeclared handling
  satisfies no policy. Only the two entries on our own Baseten deployment currently promise no
  training and no retention, so `allow_training: false` routes there until an account
  elsewhere is opted out and its entry is edited.
- `overwrites` is per vendor, decoded into a typed struct with `DisallowUnknownFields`, so a
  misspelt key or a wrong type fails the request with `routing.ErrOverwrite`, naming the
  provider and the field. `Select` then tries only that vendor's other models (OpenAI's
  realtime and Live models read different structs out of one block) and never another
  vendor, which is handed its own block and would drop the overwrite in silence. What a voice can be
  steered by this way: `elevenlabs: {voice_id, voice_settings: {style}}`,
  `inworld: {voice_id, delivery_mode}`. The recording path reads the same `elevenlabs` block.
  ElevenLabs' `style` is a number from 0 to 1, how far to exaggerate the speaker's own style,
  and not the shared `style`, which is a word to sound like. Only the models before v3 take
  it (Flash v2.5, Multilingual v2): the v3 and v4 models, the batch `eleven_v3` included,
  refuse it as an overwrite error, so `tts-quality` refuses it and `en-low-latency` is
  spoken by Flash.
- A `voice_id` in any vendor's block is the voice spoken: `startCandidate` hands it to the
  factory as the spec's voice, so Cartesia, whose factory reads no block, speaks it too. A
  voice asked only that way, with no top-level `voice`, narrows the candidates to the vendors
  that named one before anything is tried (`Router.voiced`): any other vendor would be handed
  no voice and speak its default, which nobody can hear is wrong (ElevenLabs' default is
  "Spuds Oxley - Grandpa", `elevenlabs.DefaultVoiceID`). None of them a candidate, or none
  with a factory (a recording asked in a Breeze voice), is refused as `routing.ErrRequest`.
  The Inworld recorder reads the `inworld` block as its live voice does.
  A top-level voice goes to every candidate, so nothing is left out for it.
- The voice that spoke, the provider's default included, is `voice` on the socket's `started`
  frame and on `Speech` (`tts.Voiced`). A provider that cannot say leaves it out rather than
  echo the voice asked for.

## ElevenLabs, Cartesia and Inworld record

- A recording is built by `ttsrouter.DefaultRecorderRegistry` (`ttsrouter/recordings.go`), which
  has ElevenLabs, Cartesia and Inworld. Every other vendor in `router.yaml` (Breeze, Speechify,
  Gemini, Fish, s2pro) only streams. Any ElevenLabs model is offered as a recorder, but only
  `eleven_v4` is verified (staging, 2026-10-19: an inline recording returned audio); the other
  five in `router.yaml` (`eleven_flash_v2_5`, `eleven_v4_turbo`, `eleven_multilingual_v2`,
  `eleven_v3_conversational`, `eleven_v3`) are `unverified`. On the same day a recording on
  `inworld/inworld-tts-2` or `breeze/breeze-tts-2` failed with `no factory registered`.
- Cartesia records on `POST /tts/bytes` (`cartesia.Recorder`), with the voice, model and
  language its live voice reads (an overwrite's `voice_id` included). `format` is mapped to
  `output_format`: `mp3_<rate>_<kbps>` to mp3, `pcm_<rate>` to raw `pcm_s16le`, `wav_<rate>`
  to wav, `ulaw_<rate>` and `alaw_<rate>` to raw `pcm_mulaw` and `pcm_alaw`; empty is
  `mp3_44100_128`, as at ElevenLabs. A format Cartesia has no container, rate or bit rate for
  (`opus_*`, `mp3_24000_48`, `pcm_32000`) is refused when the recorder is built, naming it.
  Speed, volume and emotion (its `generation_config`) are not sent, so `sonic-preview` does not
  declare them and a recording that asks for one is refused. A recording on Cartesia is
  `unverified` against the real API: the local key was out of credits (402) on 2026-10-19.
- Inworld records on `POST /tts/v1/voice` (`inworld.Recorder`), with the voice, model,
  `delivery_mode` and language its live voice reads (an overwrite's `voice_id` included). The
  endpoint takes the live ids (`inworld-tts-2`, `inworld-tts-2-flash`), and a model is declared
  once in `router.yaml`, so the batch entry is `inworld-tts-2-batch` and the recorder drops
  `-batch` before it sends the id. `format` is mapped to `audioConfig`: `mp3_<rate>_<kbps>` to
  `MP3` with `bitRate`, `pcm_<rate>` to `PCM` (raw 16-bit), `wav_<rate>` to `WAV`,
  `ulaw_<rate>` and `alaw_<rate>` to `MULAW` and `ALAW`, at 8000 to 48000 Hz; empty is
  `mp3_44100_128`. `opus_*` and any other name is refused when the recorder is built. One
  request takes at most 2,000 UTF-16 code units, so a longer text fails the job naming the
  limit, as a `routing.ErrRequest` (`Recordings.Record` writes no `record_failed` stat for it,
  as with a refused format, since a model's health is every customer's, and moves on to the
  next candidate where there is one): the
  router does not cut it up, because mp3 and wav files cannot be joined byte for byte. `tl`
  is sent as `fil` (Inworld refuses `tl`, probed 2026-10-20), and `temperature` as 1.1, as
  the live socket sends it. Speed (`speakingRate`) is not sent, so no Inworld entry declares
  `speed`.
- `Recordings.Check` runs before a recording is accepted (`recordSpeech` in `api/recordings.go`).
  When no candidate's vendor has a recorder, such as a pinned `breeze/breeze-tts-2` or a
  shortcut or priority list made only of vendors that stream, the request is a 400 that names
  them and the models that record. One recorder among the candidates is enough: `tts-quality`
  is served by ElevenLabs, or by Cartesia when ElevenLabs cannot be built, because `Select`
  passes over a candidate with no factory without counting it against the model.
- `Recordings.Record` fails over during the recording too. It routes with `routing.Router.Walk`,
  which is `Select` with the provider handed to a callback: one resolution of the request, with
  `Select`'s filters (voice, policy, terms, data policy), ranking and overwrite rule applied once,
  and each started candidate handed to `Record` in that order. A candidate `Select` rules out is
  never asked, and once a vendor's model refused its overwrite block no other vendor is. Classes: a vendor failure (any error from
  `Record`: a non-200, a transport error, a timeout, a body it cannot read) writes
  `record_failed` and moves on; a refusal (`routing.ErrRequest` from a build, or
  `inworld.ErrTextTooLong`) moves on without a stat; a cancelled or expired context stops.
  Empty text is refused before any candidate (`tts.Recording.Validate`). If none records it, the
  error names each candidate's (cut to `maxTriedError`, 300 bytes) and keeps `ErrRequest` when
  one refused, as `Select` does. A walk whose only error is the one recorder's (a pinned model,
  or one candidate left by the filters) fails as it did before the walk: that error, that model. The inline path's 90 s is shared by every candidate.
  A voice asked only in a streaming vendor's overwrites is still refused once routed
  (`Router.voiced`), as a failed job.
- `GET /v1/tts/routes` and `/v1/tts/routes/{target}` say per candidate whether a recording can
  use it (`can_record`, from the recorder registry). The list and its health stay the live
  router's. STT and STS leave the field out.
- A new recorder is one `Register` in `DefaultRecorderRegistry`; the check and `can_record`
  follow from it.
- `inline: true` on `POST /v1/tts/recordings` (Python `router.tts.recording(..., inline=True)`)
  speaks the text while the request waits and returns the audio, base64, in the 202 body,
  storing nothing: the cheap check that synthesis works on an app. `recordSpeech` refuses more
  than 16000 characters or a callback with a 400 and gives it 90 seconds; `Check` runs first,
  so a model that only streams is a 400 here too. A failed synthesis is still a 202, with
  `status: failed`. `Speech.voice` says which voice spoke it.

## Adding an option

1. A field on `options.TTS`, with `Merge` and a `Term` plus a line in `Terms()` if it is
   optional behaviour.
2. The same field on `TtsOptions`, on its Go struct in
   `internal/api`. Then run
   `go run ./cmd/openapi` and regenerate all three clients.
3. Read it in each provider that can express it, refuse it where the vendor has a range and the
   request is outside it, and declare it in `supports:`.
4. A test for the refusal, not only for the happy path.

# Routing text to speech

The per-modality half of [router-interface](../router-interface/SKILL.md). The vocabulary is
[`options.TTS`](../../../acceleration/internal/options/options.go); who can express what is
declared per model in [`router.yaml`](../../../acceleration/internal/routing/router.yaml).

Two paths again. A live voice is a socket at `/v1/tts/stream`, which streams PCM back a chunk
at a time and is judged on time-to-first-byte. A recording is a job at `/v1/tts/recordings`,
which returns one file — nobody is listening to an audiobook while it is being made, and that
is exactly what lets a codec and a bitrate be chosen instead of raw PCM.

## The three that carry the live path, and what each calls the same thing

`eleven_v3_conversational`, Sonic 3.6 and Realtime TTS-2 are the models the router leans on.
`eleven_flash_v2_5` is in the fourth column because it is where most of this vocabulary came
from, and it is the only one of the four that still has all of it.

| Option | ElevenLabs v3 conversational | Cartesia Sonic 3.6 | Inworld Realtime TTS-2 | ElevenLabs flash v2.5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| endpoint | `/v1/text-to-dialogue/stream-input` | `/tts/websocket` | `voice:streamBidirectional` | `.../multi-stream-input` |
| `voice` | `voices: [id]`, exactly one per socket | `voice.id` | `create.voiceId` | in the path |
| `languages` | `language_code` query, ISO 639-1 | `language` base code **or** `locale` (`en-GB`, 3.6+), never both, plus `accent` | `language` BCP-47, inferred from the text when absent | `language_code` query |
| `speed` | — | `generation_config.speed`, 0.6–1.5 | `audioConfig.speakingRate`, 0.5–1.5, above 0.8 recommended | `voice_settings.speed`, 0.7–1.2 |
| `volume` | — | `generation_config.volume`, 0.5–2.0 | — | — |
| `emotion`, `style` | audio tags in the text | `generation_config.emotion`, closed enum, English only, beta | `[bracket]` prose, or an `instruction` field on HTTP | — |
| `stability` | `voice_settings.stability`, first message only, 0–1 | — | `deliveryMode`: `STABLE`, `BALANCED`, `CREATIVE` | `voice_settings.stability`, continuous |
| `similarity` | — | — | — | `similarity_boost` |
| elevenlabs overwrite `voice_settings.style` | — (refused) | — | — | `voice_settings.style`, 0–1 |
| `format` | `output_format=pcm_<rate>` | `output_format.{container,encoding,sample_rate}`, `raw` only on the socket | `audioConfig.{audioEncoding,sampleRateHertz,bitRate}` | `output_format` |
| `pronunciations` | `pronunciation_dictionary_locators`, first message only | `pronunciation_dict_id` | — | same as v3 |
| `chunk_schedule` | — | `max_buffer_delay_ms`, 0–5000, default 3000 | `maxBufferDelayMs` and `bufferCharThreshold` (≤1000) | `generation_config.chunk_length_schedule` |

What the table is saying:

- **The best model has the fewest knobs.** `eleven_v3_conversational` takes one setting,
  `stability`, and takes it only on the first message. No speed, no similarity, no chunk
  schedule. Everything else it can do is said in the text, which is why it is the one that
  answers `Performs()` and ships [`AudioTagPrompt`](../../../acceleration/internal/tts/elevenlabs).
- **Speed ranges do not overlap, and one provider has none.** 0.6–1.5, 0.5–1.5, 0.7–1.2, and
  nothing at all. `speed` is not one number every voice accepts, and a provider asked for a
  speed outside its own range refuses.
- **`stability` is a dial at ElevenLabs and three modes at Inworld.** ElevenLabs documents
  0 to 1, and a live 0.3 spoke on v3 conversational, v4 and v4 Turbo (2026-10-15); a
  third-party claim that v3 takes only 0.0 / 0.5 / 1.0 is in no ElevenLabs doc. Inworld has
  `STABLE`, `BALANCED`, `CREATIVE` (its `delivery_mode` overwrite). `similarity` survives
  only on the v2 models.
- **"Sound urgent" has three incompatible shapes.** A closed enum of 58 words, English only
  (Cartesia). Free English prose that persists until `[reset]`, like a stage direction
  (Inworld). Tags the model acts as it reads them (ElevenLabs v3). Prose does not reduce to
  `angry`, and `angry` throws away everything a director would actually say. A single
  `emotion` string is expressible by Cartesia and nobody else; the other two want the
  direction in the text.
- **`volume` is Cartesia's alone**, and Inworld's nearest equivalent is `[very quiet]` — prose
  again, not a number.
- **`pronunciations` is not a per-request map anywhere.** ElevenLabs and Cartesia both want a
  dictionary uploaded first and referenced by id; Inworld has nothing. `map[string]string` on
  the options is the wrong shape, and the honest fix is the voice-catalogue treatment: prepare
  it once, reference it per session.
- **`chunk_schedule` is characters for one vendor and milliseconds for two.** It is really
  "how long to buffer before speaking". v3 conversational decides for itself — it waits for
  roughly 40 characters and 8 words — and gives you `flush` as the only lever, which is what
  `Final` already sends.
- **Format barely matters live.** Every socket here is PCM. It is the recorded path that needs
  it: `mp3_44100_128` for a file somebody downloads, `ulaw_8000` for telephony.

## Model ids drift, and two of these have

- Sonic 3.6 went generally available as `sonic-3.6`. `sonic-preview` — which
  [`cartesia.go`](../../../acceleration/internal/tts/cartesia/cartesia.go) still pins and its
  own comment predicted — now means the beta channel that tracks whatever is next, explicitly
  not for production.
- The router ships `inworld-tts-2-flash`, five times faster to first byte than `inworld-tts-2`
  and the cheapest of the four. It also ignores steering entirely: bracket instructions and
  the `instruction` field are dropped, though non-verbals like `[laugh]` still work. Steering is
  `inworld-tts-2` only, so declaring `emotion` on the flash entry would be a lie. `temperature`
  is ignored across the TTS-2 family; `deliveryMode` replaced it.
- `eleven_v3_conversational` registers exactly one voice per socket. `eleven_v3` allows ten,
  which is what makes it the scripted-dialogue model rather than the conversational one.

## What the router refuses to fake

A voice asked to sound urgent that speaks flatly is worse than one that says it cannot: the
caller cannot tell the difference from the audio, and the whole point of routing is that they
did not have to know which vendor answered. So options become `Terms()`, and only models whose
`supports:` lists every term asked for are candidates.

Today the batch entry `elevenlabs/eleven_v3` declares `[stability, similarity, format]`, which is the recorded path; it declares no `speed`, so a recording that asks for one is refused. `cartesia/sonic-3.6` is its batch entry (`realtime: false`, `[format]`), the one a priority list asked for a recording reaches, and `en-recorded` still prefers `eleven_v3`; the live `cartesia/sonic-preview` also declares `[format]`; its live factory refuses a format as `routing.ErrRequest`, since a live voice streams raw audio. Inworld is the same: `inworld/inworld-tts-2-batch` is its batch entry (`realtime: false`, `[format]`), and the live `inworld-tts-2` and `inworld-tts-2-flash` declare `[format]` and refuse it live. Of the live entries, `eleven_flash_v2_5` and `eleven_multilingual_v2`
declare `[speed, stability, similarity]`, sent as `voice_settings` when each context opens (stability 0.5,
similarity 0.8 when not asked); a speed outside 0.7–1.2 or a stability or similarity outside
0–1 is refused when the provider is built. The dialogue models (v3 conversational, v4, v4
Turbo) declare `[stability]` and have no speed, so a request naming one routes past them, and
`NewDialogue` refuses a speed or a similarity rather than drop it. A refused value, a speed
included, is the caller's mistake (`routing.ErrRequest`): no stat is recorded, so it cannot
mark the model unavailable for everyone. Every other live entry declares nothing, so it
serves requests that ask only for a target, a voice and a language. Cartesia
(`generation_config.speed`, 0.6–1.5) and Inworld (`audioConfig.speakingRate`, 0.5–1.5) can
express a speed but do not send one yet; wire it in their package, refuse outside their range,
then add `speed` to their `supports:`. Adding to that list means sending the field in that
provider's package under [`internal/tts`](../../../acceleration/internal/tts) first.

An agent's voice session passes no voice options: `startVoice` builds its request with a
target and a voice, and no voice options (`internal/agent/pipeline.go`), and the agent config has no `speed`
or other voice setting since it was taken out on purpose ("a voice speaks at its own pace").
A speed, stability, similarity or overwrite reaches a voice only through a request to
`/v1/tts/stream` or `/v1/tts/recordings`.

Batch v3 has no `speed` because it ignores one. Live on 2026-10-16 a speed of 0.7, 1.0, 1.2 and
1.5 all got a 200 from `eleven_v3`, in times that did not follow the speed, where Flash answered
1.5 with a 400. None of the ElevenLabs pages opened (best-practices, models,
text-to-speech/convert) says so either way, so re-probe before adding it back.

Voice ids are not a term. They are resolved by the voice catalogue in
[`internal/tts/voices`](../../../acceleration/internal/tts/voices), so a name that no provider
has is a 404 rather than a routing failure. `custom:` in front of one says it is the
customer's own and nothing else, so a name that is not theirs is refused rather than passed to
the provider's library.

A voice that is not the customer's own is checked when the voice opens (`Resolver.ResolveVoice`,
`Catalogue.Check`), for every caller: the socket, a session's agent and a recording.

- A voice in the provider's cached listing (`libraryTTL`, an hour) goes through with no
  round trip. Any other voice is looked up, and one that exists is remembered for an hour.
- Only the provider's own "no such voice" refuses. ElevenLabs answers that as
  `detail.code: voice_not_found`, with a 404 or a 400, so the code decides and not the status.
  The refusal is `routing.ErrRequest` and names the closest listed voice by edit distance over
  id and name. When none takes the voice the caller gets the refusal, not "every candidate failed".
- A refused voice is not handed to a vendor that cannot look voices up (Cartesia, Inworld,
  any vendor with no library): it would start and fail on the first line (`tts-quality` did,
  on Inworld and Cartesia, before AI-1395's second PR). `Select` asks the resolver once,
  before the first candidate (`routing.VoiceVetter`, `Resolver.Unvouched`,
  `Catalogue.Unvouched`), so the answer does not depend on which vendor health ranks first.
  Such a vendor still takes the voice when its own cached listing holds that id: a listed
  name does not count, since Cartesia and Inworld speak a voice by id. A listing that cannot
  be read holds nothing.
- That first ask is made only for a voice shaped like an ElevenLabs id: 20 letters and digits
  (`Finder.Shaped`; ElevenLabs does not document the format, every id seen live on 2026-10-16
  has it). A Cartesia UUID, an Inworld name such as `Ashley`, a mistyped name such as
  `Rachell`, `custom:` and no voice are not asked about and route as #989 left them: a name
  ElevenLabs refuses on a shortcut that also reaches Cartesia or Inworld still starts there
  and fails on the first line. Staging's Inworld key could not list voices (403, 2026-10-16, until
  its scopes were widened on 2026-10-19), so leaving Inworld out for a name its listing does
  not vouch for would refuse every Inworld voice on any key like it.
- ElevenLabs answers an id that cannot be one of its voices, such as a Cartesia UUID, with
  400 `detail.status: invalid_uid` (live 2026-10-16). `Exists` returns `errNotAVoiceID`, and
  `Check` lets the voice through without a warning and without turning the check off.
- Nothing is left out when no candidate can look the voice up, when the lookup failed, for a
  customer's own voice, for `custom:`, or for a candidate whose overwrites name a `voice_id`.
- A lookup that fails another way (a bad key, a 5xx, past `lookupTimeout`, 3s) lets the voice
  through as before. An unreadable listing still refuses, without a suggestion.
- ElevenLabs looks twice, `GET /v1/voices/{id}` and then `GET /v1/shared-voices?search={id}`,
  matched on the exact id. The first alone says `voice_not_found` for a Voice Library voice
  that speaks (ElevenLabs adds it to the account the first time it does). Do not probe a
  Voice Library voice with a synthesis: that adds it to the account.
- `/v1/voices?show_legacy=false` leaves legacy voices out of the listing, so
  `21m00Tcm4TlvDq8ikWAM` is looked up, found and spoken. "Not in the listing" is not a
  refusal.
- A "no such voice" answer is remembered for `rememberFor` (30s), and so is a failed listing
  or lookup per provider, so one `Start` that tries five ElevenLabs models asks once and the
  refusal is worded once; a failing or hanging vendor costs one lookup per window, not one per open.
- A candidate whose `overwrites.<vendor>.voice_id` is set is not checked: the overwrite is the
  voice spoken (`routing.VoiceOverwritten`, `ttsrouter/registry.go` `voiceOr`), so the
  request's `voice` is never asked of the provider.
- Not checked: Cartesia and Inworld voices on a target with no ElevenLabs candidate (their listers have no `Exists`), a router with no database (no resolver) and the standalone `cmd/agent` binary.

`GET /v1/agents/voices/library` lists the libraries `buildLibrary` wires (`cmd/router/main.go`):
ElevenLabs, Cartesia and Inworld, each only with a key here. Listings are cached for
`libraryTTL` (an hour), so a picker pays for a vendor's paging once an hour, not per request.

- Cartesia is read in full: pages of 100 until `has_more` is false or `next_page` is empty,
  with `next_page` sent back as `starting_after`
  ([docs](https://docs.cartesia.ai/api-reference/voices/list); 1,049 voices over 11 pages on
  2026-10-19). Past `cartesiaMaxPages` (100), or when a `next_page` comes back, the listing
  is an error and the catalogue keeps the list it had: a shortened list is never cached.
- Fish is not browsable. Its public `GET /model` stopped at 1,000 models (`window_limited`) at
  2.78-2.93s a page of 100 on 2026-10-19, so `provider=fish` answers how to use a Fish voice
  instead (`unbrowsable` in `library.go`): by its model id, which the router sends to Fish as
  `reference_id` ([docs](https://docs.fish.audio/developer-guide/core-features/text-to-speech)).
  Any other provider with no library still says it `publishes no voice library`.
- A listing the vendor answers with a 401 or 403 says the key cannot list voices
  (`listRefused`); a refused voice, a preview and a 5xx keep `refused`'s wording. That error
  reaches the caller only when it asked for one provider; with several, the provider is in
  `unavailable` and the error goes to a warn log (`internal/api/voices.go`).

- A `voice_id` in any vendor's block is the voice spoken: `startCandidate` hands it to the

  The Inworld recorder reads the `inworld` block as its live voice does.
  A top-level voice goes to every candidate, so nothing is left out for it.

  echo the voice asked for.

## ElevenLabs, Cartesia and Inworld record

- A recording is built by `ttsrouter.DefaultRecorderRegistry` (`ttsrouter/recordings.go`), which
  has ElevenLabs, Cartesia and Inworld. Every other vendor in `router.yaml` (Breeze, Speechify,
  Gemini, Fish, s2pro) only streams. Any ElevenLabs model is offered as a recorder, but only
  `eleven_v4` is verified (staging, 2026-10-19: an inline recording returned audio); the other
  five in `router.yaml` (`eleven_flash_v2_5`, `eleven_v4_turbo`, `eleven_multilingual_v2`,
  `eleven_v3_conversational`, `eleven_v3`) are `unverified`. On the same day a recording on
  `inworld/inworld-tts-2` or `breeze/breeze-tts-2` failed with `no factory registered`.
- Cartesia records on `POST /tts/bytes` (`cartesia.Recorder`), with the voice, model and
  language its live voice reads (an overwrite's `voice_id` included). `format` is mapped to
  `output_format`: `mp3_<rate>_<kbps>` to mp3, `pcm_<rate>` to raw `pcm_s16le`, `wav_<rate>`
  to wav, `ulaw_<rate>` and `alaw_<rate>` to raw `pcm_mulaw` and `pcm_alaw`; empty is
  `mp3_44100_128`, as at ElevenLabs. A format Cartesia has no container, rate or bit rate for
  (`opus_*`, `mp3_24000_48`, `pcm_32000`) is refused when the recorder is built, naming it.
  Speed, volume and emotion (its `generation_config`) are not sent, so `sonic-preview` does not
  declare them and a recording that asks for one is refused. A recording on Cartesia is
  `unverified` against the real API: the local key was out of credits (402) on 2026-10-19.
- Inworld records on `POST /tts/v1/voice` (`inworld.Recorder`), with the voice, model,
  `delivery_mode` and language its live voice reads (an overwrite's `voice_id` included). The
  endpoint takes the live ids (`inworld-tts-2`, `inworld-tts-2-flash`), and a model is declared
  once in `router.yaml`, so the batch entry is `inworld-tts-2-batch` and the recorder drops
  `-batch` before it sends the id. `format` is mapped to `audioConfig`: `mp3_<rate>_<kbps>` to
  `MP3` with `bitRate`, `pcm_<rate>` to `PCM` (raw 16-bit), `wav_<rate>` to `WAV`,
  `ulaw_<rate>` and `alaw_<rate>` to `MULAW` and `ALAW`, at 8000 to 48000 Hz; empty is
  `mp3_44100_128`. `opus_*` and any other name is refused when the recorder is built. One
  request takes at most 2,000 UTF-16 code units, so a longer text fails the job naming the
  limit, as a `routing.ErrRequest` (`Recordings.Record` writes no `record_failed` stat for it,
  as with a refused format, since a model's health is every customer's, and moves on to the
  next candidate where there is one): the
  router does not cut it up, because mp3 and wav files cannot be joined byte for byte. `tl`
  is sent as `fil` (Inworld refuses `tl`, probed 2026-10-20), and `temperature` as 1.1, as
  the live socket sends it. Speed (`speakingRate`) is not sent, so no Inworld entry declares
  `speed`.
- `Recordings.Check` runs before a recording is accepted (`recordSpeech` in `api/recordings.go`).
  When no candidate's vendor has a recorder, such as a pinned `breeze/breeze-tts-2` or a
  shortcut or priority list made only of vendors that stream, the request is a 400 that names
  them and the models that record. One recorder among the candidates is enough: `tts-quality`
  is served by ElevenLabs, or by Cartesia when ElevenLabs cannot be built, because `Select`
  passes over a candidate with no factory without counting it against the model.
- `Recordings.Record` fails over during the recording too. It routes with `routing.Router.Walk`,
  which is `Select` with the provider handed to a callback: one resolution of the request, with
  `Select`'s filters (voice, policy, terms, data policy), ranking and overwrite rule applied once,
  and each started candidate handed to `Record` in that order. A candidate `Select` rules out is
  never asked, and once a vendor's model refused its overwrite block no other vendor is. Classes: a vendor failure (any error from
  `Record`: a non-200, a transport error, a timeout, a body it cannot read) writes
  `record_failed` and moves on; a refusal (`routing.ErrRequest` from a build, or
  `inworld.ErrTextTooLong`) moves on without a stat; a cancelled or expired context stops.
  Empty text is refused before any candidate (`tts.Recording.Validate`). If none records it, the
  error names each candidate's (cut to `maxTriedError`, 300 bytes) and keeps `ErrRequest` when
  one refused, as `Select` does. A walk whose only error is the one recorder's (a pinned model,
  or one candidate left by the filters) fails as it did before the walk: that error, that model. The inline path's 90 s is shared by every candidate.
  A voice asked only in a streaming vendor's overwrites is still refused once routed
  (`Router.voiced`), as a failed job.
- `GET /v1/tts/routes` and `/v1/tts/routes/{target}` say per candidate whether a recording can
  use it (`can_record`, from the recorder registry). The list and its health stay the live
  router's. STT and STS leave the field out.
- A new recorder is one `Register` in `DefaultRecorderRegistry`; the check and `can_record`
  follow from it.
- `inline: true` on `POST /v1/tts/recordings` (Python `router.tts.recording(..., inline=True)`)
  speaks the text while the request waits and returns the audio, base64, in the 202 body,
  storing nothing: the cheap check that synthesis works on an app. `recordSpeech` refuses more
  than 16000 characters or a callback with a 400 and gives it 90 seconds; `Check` runs first,
  so a model that only streams is a 400 here too. A failed synthesis is still a 202, with
  `status: failed`. `Speech.voice` says which voice spoke it.

## Adding an option

1. A field on `options.TTS`, with `Merge` and a `Term` plus a line in `Terms()` if it is
   optional behaviour.
2. The same field on `TtsOptions`, on its Go struct in
   `internal/api`. Then run
   `go run ./cmd/openapi` and regenerate all three clients.
3. Read it in each provider that can express it, refuse it where the vendor has a range and the
   request is outside it, and declare it in `supports:`.
4. A test for the refusal, not only for the happy path.

skills.name: scheduled-tasks
skills.desc: Walks a developer through scheduled tasks end to end - what they do, turning them on for an agent config, scheduling one locally or on staging through the agent's tool or the REST API, watching it run, and what to check when nothing arrived. Read before you schedule a task, test the feature, or debug a reminder that never came.
skills.body:
---
name: scheduled-tasks
description: Walks a developer through scheduled tasks end to end - what they do, turning them on for an agent config, scheduling one locally or on staging through the agent's tool or the REST API, watching it run, and what to check when nothing arrived. Read before you schedule a task, test the feature, or debug a reminder that never came.
---

# Scheduled tasks

A scheduled task is something the agent agreed to do for one user later: once, or on a
repeat, at a wall-clock time in that user's zone. When it comes due, the router wakes the
agent in the user's own conversation with the task's instructions. The agent's answer is
the delivery.

How the code works, its terms and the tests behind each rule:
`acceleration/internal/scheduling/AGENTS.md`. What is decided and what is not done:
`.factory/features/scheduled-tasks.md`. Paths below are under `acceleration/`.

## One example, start to end

```
 Alice, 14:02 (Europe/Amsterdam): "remind me to call the dentist in 20 minutes"
   agent -> schedule_task {title: "Dentist", instructions: "Remind Alice to call the dentist.", in: "PT20M"}
   tool  -> {"id": "...", "schedule": "Once, Wed 21 Oct 2026 at 14:22 (Europe/Amsterdam)", "next": "..., in 20 minutes"}
 14:22  worker claims the occurrence -> run "running"
        agent is sent <scheduled_task ...>Remind Alice to call the dentist.</scheduled_task>
        agent writes "Time to call the dentist!" in Alice's conversation
        run "delivered", delivered_to "conversation"; task "completed"
```

The tool and its fields: `internal/session/schedule_tools.go:36`. The prompt the agent is
sent: `scheduledPrompt`, `internal/api/scheduled_delivery.go:456`.

## Turn it on

Scheduling is a block on the agent config (`AgentScheduling`, `internal/api/configs.go:2103`):

| Field | What it does | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `scheduling.enabled` | Offers the model the four tools: `schedule_task`, `list_scheduled_tasks`, `update_scheduled_task`, `cancel_scheduled_task` | off |
| `scheduling.max_tasks_per_user` | Active tasks one user may hold on this config, 1 to 100 | 25 (`scheduling.MaxActivePerUser`) |
| `scheduling.default_timezone` | The IANA zone a task takes when neither the call, the session nor the user names one. An unknown zone is a 400 `invalid_timezone` | none: a task with no zone is refused with `timezone_unknown` |

The tools also need (`Manager.schedulingRunner`, `internal/session/schedule_tools.go:106`):

- a router with a database;
- a session that is not incognito, opened on a config;
- a caller that is a verified user or a backend acting for one (`X-Stream-User-Id`), or the
  person who wrote in an SMS (Telnyx) or WhatsApp thread or a 1:1 iMessage (Linq) chat, and
  only when that person writes, not someone else in the thread (the task is theirs and keeps
  the thread). A Linq chat is 1:1 only while its latest message says `data.chat.is_group`
  `false`: the bridge then records the sender as the chat's person
  (`channel_threads.chat_person`). A group chat, a chat whose message does not say, a thread
  linked before that column, and a Slack thread get no tools. A guest or an anonymous caller
  gets no tools.

A task made in an SMS or WhatsApp thread or a 1:1 iMessage chat comes back in that thread:
the router opens the thread's conversation, the agent answers the task there, and the reply is
texted to the person from the line. Its run says `delivered_to` `sms`, `whatsapp` or
`imessage` once the line took the
reply; a reply the line refused is `delivery_failed`, and the retry sends the same reply,
files included, without a second turn; a thread removed while the turn ran is `thread_gone`,
final (`internal/api/scheduled_thread_delivery.go`); a Linq chat that became a group is
`thread_gone`, final, too. Such a task's `deliver_to` reads `sms`, `whatsapp` or `imessage`
and cannot be changed.

The REST create does not need `scheduling.enabled` (`internal/api/scheduled_tasks.go:752`).

A follow-up needs a kept conversation, and a conversation is kept only in Stream Chat. A
router without a usable Stream app refuses every session that is not incognito with 400
`not_configured` (`session.ErrNoStreamKeys`, `ErrStreamKeysRejected` in
`internal/session/stream_keys.go`), so it has no conversation to deliver a task into.

## Schedule one locally

1. Run the router per the repo-root `AGENTS.md` (Local dev) with `ROUTER_AUTH_MODE=proxy`
   (the Volt override sets it, `.claude/skills/dashboard/SKILL.md`). The commands below name
   the app with `X-Customer-Id`, which only `proxy` mode reads; in `api_key` mode send the
   credentials of "Schedule one on staging" instead. In `noauth` mode the router reads no `X-Stream-User-Id`
   (`internal/auth/auth.go:89`), so a create is refused ("name the user the task is for
   with X-Stream-User-Id") and no session gets the tools.
2. Make a config with scheduling on. In `proxy` mode without `proxy_declares_kind`, a request
   naming its app with `X-Customer-Id` and no `Stream-Auth-Type` is a backend
   (`internal/auth/auth.go:291`):

   ```bash
   R=http://localhost:8080
   H=(-H 'X-Customer-Id: examples' -H 'Content-Type: application/json')
   curl -s "$R/v1/agents/configs" "${H[@]}" -d '{
     "name": "reminders",
     "instructions": "You are a helpful assistant.",
     "scheduling": {"enabled": true, "default_timezone": "Europe/Amsterdam"}
   }'
   ```

   A config with that name already exists on a second run (409 `name_taken`). Use another
   name, or give the existing config the same block with `PATCH /v1/agents/configs/{id}`.
3. Schedule through the agent: open a session for a user, then write to it.

   ```bash
   U=(-H 'X-Stream-User-Id: alice')
   SID=$(curl -s "$R/v1/agents/sessions" "${H[@]}" "${U[@]}" \
     -d '{"agent": "reminders", "timezone": "Europe/Amsterdam"}' | jq -r .id)
   curl -s "$R/v1/agents/sessions/$SID/respond" "${H[@]}" "${U[@]}" \
     -d '{"text": "remind me to stretch in 20 minutes", "request_id": "remind-1"}'
   curl -s "$R/v1/agents/sessions/$SID/commands/remind-1" "${H[@]}" "${U[@]}"   # state: thinking, then completed
   ```

   A text session with a named user needs a durable command, so `respond` takes a
   `request_id` (without it: 400 `personal conversations require a command ID`,
   `internal/session/session.go:507`). `GET .../commands/{request_id}`
   (`internal/api/sessions.go:1147`) answers the command's `state` (`thinking`, then
   `completed`), not the reply text: read that in the conversation on the dashboard. The
   model has made the task when the list in step 4 shows it.

   Or through REST (`createScheduledTask`, `internal/api/scheduled_tasks.go:742`). Name the
   agent with `agent`, `config_id` or `session_id`:

   ```bash
   TASK=$(curl -s "$R/v1/agents/scheduled-tasks" "${H[@]}" "${U[@]}" -d '{
     "agent": "reminders", "title": "Stretch",
     "instructions": "Remind Alice to stretch and ask how her back is.",
     "schedule": {"at": "09:00", "repeat": "FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=MO,TU,WE,TH,FR"}
   }' | jq -r .id)
   ```

   `TASK` is the new task's id. A task the tool made: take its id from the list in step 4
   (with one task, `jq -r '.items[0].id'` gives it).

   Without `session_id`, the first occurrence opens a session for the user.
4. Watch it. Fire it now without moving the schedule, then read its runs:

   ```bash
   curl -s "$R/v1/agents/scheduled-tasks?state=active" "${H[@]}" "${U[@]}" | jq '.items[] | {id, title, next_run_at, last_run_at}'
   curl -s -X POST "$R/v1/agents/scheduled-tasks/$TASK/run" "${H[@]}" "${U[@]}"   # 202, the run
   curl -s "$R/v1/agents/scheduled-tasks/$TASK/runs" "${H[@]}" "${U[@]}" | jq '.items[] | {scheduled_for, trigger, state, delivered_to, error}'
   docker compose logs -f router | grep -i 'scheduled task' | grep -v 'Failed to forward'
   ```

   The `grep -v` drops the job queue's `Failed to forward scheduled tasks` noise. A delivered
   run logs nothing; its run row says `delivered`. Open the session on the
   dashboard to read the agent's message.

## Schedule one on staging

Staging is `https://accelerate-staging.gcp.stream-io-api.com`, behind Stream's proxy. The proxy
wants `api_key` and `stream-auth-type: jwt` for any token, and a server token is HS256
`{"server": true}` signed with the app's secret (`sdks/js/src/backend.ts:318`,
`signToken` at `:486`). Never print the secret or the token.

```bash
set -a; . ./.env; set +a          # STREAM_API_KEY, STREAM_API_SECRET; prints nothing
# node 22 reads the secret from its environment, so it never appears in a command line
TOKEN=$(node -e '
const c = require("node:crypto");
const b = (v) => Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(v)).toString("base64url");
const now = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);
const input = b({ alg: "HS256", typ: "JWT" }) + "." + b({ server: true, iat: now, exp: now + 3600 });
process.stdout.write(input + "." + c.createHmac("sha256", process.env.STREAM_API_SECRET).update(input).digest("base64url"));
')
R=https://accelerate-staging.gcp.stream-io-api.com
A=(-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'stream-auth-type: jwt' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'X-Stream-User-Id: alice')
curl -s "$R/v1/agents/scheduled-tasks?api_key=$STREAM_API_KEY" "${A[@]}" | jq '.items | length'
```

Every call from "Schedule one locally" works with `"${A[@]}"` in place of
`"${H[@]}" "${U[@]}"` and `api_key=$STREAM_API_KEY` on the URL: after `?` when the URL has no
query yet, after `&` when it has one (`...?state=active&api_key=$STREAM_API_KEY`). Staging logs: the `deploy`
skill.

## Nothing arrived?

Read the task, then its runs, then the logs, in that order.

| Check | How | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Task `state` | `GET /v1/agents/scheduled-tasks/{id}` | `paused`: a pause, or its config was deleted (`internal/api/configs.go:308`). `failed`: five failed occurrences in a row (`maxConsecutiveFailures`), or a last occurrence that failed; resume clears it. A failed task with no occurrence left, or a paused one that did not sleep through its time, answers resume with 400 `schedule_in_past`: PATCH a new schedule first, 15 min out at the soonest. A paused one-shot whose time passed while paused is completed with a `missed` run (`task_paused`). `completed`: a one-shot ran, or the repeat has nothing left |
| `next_run_at`, `upcoming` | same | In the task's zone. Wrong hour: the zone (below) |
| `schedule.timezone` | same | Resolved at create from the call, the session, `users.timezone`, then `default_timezone`. A session opened with a zone moves `users.timezone` (`internal/api/session_create.go:76`) |
| `quiet_hours` | same | An occurrence due inside them is held to their end: its run stays `running` with nothing sent. A run by hand is never held |
| The runs | `GET /v1/agents/scheduled-tasks/{id}/runs` | No run at all: the occurrence was never claimed (worker logs). `running` long after `scheduled_for`: held, or a worker is on it; a run by hand whose router stopped stays `running` until the daily prune writes it `missed`, a day after it started |
| Run `state` `missed` | same | Too late: a one-shot over 24 h, a repeat over 1 h (`scheduler.go:51`), a call over 15 min (a run by hand too), or with under 11.5 min of the occurrence left. Or `error` `task_paused`: a one-shot resumed after its time, or an occurrence a move's cut-over skipped whose run the source had started |
| Run `error` | same | See the reason table below |
| Limit | create or resume answers 409 `too_many_tasks` | The user holds `max_tasks_per_user` active tasks on this config |
| Edit refused | update, pause or resume answers 409 `task_changed` | The task changed between the request's read and its save (another edit or pause, or a worker's claim, hold, finish or session write; a lease renewal is not a change): nothing was saved, so read it again and retry. The agent's `update_scheduled_task` is refused the same way |
| The tools | the model never calls `schedule_task` | `scheduling.enabled` off, incognito, a guest or anonymous caller, or a `noauth` router |
| Device PATCH refused | `PATCH /v1/agents/scheduled-tasks/{id}` answers 400 `interval_too_short` | A device moves `next` only to or past the run still pending (`scheduling.CheckLater`), and a `schedule` whose first run is earlier than a pending one. While that run is due or in flight, the `schedule` starts no earlier than the stored schedule's next occurrence after it (`owedRun`); with none after it, an active task is refused, and so is a paused one whose due run already ran (a pause over a run in flight settles it). A paused task that slept through its time, or a failed one, keeps the floor. With no run pending, `next` has nothing to move. A backend key keeps the 15 min floor (`scheduling.CheckMove`) |
| Tool refused | `schedule_task` answers `interval_too_short` or `scheduled_turn` | The agent's first run is 15 min from now at the soonest (`scheduling.MinMove`). A turn a task fired cannot schedule a task, nor reschedule, snooze or resume one; it may list, pause, skip and cancel |
| Old history gone | a completed or failed task 404, or old runs missing | A daily job deletes runs finished over 90 days ago, and completed or failed tasks over 90 days old (`ScheduledTasksKept`); active and paused tasks stay. It redacts the changes recorded of what it deletes (`ScheduledTasks.Prune`), and deleting a task redacts those of it and its runs (`ScheduledTasks.Delete`) |
| Session deleted | task 404 | Deleting a session deletes the tasks made in it or following up in it, with their runs, and redacts the changes recorded of them (`DeleteForSession`) |
| User forgotten | task 404, its runs gone | `router usage forget-user` deleted every task of that user in the app, with its runs, and redacted the changes recorded of them (`ForgetUserTasks`) |
| Team left | a device's task 404, missing from its list | In an app with `agent_teams`, a task on a config of a team the user is no longer in is not there to their device, nor one on a deleted config, except to pause or delete it; their backend still reaches it. A router holds a user's teams for 30 s, so a removal is seen within that; held teams that refuse ask Stream again first, at most once a second, and stand while it cannot be asked |

Run `error` codes (`internal/scheduling/scheduler.go:105`):

| Code | Meaning | Retried |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `delivery_failed` | Any other failure, or the occurrence was claimed three times (`maxScheduledTaskRunAttempts`: the first claim, the take-up after a hold, one after a lost worker) with no call placed; with a call placed, the cap keeps the reason that call ended under, or gives `already_called` (`capFailure`) | yes, unless it was claimed three times or a call was already placed (`scheduled_delivery.go:783`, `:857`) |
| `timed_out` | The occurrence used its 20 min (`occurrenceBudget`) | no |
| `schedule_unreadable` | The stored schedule no longer parses; the task is paused | no |
| `user_on_call` | The user stayed on a call through the 10 min window | yes |
| `channel_unreachable` | SMS, WhatsApp or iMessage would refuse: never wrote on it, opted out, outside WhatsApp's 24 h window, no line. On a thread task: opted out (before the turn or by the time the reply is sent), or the sandbox gate holds it back (a thread task's text refused for money is not this: it has the money codes below) | yes; not for a thread task's opted-out person |
| `outside_window` | A WhatsApp thread task whose person last wrote over 24 h ago, with no template to send after the window | no |
| `thread_gone` | A thread task's thread no longer exists, or is not its user's thread of its customer | no |
| `connection_removed` | A thread task's line (its connection) was removed | no |
| `not_in_team` | In an app that keeps each team's agent configs to its own users (`agent_teams`), the end user the task is for is no longer in its config's team: one they made (`caller_kind` not `server`), or one the agent made talking with them (`created_by` `agent`, outside a thread), whoever opened that chat. The agent is not run and no session is opened. A task the backend made through the API, or the agent made on an SMS, WhatsApp or iMessage thread, is not checked; teams Stream could not read fail the attempt as `delivery_failed`, retried | no |
| `no_reply` | The agent said nothing and made no file to carry | yes |
| `reply_failed` | The reply failed, or was cancelled or interrupted and, when run once more under `st_<run>_r1`, was cut off again (a text channel's or a thread task's first cut-off also gives it, and the retry runs it again) | yes |
| `no_phone_number` | The user never texted this agent by SMS; a number used only on WhatsApp is not rung | yes |
| `no_agent_number` | The config has no SMS line to ring from | yes |
| `not_answered` | Nobody picked up within the 90 s ring | no |
| `already_called` | A call was placed for this occurrence already, and its end is not recorded; no channel after `phone` is tried. That call may have carried the task out, so the run leaves the failure streak as it is and the task moves on as after a run that did not fail (a one-shot is `completed`) | no |
| `account_suspended`, `insufficient_credits`, `system_limit_reached`, `spend_limit_reached`, `user_limit_reached` | A step the organization may not pay for was refused for money (suspended, no credit left, or a spent limit): an SMS, WhatsApp or iMessage text or a thread task's reply (`dlc.ErrUnpaid`, or its reservation), the task's session opening or being carried on, a turn the model refuses, on a text channel (`captureReply`, which ends the walk over the channels, `refusedTurn`), in the conversation (`followUpInConversation` waits for the turn to end; a turn that ends any other way is still `delivered`) or on a thread task (`deliverOnThread`), or its call, placed or not: a placed call whose session cannot open fails under the refusal's code (`carryOutOnCall`); on an answered call, a turn refused before the agent answered anything hangs up (`carryOutAnswered`), the task's turn cut off by the caller included, and a refusal after that is a later turn's, still `delivered`: a refusal for money names no turn, so a call's session keeps it (`Session.UnansweredRefusal`, which `carryOutAnswered` reads) and gives it to the conversation, transcript or not, only while the agent has not answered since the task's turn was typed (`Session.refusedUnanswered`). The other steps read how the turn ended from the conversation, which keeps the error that failed the reply (`Session.FollowUpFailure`, `turnRefusal`), never from the session's events alone, which a watcher that falls behind loses; a text channel carries only its own follow-up's reply, read back once its turn ends (`readBackReply`). A turn that ended while no attempt watched it, such as one an attempt cut short left running, fails the same way while the session that ran it is still open. A refusal for money is kept on the failed reply's message in Chat (`support_money_refusal`, read back by `commandsIn`), so it survives the conversation being opened again (a restart, a drain, or the end of the session's unwatched grace): the retry ends under the same code, as before the reopen. The run records the refusal's own code (`deliveryReason`, `scheduled_delivery.go:356`), never `channel_unreachable` or `delivery_failed`, and the router warns, naming the task | no (`unpaid`, `scheduled_delivery.go:400`) |
| `spend_check_unavailable` | The router could not check what the organization has spent, so it refused the step for now (`policy.Transient`). A turn it refused runs once more on the retry, under `st_<run>_r1`: the scheduler hands the next attempt the reason this one failed under (`deliverWithRetries`) and records it on the run, so a router that takes the run over after a crash or a lost lease reruns the turn too, a hand-off to the router holding the session carries it (`scheduledHandOff.Earlier`), and `replyCommand` reruns a failed reply after a money code. A conversation rerun refused as well fails the attempt under the same code (`followUpInConversation`), so the run fails once its retries are spent. A reply that failed for any other reason is read back as it was. A placed call is rung once: refused this way, its session or its answered turn fails the run under this code, final, with the call kept on the run (`callEnded`), so the user is not rung again | yes (`unpaid` leaves it retryable) |
| `task_paused` | On a `missed` run: a one-shot whose time came while it was paused, or an occurrence the cut-over of a move skipped whose run the source had started | — |

A failure is retried after 30 s, 2 min and 10 min (`deliveryRetries`) only when the failure
is not final; with several channels, it is final only when every channel's failure is.

Worker log lines, as the code writes them (`grep -i 'scheduled task'` finds all of them;
